The score in <a href="#eq:classical-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-score">[eq:classical-score]</a> subtracts the particle information required by the observation and adds twice the time entropy conditional on the particle. Its largest asymptotic increase per unit duration is denoted by $\beta$. Theorem <a href="#thm:classical-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:classical-growth">15</a> proves $\beta\le\gamma$.

To prove this bound, assume excessive growth and localize a sequence whose scores approach the largest possible rate. The aspect penalty makes the orientations of such observations coherent. Choosing the least possible aspect produces a saturated path: its intermediate observations attain the same growth rate. There are two alternatives. An isotropic extremizer is excluded in Section <a href="#sec:isotropic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:isotropic">5</a> by combining time-fiber richness, planar projections, and a Loomis–Whitney argument. In the other alternative, the orientation and longitudinal resolutions advance at a fixed ratio $m>0$.

The latter case produces four data coordinates with resolution speeds $0,1,m,1+m$. Their particle-information profile is Lipschitz, but ordinary almost everywhere differentiability does not give a derivative on the particular plane selected by the path. Section <a href="#sec:characteristic-plane" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:characteristic-plane">6</a> proves the needed trace and affine approximation there. Planar projections then transfer lower bounds between the coordinate rates. When $m=1$, the middle coordinates share a speed and only their joint rate is available. Two conditional projection tests and a reciprocal pinned-direction argument supply the missing inequalities. The latter is related to the radial-projection bootstraps of Shmerkin and Wang and of Orponen, Shmerkin, and Wang (Shmerkin and Wang 2025; Orponen, Shmerkin, and Wang 2024) <a id="pm-cite-28"></a>[[ShmerkinWang2025Distance](#ref-ShmerkinWang2025Distance), [OrponenShmerkinWang2024Radial](#ref-OrponenShmerkinWang2024Radial)]. Section <a href="#sec:classical-closure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:classical-closure">8</a> combines these rate constraints with the saturated path’s contact and jump conditions to obtain a contradiction.

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
###### Oscillatory packets.

Write $\lambda^{-1}=\epsilon^{H_{\mathrm P}}$. At duration $t$, a packet has velocity depth $u_t=(H_{\mathrm P}-t)/2$ and position depth $u_t+t$. The packet score in <a href="#eq:packet-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:packet-score">[eq:packet-score]</a> uses squared oscillatory amplitudes, and its largest growth rate is denoted by $\beta_{\mathrm q}$. Sections <a href="#sec:packet-structure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:packet-structure">9</a>–<a href="#sec:packet-composition" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:packet-composition">10</a> construct finite decompositions, control their tails, and track the loss when only part of an assigned atom class is retained. These constructions use the Fourier-series localization and almost orthogonality underlying classical wave-packet methods (Tao 2003; Guo et al. 2025) <a id="pm-cite-29"></a>[[Tao2003](#ref-Tao2003), [GuoOhWangWuZhang2025](#ref-GuoOhWangWuZhang2025)].

Away from the uncertainty boundary, a coarser observation faithfully locates the packets, so the positive-mass estimate applies. At the boundary, a separate coherent estimate is required. It leaves a layer of fine velocity information, which must be carried to the preceding step. Section <a href="#sec:packet-repayment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:packet-repayment">11</a> proves that hypothetical growth $\beta_{\mathrm q}>\gamma/2$ increases this information by at least $(4\beta_{\mathrm q}-2\gamma)h$, up to controlled errors, at every backward step of fixed length $2h$. The layer holds at most $2h$ units, up to vanishing errors. A fixed finite number of steps therefore yields a contradiction and proves Theorem <a href="#thm:packet-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:packet-growth">35</a>: $\beta_{\mathrm q}\le\gamma/2$.

<a id="pm-h-7"></a>
###### The multiplier.

Packet growth gives the oscillatory estimate of Theorem <a href="#thm:oscillatory-estimate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:oscillatory-estimate">50</a>, with an arbitrarily small positive power loss. On a physical shell of radius $\lambda$, the Bochner–Riesz kernel has amplitude of order $\lambda^{-2-\delta}$. The pseudoconformal distance-phase change of variables used in Guo et al. (2025) <a id="pm-cite-30"></a>[[GuoOhWangWuZhang2025](#ref-GuoOhWangWuZhang2025)] puts this shell into the required phase class. Section <a href="#sec:multiplier" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:multiplier">12</a> verifies all phase and amplitude bounds uniformly in the shell and obtains the operator norm $O_{\delta,\nu}(\lambda^{-\delta+\nu})$. Choosing $0<\nu<\delta$ proves Theorem <a href="#thm:bochner-riesz" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:bochner-riesz">1</a> by summation. A beta-integral representation supplies the complex-order bounds used in Stein’s analytic interpolation theorem (Stein 1956) <a id="pm-cite-31"></a>[[Stein1956](#ref-Stein1956)], completing <a href="#eq:intro-full-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:intro-full-range">[eq:intro-full-range]</a>.

<a id="pm-h-8"></a>
#### Finite laws and order of limits

Entropy permits a common language for these geometric and analytic steps. We use finite entropy and relative entropy (Shannon 1948; Kullback and Leibler 1951) <a id="pm-cite-32"></a>[[Shannon1948](#ref-Shannon1948), [KullbackLeibler1951](#ref-KullbackLeibler1951)], conditional copies and submodularity (Tao 2010) <a id="pm-cite-33"></a>[[Tao2010Entropy](#ref-Tao2010Entropy)], and homogeneous profiles across scales. Multiscale entropy and comparable-partition methods have important precedents in Hochman and Shmerkin (2012; Hochman 2014) <a id="pm-cite-34"></a>[[HochmanShmerkin2012](#ref-HochmanShmerkin2012), [Hochman2014](#ref-Hochman2014)]. Section <a href="#sec:entropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:entropy">2</a> proves the precise finite-law statements used here.

Small normalized mutual information yields a comparison with a product law after trimming; it does not give exact independence. Theorem <a href="#thm:finite-conditioning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:finite-conditioning">8</a> specifies which labels are fixed and which remain free, so later conditioning uses the correct comparison population. For the characteristic-plane argument, first fix a homogeneous component and its limiting profile, then choose the approximation scale, and only afterwards take the finite precision small relative to that scale. Theorem <a href="#thm:characteristic-trace" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:characteristic-trace">26</a> and Corollary <a href="#cor:finite-characteristic-trace" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:finite-characteristic-trace">27</a> state these successive steps.

Packet composition also keeps two finite populations distinct. Its upper estimate concerns a retained superposition, while its earlier lower test uses the whole assigned cap class. Proposition <a href="#prop:finite-packet-composition" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:finite-packet-composition">41</a> records the loss from retention. Section <a href="#sec:packet-repayment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:packet-repayment">11</a> carries the remaining fine velocity information through a fixed finite number of cuts, using the one-step statement of Proposition <a href="#prop:finite-repayment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:finite-repayment">48</a>.

Throughout, $\mathsf H,\mathsf I$ denote entropy and mutual information divided by $\log(1/\epsilon)$, whereas $\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}},\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}$ use natural logarithms. The notation $\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(r\right)$ uses the normalized units. The Planck depth is always $H_{\mathrm P}$, distinct from entropy. A positive depth increment is fixed before the small-parameter limit; when increments subsequently shrink, that additional limit is stated separately.

<a id="sec:entropy"></a>
### Finite entropy, conditioning, and passage to profiles

The geometric arguments will use conditional point and parameter populations whose masses must remain controlled after labels are fixed. We first develop the finite probability estimates that justify those operations, and then explain their passage to limiting entropy profiles. All probability spaces in the finite statements are finite, with cardinalities allowed to depend on $\epsilon$. Put $\ell=\log(1/\epsilon)$ and write $\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}},\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}$ for natural-log entropy and mutual information, with $\mathsf H=\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}/\ell$ and $\mathsf I=\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}/\ell$. The exact particle index $T$ may have an arbitrarily large alphabet; no bound on its entropy is required. Every comparison measure is specified explicitly and need not be a marginal of the law being estimated.

<a id="pm-h-10"></a>
#### Entropy estimates with unrestricted parent alphabets

Our conventions are the usual finite entropy and relative entropy (Shannon 1948; Kullback and Leibler 1951) <a id="pm-cite-35"></a>[[Shannon1948](#ref-Shannon1948), [KullbackLeibler1951](#ref-KullbackLeibler1951)]. Conditional copies and entropy submodularity also feature in Tao’s entropy calculus (Tao 2010) <a id="pm-cite-36"></a>[[Tao2010Entropy](#ref-Tao2010Entropy)]; the comparison and retention bounds required here are proved below.

We use the chain rule, nonnegativity of conditional mutual information, and $\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(X)\le\log|\mathcal X|$ for an $\mathcal X$-valued observation. Here are the particular consequences, including quantitative restriction estimates, that we will need.

<a id="stmt-lem-entropy-restriction"></a>
<div id="lem:entropy-restriction" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:entropy-determination"></a>
<a id="eq:entropy-change"></a>
<a id="eq:entropy-ambiguity"></a>
<a id="eq:entropy-masses"></a>
<a id="eq:conditional-kl"></a>
<a id="eq:conditional-kl-bound"></a>
**Lemma 2** (Determination, masses, and restriction). *Let $A,B,D,T$ be finite observations. Then $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;B)&\le\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;A)+\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(B\mid A),\label{eq:entropy-determination}\\
 |\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(B\mid T)-\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(A\mid T)|
 &\le\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(B\mid A)+\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(A\mid B).\label{eq:entropy-change}
\end{aligned}$$ If, outside an event of probability $\zeta$, $B$ has at most $N$ possible values given $A$, and $|\mathcal B|\le M$, then $$\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(B\mid A)\le\log2+\log N+\zeta\log M.
 \label{eq:entropy-ambiguity}$$ For nonnegative numbers $m_b$ with $m_b>0$ on the support of $B$, $$\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(B)+\mathbb E\log m_B\le\log\sum_bm_b.
 \label{eq:entropy-masses}$$ Finally, let $\mathsf P,\mathsf Q$ be laws on the same space with $\mathsf Q\le K\mathsf P$, $K\ge1$. For arbitrary $B,D$, $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}^{\mathsf Q}(D\mid B)
 &=\mathbb E_{\mathsf Q}[-\log\mathsf P(D\mid B)]
   -\mathbb E_{\mathsf Q_B}
     \mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathsf Q_{D\mid B}\Vert\mathsf P_{D\mid B}),\label{eq:conditional-kl}\\
 \mathbb E_{\mathsf Q_B}
     \mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathsf Q_{D\mid B}\Vert\mathsf P_{D\mid B})
 &\le\log K.\label{eq:conditional-kl-bound}
\end{aligned}$$ In particular, restriction to an event of $\mathsf P$-mass $m>0$ costs at most $\log(1/m)$ in <a href="#eq:conditional-kl-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditional-kl-bound">[eq:conditional-kl-bound]</a>. None of these estimates depends on the cardinality of $B$ or $T$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-entropy-restriction"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-entropy-restriction</summary>

*Proof.* The chain rule gives $\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;B)\le\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;A,B)
=\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;A)+\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;B\mid A)$, proving <a href="#eq:entropy-determination" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:entropy-determination">[eq:entropy-determination]</a>. Apply the chain rule to $\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(A,B\mid T)$ in both orders to obtain <a href="#eq:entropy-change" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:entropy-change">[eq:entropy-change]</a>. Adjoining the indicator of the exceptional event costs at most $\log2$; conditioning on its two values gives <a href="#eq:entropy-ambiguity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:entropy-ambiguity">[eq:entropy-ambiguity]</a>. For <a href="#eq:entropy-masses" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:entropy-masses">[eq:entropy-masses]</a>, normalize $m$ to a probability law and use nonnegativity of its relative entropy from the law of $B$. Expanding the conditional relative entropy gives <a href="#eq:conditional-kl" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditional-kl">[eq:conditional-kl]</a>. Its expectation is at most $\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathsf Q_{B,D}\Vert\mathsf P_{B,D})$, which by marginalization is at most $\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathsf Q\Vert\mathsf P)\le\log K$. ◻

</details>

We call a determination *of zero cost* when the right side of <a href="#eq:entropy-ambiguity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:entropy-ambiguity">[eq:entropy-ambiguity]</a>, divided by $\ell$, tends to zero. This includes bounded ambiguity between comparable translated grids, provided the translation is recorded. When $|\mathcal B|\le\epsilon^{-C}$, vanishing exceptional probability is sufficient for the last term.

<a id="stmt-lem-typical-conditioning"></a>
<div id="lem:typical-conditioning" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:conditioning-likelihood"></a>
**Lemma 3** (Domination and conditioning on typical cells). *Let $\mathsf U,\mathsf V$ be probability laws on the same finite space with $\mathsf U\le A\mathsf V$, $A\ge1$, and let $C$ be a finite observation. For $0<\eta<1$, $$\mathsf U_C\{c:\mathsf U_C(c)<\eta\mathsf V_C(c)\}\le\eta.
 \label{eq:conditioning-likelihood}$$ At every other $\mathsf U_C$-positive value, $$\mathsf U(\,\cdot\mid C=c)
 \le \frac A\eta\,\mathsf V(\,\cdot\mid C=c).$$ The estimate is independent of the number of values of $C$.*

<a id="eq:retention-fibers"></a>
*In particular, let $\mathsf P$ be a finite law, let $\mathcal E$ have mass $m=\mathsf P(\mathcal E)>0$, and put $\mathsf U=\mathsf P(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal E)$ and $r_C(c)=\mathsf P(\mathcal E\mid C=c)$. Then $$\begin{gathered}
 \mathsf U_C(c)=\frac{\mathsf P_C(c)r_C(c)}m,\qquad
 \mathsf U_C\{r_C<t\}\le\frac tm\quad(t>0),\\
 \mathsf U(\,\cdot\mid C=c)
 \le r_C(c)^{-1}\mathsf P(\,\cdot\mid C=c).
 \end{gathered}
 \label{eq:retention-fibers}$$ The last inequality is asserted on positive $\mathsf U_C$ fibers. Thus for $0<\eta_0<1$, outside $\mathsf U_C$-mass $\eta_0$, their domination constants are at most $(m\eta_0)^{-1}$.*

<a id="eq:nested-retention-fibers"></a>
<a id="eq:typical-cell-entropy"></a>
<a id="eq:typical-cell-surprise"></a>
*Suppose further that $C$ is a function of a finite parent observation $X$, and write $r_X(x)=\mathsf P(\mathcal E\mid X=x)$. On every positive $C=c$ fiber, for $0<\eta_1<1$, $$\mathsf U\{r_X(X)<\eta_1r_C(c)\mid C=c\}\le\eta_1.
 \label{eq:nested-retention-fibers}$$ Removing these parent values does not change a conditional law given $X$. Let $d_-\le d_+$ be real numbers. If a finite child $Y$ satisfies, on every $(X,Y)$ value attained in $\mathcal E$, $$d_-\le-\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf P(Y\mid X)\le d_+,
 \qquad \ell=\log(1/\epsilon),$$ then there are at most $\epsilon^{-d_+}$ retained children over each parent, and, with $\mathsf U_c=\mathsf U(\,\cdot\mid C=c)$, $$d_- -\frac{\log(1/r_C(c))}{\ell}
 \le \mathsf H^{\mathsf U_c}(Y\mid X)\le d_+.
 \label{eq:typical-cell-entropy}$$ More precisely, outside $\mathsf U_c$-mass at most $\eta_1+\eta_2$, $$d_- -\frac{\log(1/(\eta_1r_C(c)))}{\ell}
 \le-\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf U_c(Y\mid X)
 \le d_+ +\frac{\log(1/\eta_2)}{\ell},
 \qquad 0<\eta_2<1.
 \label{eq:typical-cell-surprise}$$ These conclusions concern the retained support and sampled conditional values. They assert no lower mass bound for every untrimmed child.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-typical-conditioning"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-typical-conditioning</summary>

*Proof.* Summing $\mathsf U_C(c)<\eta\mathsf V_C(c)$ over the indicated values proves <a href="#eq:conditioning-likelihood" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditioning-likelihood">[eq:conditioning-likelihood]</a>. On its complement, divide $\mathsf U(\omega)\le A\mathsf V(\omega)$ by $\mathsf U_C(c)\ge\eta\mathsf V_C(c)$. This proves the first part. For an event restriction the displayed identity for $\mathsf U_C$ is exact. Summing it over $r_C<t$ proves the second assertion in <a href="#eq:retention-fibers" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:retention-fibers">[eq:retention-fibers]</a>; conditioning on $\mathcal E$ inside one $C$ fiber proves the third.

Because $C$ is determined by $X$, on a positive $C=c$ fiber we have $$\mathsf U_{X\mid c}(x)
 =\mathsf P_{X\mid c}(x)\frac{r_X(x)}{r_C(c)}.$$ Summing over $r_X<\eta_1r_C(c)$ gives <a href="#eq:nested-retention-fibers" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:nested-retention-fibers">[eq:nested-retention-fibers]</a>. The original conditional child law on this fiber is still $\mathsf P(Y\mid X)$. The upper surprise bound on $\mathcal E$ gives $\mathsf P(y\mid x)\ge\epsilon^{d_+}$ for every retained child, so summing these masses gives the support count. Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:entropy-restriction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:entropy-restriction">2</a> to $\mathsf U_c\le r_C(c)^{-1}\mathsf P(\,\cdot\mid C=c)$ for the lower bound in <a href="#eq:typical-cell-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:typical-cell-entropy">[eq:typical-cell-entropy]</a>; the support count gives its upper bound.

For a retained parent, $$\mathsf U_c(y\mid x)
 =\frac{\mathsf P(Y=y,\mathcal E\mid X=x)}{r_X(x)}
 \le\frac{\mathsf P(y\mid x)}{r_X(x)}.$$ On the parents retained in <a href="#eq:nested-retention-fibers" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:nested-retention-fibers">[eq:nested-retention-fibers]</a>, this is at most $\epsilon^{d_-}/(\eta_1r_C(c))$. On any parent fiber the support count bounds by $\eta_2$ the $\mathsf U_c$-mass of children with $\mathsf U_c(y\mid x)<\eta_2\epsilon^{d_+}$. The two exceptional sets give <a href="#eq:typical-cell-surprise" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:typical-cell-surprise">[eq:typical-cell-surprise]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-entropy-splitting"></a>
<div id="lem:entropy-splitting" class="lemma">

**Lemma 4** (Finite splitting and resampling). *For any finite tag $Q$, $$\begin{aligned}
 0\le\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(D\mid B)-\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(D\mid B,Q)&\le\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(Q),\\
 |\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;D\mid Q)-\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;D)|&\le\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(Q),\\
 \mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(U;V\mid Z,Q)&\le\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(U;V\mid Z)+\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(Q).
\end{aligned}$$ The conditional quantities on the left are averages of the quantities on the individual tag fibers. If $U,V$ are conditionally independent given $Z$ under $\mathsf P$, and $\mathsf R\le K\mathsf P$, then $$\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}^{\mathsf R}(U;V\mid Z)\le\log K.$$ Given a joint law of $(T,C,V)$ and a kernel $\kappa(u\mid T,C)$, one may adjoin $U$ by this kernel while preserving that entire joint law. The new $U$ is conditionally independent of $V$ given $(T,C)$, and its joint law with $(T,C)$ is the prescribed kernel law.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-entropy-splitting"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-entropy-splitting</summary>

*Proof.* The first difference equals $\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(D;Q\mid B)$. For the second, the chain rule gives $$\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;D\mid Q)-\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;D)
 =\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;Q\mid D)-\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(T;Q),$$ the difference of two numbers in $[0,\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(Q)]$. Likewise $$\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(U;V\mid Z,Q)-\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(U;V\mid Z)
 =\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(U;Q\mid V,Z)-\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}(U;Q\mid Z)
 \le\mathsf H_{\mathrm{nat}}(Q).$$ For the dominated law, decompose conditional relative entropy against $\mathsf P_{U\mid Z}\otimes\mathsf P_{V\mid Z}$ into conditional mutual information plus the two nonnegative marginal relative entropies. Its average is at most $\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathsf R_{U,V,Z}\Vert\mathsf P_{U,V,Z})\le\log K$. Finally the resampled joint law is exactly $\mathsf P(t,c,v)\kappa(u\mid t,c)$; summing and conditioning prove all its stated properties. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-homogenization"></a>
<div id="lem:homogenization" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:homogeneous-bin"></a>
<a id="eq:homogeneous-entropy"></a>
<a id="eq:homogeneous-surprise"></a>
**Lemma 5** (Finite homogenization). *Fix a law $\mathsf P$, a finite list $(X_j,Y_j)$, $1\le j\le q$, and numbers $A_j\ge0$ such that $|\mathcal Y_j|\le\epsilon^{-A_j}$. There is no cardinality assumption on $X_j$. For $a,\sigma,\theta>0$, there are disjoint events $E_z$ whose union has probability at least $1-q\epsilon^\sigma-\theta$, with the following properties. The number of events is at most $$J=\prod_{j=1}^q\left(1+\left\lceil\frac{A_j+\sigma}{a}\right\rceil\right),
 \qquad m_z:=\mathsf P(E_z)\ge\theta/J.$$ For each $z,j$ there is $d_{j,z}\in[0,A_j+\sigma]$ such that, on $E_z$, $$d_{j,z}\le -\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf P(Y_j\mid X_j)
 \le d_{j,z}+a.
 \label{eq:homogeneous-bin}$$ If $\mathsf R$ is any law supported on $E_z$ satisfying $\mathsf R\le K\mathsf P(\,\cdot\mid E_z)$, then $$d_{j,z}-\frac{\log(K/m_z)}\ell
 \le\mathsf H_{\mathsf R}(Y_j\mid X_j)\le d_{j,z}+a.
 \label{eq:homogeneous-entropy}$$ More precisely, for every $0<\eta<1$, outside a set of $\mathsf R$-probability at most $2\eta$, $$d_{j,z}-\frac{\log(K/(m_z\eta))}\ell
 \le-\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf R(Y_j\mid X_j)
 \le d_{j,z}+a+\frac{\log(1/\eta)}\ell.
 \label{eq:homogeneous-surprise}$$ There are at most $\epsilon^{-(d_{j,z}+a)}$ retained $Y_j$ values over each fixed $X_j$ value. The support-count assertion and <a href="#eq:homogeneous-bin" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:homogeneous-bin">[eq:homogeneous-bin]</a> are uniform on the retained support, before any further restriction is chosen.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-homogenization"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-homogenization</summary>

*Proof.* For every $x$, $$\sum_{y:\,\mathsf P(y\mid x)<\epsilon^{A_j+\sigma}}
       \mathsf P(y\mid x)\le|\mathcal Y_j|\epsilon^{A_j+\sigma}
       \le\epsilon^\sigma.$$ Discard these tails for the $q$ observations and partition the remaining surprise values into intervals of length $a$. This produces at most $J$ cells. Discard cells of mass less than $\theta/J$; their total mass is at most $\theta$. This proves the first assertions. For each retained $x,y$, <a href="#eq:homogeneous-bin" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:homogeneous-bin">[eq:homogeneous-bin]</a> gives $\mathsf P(y\mid x)\ge\epsilon^{d_{j,z}+a}$, so summing over retained $y$ gives the stated count. It follows that the upper entropy bound in <a href="#eq:homogeneous-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:homogeneous-entropy">[eq:homogeneous-entropy]</a> holds under every law on that support. The lower bound follows from <a href="#eq:conditional-kl" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditional-kl">[eq:conditional-kl]</a>, since $\mathsf R\le(K/m_z)\mathsf P$ and the original surprise is at least $d_{j,z}\ell$.

For the pointwise upper bound on conditional masses, discard $x$ for which $\mathsf R_{X_j}(x)<\eta\mathsf P_{X_j}(x)$; their total $\mathsf R$-mass is at most $\eta$. At all remaining $x$, $$\mathsf R(y\mid x)
 \le\frac{K}{m_z\eta}\mathsf P(y\mid x)
 \le\frac{K}{m_z\eta}\epsilon^{d_{j,z}}.$$ For the reverse surprise bound, on each fiber the total $\mathsf R$-mass of values with $\mathsf R(y\mid x)<\eta\epsilon^{d_{j,z}+a}$ is at most $\eta$ by the support count. Averaging in $x$ and combining the two exceptional sets proves <a href="#eq:homogeneous-surprise" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:homogeneous-surprise">[eq:homogeneous-surprise]</a>. ◻

</details>

Joint bins give a sharper version for increments. Suppose $G$ is any parent, possibly containing $T$, and on retained triples $(g,b,d)$, $$\epsilon^{b_0+a}\le\mathsf P(B=b\mid G=g)\le\epsilon^{b_0-a},
 \qquad
 \epsilon^{d_0+a}\le\mathsf P(B=b,D=d\mid G=g)\le\epsilon^{d_0-a}.$$ Dividing these inequalities gives conditional surprises for $D\mid(G,B)$ in $[d_0-b_0-2a,d_0-b_0+2a]$ and at most $\epsilon^{-(d_0-b_0+2a)}$ retained children per $(g,b)$. Indeed, the sum of the lower joint masses cannot exceed the upper parent mass. Lemma <a href="#lem:entropy-restriction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:entropy-restriction">2</a> therefore bounds entropy errors under a density loss $K$ by $2a+\log K/\ell$, independently of the size or entropy of the parent. These are estimates for retained support and for sampled conditional values; no assertion about every untrimmed conditional fiber is needed.

<a id="pm-h-11"></a>
#### From small information to explicit product comparisons

<a id="stmt-lem-zero-information"></a>
<div id="lem:zero-information" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:likelihood-tail"></a>
**Lemma 6** (Zero information and product domination). *Let $\pi$ be a law and let $\Lambda$ be a comparison probability law with $\pi\ll\Lambda$. Write $L=d\pi/d\Lambda$ and $D=\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\Vert\Lambda)$. For every $v>0$, $$\pi(\log L>v)\le\frac{D+1/e}{v}.
 \label{eq:likelihood-tail}$$ Consequently, if $D=o(\ell)$, there is $v=o(\ell)$ such that $\pi(\log L>v)=o(1)$, and the remaining subprobability is bounded by $e^v\Lambda$. This applies in particular to $$\Lambda(a,b,c)=\pi_C(c)\pi_{A\mid C}(a\mid c)
                            \pi_{B\mid C}(b\mid c),
 \qquad D=\mathsf I_{\mathrm{nat}}^\pi(A;B\mid C).$$ Conversely, if a probability law $\rho$ satisfies $\rho\le K\prod_{i=1}^k\mu_i$, then <a id="eq:product-information"></a>$$\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\rho\middle\Vert\prod_i\rho_i\right)\le\log K.
 \label{eq:product-information}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-zero-information"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-zero-information</summary>

*Proof.* Since $x\log(1/x)\le1/e$ on $0\le x\le1$, $\mathbb E_\pi(\log L)_-\le1/e$. Thus $\mathbb E_\pi(\log L)_+\le D+1/e$, and Markov’s inequality gives <a href="#eq:likelihood-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:likelihood-tail">[eq:likelihood-tail]</a>. For example, when $\ell\to\infty$ and $D=o(\ell)$ take $v=\sqrt{(D+1)\ell}$. For the converse, expand $$\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\rho\middle\Vert\prod_i\mu_i\right)
 =\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\rho\middle\Vert\prod_i\rho_i\right)
       +\sum_i\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho_i\Vert\mu_i)\le\log K.\qedhere$$ ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-marginal-core"></a>
<div id="lem:marginal-core" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:core-comparison"></a>
<a id="eq:core-actual"></a>
**Lemma 7** (Simultaneous replacement by actual marginals). *Let $\nu$ be a subprobability of mass $m>0$ on a finite space. For $1\le l\le r$, suppose a tuple of observations $(F_{l1},\ldots,F_{lk_l})$ satisfies $$\nu_{F_{l1},\ldots,F_{lk_l}}
       \le A_l\prod_{j=1}^{k_l}\mu_{lj},
 \label{eq:core-comparison}$$ where every $\mu_{lj}$ is a specified probability law. Put $q=\sum_l k_l$. Repeated occurrences of an observation with different comparison laws are counted separately. For $0<\eta<m/q$ there is a restriction $\nu'$ of $\nu$, of mass $M\ge m-q\eta$, such that $\rho=\nu'/M$ satisfies all the bounds $$\rho_{F_{l1},\ldots,F_{lk_l}}
 \le A_l M^{k_l-1}\eta^{-k_l}
           \prod_{j=1}^{k_l}\rho_{F_{lj}}.
 \label{eq:core-actual}$$ Support counts persist, and every marginal mass upper bound for $\nu$ persists for $\rho$ with the factor $M^{-1}$. In particular, taking $\eta=m/(2q)$ retains mass at least $m/2$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-marginal-core"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-marginal-core</summary>

*Proof.* Starting with $\nu$, repeatedly remove all points with $F_{lj}=v$ whenever its current positive marginal is less than $\eta\mu_{lj}(v)$. Once a value is removed its marginal remains zero, so this procedure terminates. Charge the mass removed at such a step to the pair $((l,j),v)$. Each pair is charged at most once, by less than $\eta\mu_{lj}(v)$; summing proves the loss bound $q\eta$. On every surviving factor value, $\mu_{lj}(v)\le\nu'_{F_{lj}}(v)/\eta
=M\rho_{F_{lj}}(v)/\eta$. The old upper bounds hold for the restricted subprobability. Insert these factor inequalities into <a href="#eq:core-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:core-comparison">[eq:core-comparison]</a> and divide by $M$ to obtain <a href="#eq:core-actual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:core-actual">[eq:core-actual]</a>. Restriction can only remove support, and normalization has precisely the claimed effect on masses. ◻

</details>

The next theorem specifies the laws compared when labels are fixed. A point may be an exact finite particle or a tuple of spatial observations. Additional finite tags may be included in a label.

<a id="stmt-thm-finite-conditioning"></a>
<div id="thm:finite-conditioning" class="theorem">

<a id="eq:star-independent"></a>
<a id="eq:star-pair"></a>
**Theorem 8** (Finite stars and conditioning with named comparison laws). *Let $\pi(p,b)$ be a probability law with $\mu=\pi_P$, $\lambda=\pi_B$. Let $E$ be an allowed set with $\pi(E)\ge1-\zeta$ and suppose <a id="eq:pair-product"></a>$$\boldsymbol1_E(p,b)\pi(p,b)\le K\mu(p)\lambda(b),\qquad K\ge1.
 \label{eq:pair-product}$$ Choose $0<\alpha<1$ with $\zeta<1-\alpha$, retain only point fibers with $r(p):=\pi(E\mid P=p)\ge\alpha$, and normalize the pairs in these fibers and in $E$ to a law $q$. Its retained mass $M_0$ satisfies <a id="eq:star-kernel"></a>$$M_0\ge1-\frac{\zeta}{1-\alpha},\qquad
 q(p,b)\le M_0^{-1}\pi(p,b),\qquad
 q(b\mid p)\le c\lambda(b),\quad c:=K/\alpha.
 \label{eq:star-kernel}$$ For a fixed integer $n\ge1$, sample $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ independently given $P$ with kernel $q(b\mid p)$, and let $$S(p,b_1,\ldots,b_n)=q_P(p)\prod_{i=1}^nq(b_i\mid p).$$ The following are comparison probability laws on the whole star: $$\begin{aligned}
 \Lambda_0&=q_P\otimes\lambda^{\otimes n},
 &S&\le c^n\Lambda_0,\label{eq:star-independent}\\
 \Lambda_i&=q_{P,B_i}\otimes\bigotimes_{j\ne i}\lambda_{B_j},
 &S&\le c^{n-1}\Lambda_i\quad(1\le i\le n).
 \label{eq:star-pair}
\end{aligned}$$ Here $q_{P,B_i}$ is a copy of the retained pair law $q$. It may be replaced by the original $\pi$ in <a href="#eq:star-pair" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:star-pair">[eq:star-pair]</a> at the additional cost $M_0^{-1}$.*

<a id="eq:conditional-independent"></a>
<a id="eq:conditional-pair"></a>
<a id="eq:fixed-comparison-zero"></a>
<a id="eq:fixed-comparison-pair"></a>
<a id="eq:free-comparison-pair"></a>
*Let $R=wS/m$, where $0\le w\le1$ and $m=\mathbb E_Sw>0$. Fix an index set $J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of *fixed labels*; write $F=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus J$ for the *free labels*. Choose any observation $$C=(B_J,Z),\qquad Z=f(P,B_J).$$ Thus the function defining $Z$ involves the point and the fixed labels only. For every $0<\eta<1/(n+1)$, there is a set of $C$ values of $R_C$-mass at least $1-(n+1)\eta$ on which, simultaneously, $$\begin{aligned}
 R(\,\cdot\mid C)&\le\frac{c^n}{m\eta}\Lambda_0(\,\cdot\mid C),
 \label{eq:conditional-independent}\\
 R(\,\cdot\mid C)&\le\frac{c^{n-1}}{m\eta}
                 \Lambda_i(\,\cdot\mid C),\quad1\le i\le n.
 \label{eq:conditional-pair}
\end{aligned}$$ For a fixed value $C=(b_J,z)$, put $z_{b_J}(p)=f(p,b_J)$. Ignoring the deterministic coordinates $B_J$, these comparison laws are exactly $$\begin{aligned}
 \Lambda_0(\,\cdot\mid b_J,z)
 &=q_P(\,\cdot\mid z_{b_J}(P)=z)
                            \otimes\bigotimes_{j\in F}\lambda_{B_j},
 \label{eq:fixed-comparison-zero}\\
 \Lambda_i(\,\cdot\mid b_J,z)
 &=q_P(\,\cdot\mid B_i=b_i,z_{b_J}(P)=z)
                            \otimes\bigotimes_{j\in F}\lambda_{B_j},
                  &&i\in J,\label{eq:fixed-comparison-pair}\\
 \Lambda_i(\,\cdot\mid b_J,z)
 &=q_{P,B_i}(\,\cdot\mid z_{b_J}(P)=z)
                       \otimes\bigotimes_{j\in F\setminus\{i\}}\lambda_{B_j},
                  &&i\in F.\label{eq:free-comparison-pair}
\end{aligned}$$ Conditionals in this display need only be defined when their conditioning event has positive comparison mass; the inequalities hold at every $R$-positive value under consideration.*

<a id="eq:actual-point-free"></a>
*There is also a direct comparison using the actual point marginal. There is a set $G$ of $(P,C)$ values with $R(G)\ge1-\eta$ such that, for every $C$ value, as an inequality of subprobabilities, $$\boldsymbol1_G(p,C)R(p,b_F\mid C)
 \le\frac{c^{|F|}}{m\eta}R_P(p\mid C)
                             \prod_{j\in F}\lambda(b_j).
 \label{eq:actual-point-free}$$ For $0<\tau<1$, outside $C$ values of $R_C$-mass at most $\eta/\tau$, the subprobability on the left has mass at least $1-\tau$. In any of these conditionals, all applicable product comparisons, including product comparisons for coordinate tuples at several fixed labels, may be converted *simultaneously* to comparisons using their actual retained marginals by Lemma <a href="#lem:marginal-core" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:marginal-core">7</a>. If the subprobability after all prior trims, including intersection with $G$ when used, has conditional mass $u$ and the resulting list has $N_{\mathrm{fac}}$ factor occurrences, its core has conditional mass at least $u/2$ and each $k$-factor comparison constant $A$ becomes at most $A(2N_{\mathrm{fac}}/u)^k$. All exceptional-mass and domination estimates above are independent of the number of possible values of $C$, $P$, and the labels.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-finite-conditioning"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-finite-conditioning</summary>

*Proof.* The probability under $\mu$ of $r(P)<\alpha$ is at most $\zeta/(1-\alpha)$. More exactly, on that set, $r\le\alpha(1-r)/(1-\alpha)$, whence $$M_0=\mathbb E_\mu r-\mathbb E_\mu[r\boldsymbol1_{r<\alpha}]
 \ge1-\zeta-\frac{\alpha\zeta}{1-\alpha}
 =1-\frac{\zeta}{1-\alpha}.$$ On retained point fibers, $q(b\mid p)=\pi(b\mid p)\boldsymbol1_E(p,b)/r(p)
\le(K/\alpha)\lambda(b)$. Multiplying the $n$ kernel bounds proves <a href="#eq:star-independent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:star-independent">[eq:star-independent]</a>. Leaving the $i$th pair unestimated and bounding the other $n-1$ kernels proves <a href="#eq:star-pair" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:star-pair">[eq:star-pair]</a>.

Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:typical-conditioning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:typical-conditioning">3</a> to $\mathsf U=R$ and each of $\mathsf V=\Lambda_0,\ldots,\Lambda_n$, with $A=c^n/m$ or $c^{n-1}/m$. A union bound proves <a href="#eq:conditional-independent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditional-independent">[eq:conditional-independent]</a>–<a href="#eq:conditional-pair" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditional-pair">[eq:conditional-pair]</a>. The factorizations <a href="#eq:fixed-comparison-zero" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fixed-comparison-zero">[eq:fixed-comparison-zero]</a>–<a href="#eq:free-comparison-pair" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:free-comparison-pair">[eq:free-comparison-pair]</a> follow by inserting $B_J=b_J$ and $z_{b_J}(P)=z$ in the displayed product laws. No factor depending on a free label is conditioned on except the pair factor in <a href="#eq:free-comparison-pair" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:free-comparison-pair">[eq:free-comparison-pair]</a>.

For <a href="#eq:actual-point-free" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:actual-point-free">[eq:actual-point-free]</a>, independence in $S$ gives $$S(p,b_F,C)=S_{P,C}(p,C)\prod_{j\in F}q(b_j\mid p).$$ Apply <a href="#eq:conditioning-likelihood" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditioning-likelihood">[eq:conditioning-likelihood]</a> to the marginals $R_{P,C},S_{P,C}$ and set $G=\{R_{P,C}\ge\eta S_{P,C}\}$. Using $R\le S/m$ and the kernel bounds gives $$\boldsymbol1_G R(p,b_F,C)
 \le\frac{c^{|F|}}{m\eta}R_{P,C}(p,C)
                                   \prod_{j\in F}\lambda(b_j).$$ Divide by $R_C(C)$. Since $R(G^c)\le\eta$, Markov’s inequality bounds by $\eta/\tau$ the mass of conditionals losing more than $\tau$. Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:marginal-core" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:marginal-core">7</a> to the subprobability in each selected conditional, with its complete finite list of factor comparisons and threshold $u/(2N_{\mathrm{fac}})$. Its mass $M\le1$ makes the bound in <a href="#eq:core-actual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:core-actual">[eq:core-actual]</a> at most $A(2N_{\mathrm{fac}}/u)^k$. ◻

</details>

We spell out two consequences of the theorem to make its uses precise. First, take $Z$ trivial and $i\in J$. For typical fixed values $b_J$, <a id="eq:fixed-pair-inheritance"></a>$$R_P(\,\cdot\mid B_J=b_J)
       \le\frac{c^{n-1}}{m\eta}q_P(\,\cdot\mid B_i=b_i).
 \label{eq:fixed-pair-inheritance}$$ Thus if at label $b_i$ a coordinate tuple $\Phi_i(P)$ has a bound $q_{\Phi_i\mid b_i}\le A_i\prod_l\mu_{il}$, its law after fixing all of $B_J$ has bound $c^{n-1}A_i/(m\eta)$ against exactly those factors. This is true for every $i\in J$ simultaneously. Applying the core lemma to the combined list supplies actual marginals for all of them in one retained law. Counts on the original pair support are preserved. If $Z$ is nontrivial, the comparison is instead the conditional law $q_P(\,\cdot\mid B_i=b_i,z_{b_J}(P)=z)$ in <a href="#eq:fixed-comparison-pair" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fixed-comparison-pair">[eq:fixed-comparison-pair]</a>; additional coordinate product bounds must be conditioned by <a href="#eq:conditioning-likelihood" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditioning-likelihood">[eq:conditioning-likelihood]</a>, with their factors explicitly identified.

Second, suppose $\rho(a,b)\le K\mu(a)\lambda(b)$ and $C=f(A)$. Outside $\rho_C$-mass at most $\eta$, <a id="eq:parent-product"></a>$$\rho(a,b\mid C=c)\le\frac K\eta
                      \mu(a\mid C=c)\lambda(b).
 \label{eq:parent-product}$$ The measure on children is the original $\mu$ conditioned on its parent; there is no factor $\mu_C(c)^{-1}$ in addition to the displayed likelihood loss. Any number of parent cells, in particular polynomially many, is allowed. Subsequent simultaneous marginal replacement uses the actual child and parameter populations retained in that cell. An observation depending on a free label does not have the factorization used in <a href="#eq:actual-point-free" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:actual-point-free">[eq:actual-point-free]</a>; it must first be included among fixed labels or handled by a separately verified comparison law.

For example, if a final retained point law has $$\rho_{X,U_0}\le A\rho_X\rho_{U_0},\qquad
 \rho_{X,N,L,Z}\le B\rho_X\rho_{N,L}\rho_Z,$$ then conditioning the second inequality on $(X,N)=(x,n)$ gives <a id="eq:full-precision-slice"></a>$$\rho(l,z\mid x,n)
 \le B\frac{\rho_X(x)\rho_N(n)}{\rho_{X,N}(x,n)}
                     \rho(l\mid n)\rho_Z(z).
 \label{eq:full-precision-slice}$$ The factor in the fraction exceeds $1/\eta$ on a set of $\rho_{X,N}$-mass at most $\eta$. This follows by summing $\rho_{X,N}(x,n)$ over the exceptional values, so it is valid also for labels recorded at the finest precision. The first displayed comparison remains available on the same law; it is not replaced by a marginal from an earlier trim.

<a id="stmt-cor-point-slicing"></a>
<div id="cor:point-slicing" class="corollary">

**Corollary 9** (Point slicing after a fixed-label core). *Fix the values of some labels. On that fiber let $\nu$ be a retained probability law of a point $P$ and free labels $(B_j)_{j\in F}$, with $$\nu\le A\nu_P\otimes\bigotimes_{j\in F}\lambda_j.$$ The comparison laws $\lambda_j$ may be the actual marginals obtained by a simultaneous core on this fiber. If $Z=f(P)$, then on every positive $Z$ fiber, $$\nu(p,b_F\mid Z=z)
 \le A\nu_P(p\mid Z=z)\prod_{j\in F}\lambda_j(b_j).$$ Thus the comparison label populations are those *before* the point slice, and any mass upper bounds already proved for them remain available. After a further restriction and core of conditional mass $M>0$, each new actual label marginal is bounded by $A/M$ times its respective $\lambda_j$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cor-point-slicing"><summary>Proof of stmt-cor-point-slicing</summary>

*Proof.* The comparison $Z$ marginal equals $\nu_Z$, so restricting to a $Z$ fiber and dividing by this common mass proves the assertion. Integrating the point and other labels proves the marginal upper bound before the final restriction; restriction and normalization cost at most $M^{-1}$. ◻

</details>

All these conclusions concern a fixed finite star. They supply no lower bound for the density of an arbitrary graph of cyclic incidences. If $K$, $M_0^{-1}$, $m^{-1}$, $u^{-1}$, $\eta^{-1}$ and $\alpha^{-1}$ have logarithms $o(\ell)$ and $n,N_{\mathrm{fac}}$ are fixed, every displayed loss is $\epsilon^{-o(1)}$. For a normalized retained incidence law $\rho\le A\mu\otimes\lambda$, its support has $(\mu\otimes\lambda)$-mass at least $A^{-1}$, simply by integrating the domination inequality. This is the dense-graph conclusion used in the projection theorem.

<a id="pm-h-12"></a>
#### Countable profiles and the order of the limits

The use of entropy at successive resolutions is related to the local entropy averages and comparable-partition arguments of Hochman and Shmerkin (2012, sec. 3.3 and 4.2) <a id="pm-cite-37"></a>[[HochmanShmerkin2012](#ref-HochmanShmerkin2012)] and Hochman (2014, sec. 3). Here we need a finite-law diagonal with explicit retention properties, which we establish directly.

A conditional observation is *homogeneous with exponent $d$* if its realized conditional surprise, divided by $\ell$, converges to $d$ in probability and its normalized conditional entropy also converges to $d$. When further restrictions will be made, we first retain the uniform bins of Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a>. Convergence in probability by itself is insufficient for this purpose. For example, let $\ell\to\infty$, give one atom mass $1-e^{-\sqrt\ell}$, and distribute the remaining mass uniformly among $\lceil e^\ell\rceil$ atoms. Normalized surprise converges to zero in probability, but restriction to the latter atoms has density $e^{\sqrt\ell}$ and entropy tending to one in normalized units. The support and bin requirements in Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a> exclude precisely this issue.

<a id="stmt-lem-profile-diagonal"></a>
<div id="lem:profile-diagonal" class="lemma">

**Lemma 10** (Profiles, countable homogenization, and diagonals). *The following three statements hold.*

1.  *Suppose for each $\epsilon\to0$ there is a countable list $(X_j,Y_j)_{j\ge1}$, with $|\mathcal Y_j|\le\epsilon^{-A_j}$ for each fixed $j$. One can partition all but $o(1)$ of the law into $\epsilon^{-o(1)}$ parts, each of mass at least $\epsilon^{o(1)}$, such that the following holds. From any choice of one retained part at each scale, a subsequence can be extracted on which every listed observation is homogeneous. The same exponents are inherited by every sequence of laws supported on those parts whose density relative to their normalized laws is at most $\epsilon^{-o(1)}$. The assertion is simultaneous for joint observations and observations conditional on an exact particle index, when these are included in the list.*

2.  *Let $v$ range over a compact rectangle of depth parameters. Suppose observations $Y_v$, conditional on any $X$, obey, uniformly for fixed $u,v$, the two ambiguity bounds $$\log N(Y_v\mid Y_u,X),\ \log N(Y_u\mid Y_v,X)
           \le C\ell\|u-v\|_1+o(\ell),$$ and have bounded normalized alphabet sizes at one reference depth. Their normalized entropy profiles have subsequences converging on all depths to a $C$-Lipschitz function, after extraction on a countable dense set. Homogeneous surprise exponents on that dense set extend to the same function at every fixed depth, provided the ambiguity bounds also hold on the retained support.*

3.  *Suppose a finite construction at each fixed $h>0$ has finitely many normalized errors tending to zero as $\epsilon\to0$. Given any sequence of permissible $h_k\downarrow0$, and any countable sequence of such requirements, a diagonal can be chosen so that the first $k$ requirements have errors at most $h_k/k$ and $h_k\log(1/\epsilon_k)\to\infty$. Thus errors may be made $o(h)$ before passing to the scale $\epsilon^h$. This assertion supplies no rate uniform in $h$ or in the limiting profile.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-profile-diagonal"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-profile-diagonal</summary>

*Proof.* For the first assertion, apply Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a> to lists of length $q_k\uparrow\infty$, meshes $a_k\downarrow0$, and, for example, $\sigma=1$, $\theta_k\downarrow0$. At stage $k$ the number $J_k$ is finite and independent of $\epsilon$. Choose the stages sufficiently slowly that $q_k\epsilon\to0$ and $\log(J_k/\theta_k)=o(\ell)$. The discarded mass tends to zero and every retained part has the claimed lower mass. For each fixed $j$ the bin centers stay in the compact interval $[0,A_j+1]$. Successive extraction and a diagonal make all those centers converge. Equations <a href="#eq:homogeneous-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:homogeneous-entropy">[eq:homogeneous-entropy]</a> and <a href="#eq:homogeneous-surprise" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:homogeneous-surprise">[eq:homogeneous-surprise]</a>, with $\eta\downarrow0$ sufficiently slowly and $\log(1/\eta)=o(\ell)$, prove homogeneity. The same estimates prove its asserted inheritance for any dominated sequence; no exceptional set from before binning is reused. All bounds depend on the child alphabets only.

For the second assertion, the chain rule bounds the difference of conditional entropies by the two ambiguity logarithms. A bounded sequence of profiles therefore has, by diagonal extraction on a dense countable set, a limit satisfying the Lipschitz inequality there. Extend it continuously. Approximation of any fixed parameter by dense parameters and the same inequality proves convergence there. For surprises, the identity $$-\log\mathsf P(Y_v\mid X)+\log\mathsf P(Y_u\mid X)
 =-\log\mathsf P(Y_v\mid Y_u,X)
       +\log\mathsf P(Y_u\mid Y_v,X)$$ is exact at sampled values. For an observation with at most $N$ values on each conditional fiber, the conditional-surprise tail above $\log N+t$ has probability at most $e^{-t}$, by summing masses less than $e^{-t}/N$. Apply this to both terms. Since conditional surprises are nonnegative, their difference in absolute value is at most the larger of their two upper bounds outside probability $2e^{-t}$. Take, for instance, $t=\sqrt\ell$, then approximate $v$ by the dense set. This proves the assertion about surprise.

For the last assertion, fix $h_k$ first. The defining small-parameter convergences give a sufficiently small $\epsilon_k$ for the first $k$ errors to be at most $h_k/k$. Decrease $\epsilon_k$ further so that $h_k\log(1/\epsilon_k)\ge k$ and the scales decrease strictly. This inductive choice proves the claim. If a profile must first be chosen and differentiated, choose its regular points and admissible $h_k$ before making this final small-parameter selection. ◻

</details>

In applications with a block length $h$, “subpower loss” means $\log K=o(h\ell)$, not merely $o(\ell)$. For example the logarithm of a conditional $k$-factor core constant in Theorem <a href="#thm:finite-conditioning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:finite-conditioning">8</a> is bounded by a fixed linear combination of $$n\log(K/\alpha),\quad\log(1/M_0),\quad\log(1/m),\quad
 \log(1/\eta),\quad k\log(2N_{\mathrm{fac}}/u).$$ These quantities must be chosen $o(h\ell)$ with $h$ fixed first. The finite numbers of observations and replicas are also fixed at that stage. Lemma <a href="#lem:profile-diagonal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:profile-diagonal">10</a> then permits increasing them slowly and shrinking $h$ afterwards. When an increment has a much larger parent entropy, <a href="#eq:conditional-kl-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:conditional-kl-bound">[eq:conditional-kl-bound]</a> and the uniform child counts give the same $o(h)$ error without multiplying by that parent entropy.

Finally, the use of universal bounds after conditioning is a selection principle for a specified array of conditional laws. At each scale fix a class $\mathcal A_\epsilon$ of laws and parameters such that every sequence selected from these classes is admissible for the asserted universal bound. In particular, all vanishing-error hypotheses must have common deterministic envelopes within the array: a hypothesis $\log K=o(\ell)$ is represented there by $\log K\le r_\epsilon\ell$ with one $r_\epsilon\to0$. If $F_\epsilon(\mathsf P,\vartheta)$ has $\limsup F_\epsilon\le0$ along every such selected sequence, then $$\sup_{(\mathsf P,\vartheta)\in\mathcal A_\epsilon}
               F_\epsilon(\mathsf P,\vartheta)\le o(1).$$ Otherwise choose a violating law and parameter at each of a sequence of scales. The same upper bound holds for any average over conditional laws in this array, regardless of the number of conditioning cells. The envelopes may depend on the construction; this argument asserts no uniform convergence over all possible sequences satisfying an unspecified subpower condition. When the universal statement is initially given for fixed parameters, this argument requires stability under convergent parameters; compactness alone does not supply that stability. The geometric applications below verify it by bounded box enlargements and $O(\|\vartheta-\vartheta'\|)$ changes in depth weights.

<a id="sec:projection"></a>
### The planar projection estimate

The geometric input is the discrete planar Furstenberg theorem of Ren and Wang. We state precisely the consequence used below, including weighted populations, extra parameter labels, and incomplete incidence graphs. No restriction estimate in three dimensions is used as an input.

For a bounded set $E$, let $\abs E_\rho$ denote the number of half-open dyadic $\rho$-squares meeting $E$, where replacing a scale by a comparable dyadic scale is harmless. A finite family of dyadic $\rho$-squares $\mathcal P$ is a $(\rho,d,C)$-set if $$\#\{p\in\mathcal P:p\cap B(z,r)\ne\varnothing\}
 \le C r^d\#\mathcal P,\qquad \rho\le r\le1,$$ up to a fixed enlargement of the ball. We use dyadic tubes in a fixed bounded slope chart. The same definition for tubes refers to their slope–intercept parameters. For tubes meeting one fixed $\rho$-square, this nonconcentration condition is equivalent, within fixed factors, to the corresponding condition on slopes.

<a id="stmt-thm-ren-wang"></a>
<div id="thm:ren-wang" class="theorem">

**Theorem 11** (Ren–Wang, discrete form). *Fix $0<s\le1$, $0<d\le2$, and $\alpha>0$. There are $\eta_0=\eta_0(\alpha,s,d)>0$ and $\rho_0=\rho_0(\alpha,s,d)>0$ with the following property. Suppose $\mathcal P$ is a nonempty $(\rho,d,\rho^{-\eta_0})$-set of squares, with $0<\rho<\rho_0$. For each $p\in\mathcal P$, let $\mathcal T(p)$ be a family of tubes meeting $p$, of cardinality comparable to $M$, and forming a $(\rho,s,\rho^{-\eta_0})$-set. Then <a id="eq:ren-wang-discrete"></a>$$\#\bigcup_{p\in\mathcal P}\mathcal T(p)
 \gtrsim_\alpha
 \rho^{-\min\{1,d,(d+s)/2\}+\alpha}M .
 \label{eq:ren-wang-discrete}$$ The statement is unchanged by fixed bounded domains, finitely many coordinate charts, or fixed-factor enlargements of the grids and tubes, after decreasing $\eta_0,\rho_0$ if necessary.*

</div>

This is Theorem 4.1 of Ren and Wang (2025) <a id="pm-cite-38"></a>[[RenWang2025](#ref-RenWang2025)], expressed using its Definition 3.1 of a nice configuration. That definition already permits each $\mathcal T(p)$ to be a selected subfamily of the tubes meeting $p$. The reduction below additionally handles probability weights, auxiliary tags that may share a slope, and incidence graphs of positive product mass. The fixed-factor variants follow by taking comparable dyadic scales, covering by boundedly many grid pieces, and absorbing the resulting fixed constants into the input loss. The order of the quantifiers is important: the desired output loss $\alpha$ is fixed before the admissible input loss $\eta_0$.

A tag is a slope together with any auxiliary labels; distinct tags may have the same slope. Keeping the full tag allows its set of neighboring points to depend on that additional information.

<a id="stmt-thm-planar-projection"></a>
<div id="thm:planar-projection" class="theorem">

<a id="eq:projection-populations"></a>
<a id="eq:weighted-projection-finite"></a>
**Theorem 12** (Weighted projection bound with parameter tags). *Fix $0<d\le2$, $0<s\le1$, and $\alpha>0$, and fixed bounded point and slope domains. There are $\eta>0$ and $\rho_1>0$ such that the following holds for $0<\rho<\rho_1$. Let $\mu$ be a finite probability population of points in $\mathbb R^2$. Let $\nu$ be a finite probability population of tags $b$, with a slope $a(b)$ assigned to each tag. Suppose $$\begin{aligned}
 \mu(B(z,r))&\le \rho^{-\eta}r^d,
 & (a_*\nu)(I)&\le \rho^{-\eta}r^s
 \label{eq:projection-populations}
\end{aligned}$$ for all balls and intervals of radius or length comparable to $r\in[\rho,1]$. Let $G$ be a graph of point–tag incidences with $(\mu\times\nu)(G)\ge\rho^\eta$. For each tag $b$, suppose that the projection $\pi_{a(b)}(x)$ of its neighbors can be covered by at most $M$ intervals of length $\rho$. Here $\pi_a(x_1,x_2)=x_2-a x_1$. One may multiply these maps by scalars whose absolute values have fixed positive lower and upper bounds. Then $$M\ge \rho^{-\min\{1,d,(d+s)/2\}+\alpha}.
 \label{eq:weighted-projection-finite}$$ Changing the implicit fixed factors in the domains, projections, and interval lengths changes only $\eta,\rho_1$.*

*In particular, along any sequence with subpower nonconcentration constants, graph product mass $\rho^{o(1)}$, and conditional projection count at most $\rho^{-l-o(1)}$, one has <a id="eq:weighted-projection-limit"></a>$$l\ge \min\{1,d,(d+s)/2\}.
 \label{eq:weighted-projection-limit}$$ The limiting assertion for $d=0$ is immediate.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-planar-projection"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-planar-projection</summary>

*Proof.* Absorb any allowed scalar factors into the interval lengths, and use $\pi_a(x_1,x_2)=x_2-a x_1$. Normalized orthogonal projections also have this form on boundedly many direction charts, after an orthogonal coordinate change and such a bounded scalar factor. Write $q=(\mu\times\nu)(G)$, and independently sample $$N=\lceil\rho^{-d}\rceil\quad\hbox{points},\qquad
 Q=\lceil\rho^{-s}\rceil\quad\hbox{whole tags}.$$ The tags, including any information besides their slope, are sampled without alteration.

<a id="eq:sampled-point-count"></a>
<a id="eq:sampled-slope-count"></a>
We give the finite loss accounting. In this proof $C$ denotes a fixed numerical constant, enlarged a finite number of times; it does not depend on $\rho,\eta$, or the population cardinalities. For fixed $\eta>0$ and sufficiently small $\rho$, the sampled multisets have, simultaneously for all dyadic balls or intervals at scales between $\rho$ and $1$, $$\begin{aligned}
 \#\{x_i\in B(z,r)\}
 &\le C\rho^{-3\eta}(r/\rho)^d, \label{eq:sampled-point-count}\\
 \#\{a(b_j)\in I\}
 &\le C\rho^{-3\eta}(r/\rho)^s. \label{eq:sampled-slope-count}
\end{aligned}$$ Moreover, the failure probability is smaller than every fixed power of $\rho$. Indeed each count is binomial, its expectation is bounded by $\rho^{-\eta}N r^d$, or $\rho^{-\eta}Q r^s$, and the displayed threshold has an additional factor at least a fixed multiple of $\rho^{-2\eta}$. The standard exponential Markov estimate $$\mathbb P(X\ge t)\le (e\,\mathbb EX/t)^t,\qquad t\ge \mathbb EX,$$ follows by applying Markov’s inequality to $\exp(\theta X)$ and optimizing $\theta$. Here the smallest nonvacuous threshold is a positive multiple of $\rho^{-3\eta}$. A union bound over the polynomially many dyadic cells and scales proves the assertion. Every ball or interval is covered by boundedly many such cells of comparable scale.

The expected sampled edge count is $qNQ$, whereas its maximum is $NQ$. The occupancy failure event therefore contributes at most $o(qNQ)$ to this expectation. Some sample obeys <a href="#eq:sampled-point-count" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sampled-point-count">[eq:sampled-point-count]</a>–<a href="#eq:sampled-slope-count" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sampled-slope-count">[eq:sampled-slope-count]</a> and has at least $qNQ/2$ edges. Delete point vertices of degree less than $qQ/4$. At least $qNQ/4$ edges remain, hence there are at least $qN/4$ remaining point vertices.

A finest point square contains at most $C\rho^{-3\eta}$ sampled vertices. Keep one remaining vertex in each occupied square; the resulting point-square family has cardinality at least $C^{-1}q\rho^{3\eta}N$. Each selected vertex still has at least $qQ/4$ incident sampled tags.

For a tag and one of its allowed projection intervals, its slope and projection bin specify a tube through the corresponding incident point. Rounding these data to the tube grid and using a bounded enlargement costs only fixed factors. At one selected point square, only boundedly many different intercept bins in a fixed slope bin can give tubes through that square. By <a href="#eq:sampled-slope-count" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sampled-slope-count">[eq:sampled-slope-count]</a>, a tube there can be represented by at most $C\rho^{-3\eta}$ of the sampled tags, up to the same bounded neighboring-bin multiplicity. Remove such coincidences. Each selected point is incident to at least $C^{-1}q\rho^{3\eta}Q$ distinct tubes.

<a id="eq:projection-retained-sizes"></a>
Pigeonhole the point vertices according to dyadic ranges of this last degree. There are $O(\log(1/\rho))$ ranges. Keep a range containing at least that fraction of the selected points, and prune the tube families to a common size $M_0$ within a factor of two. For small $\rho$, all these operations give $$\#\mathcal P\ge \rho^{C\eta}N,\qquad
 M_0\ge \rho^{C\eta}Q .
 \label{eq:projection-retained-sizes}$$ The original sampled count bounds remain upper bounds on every retained subset. Dividing them by the retained cardinalities in <a href="#eq:projection-retained-sizes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:projection-retained-sizes">[eq:projection-retained-sizes]</a> proves that $\mathcal P$ is a $(\rho,d,\rho^{-C\eta})$-set and every $\mathcal T(p)$ is a $(\rho,s,\rho^{-C\eta})$-set. The constants can be taken uniform through the finite grid changes.

On the other hand, each of the $Q$ sampled tags has at most $M$ allowed projection bins, so the total number of distinct tubes is at most $CQM$. Put $$\chi=\min\{1,d,(d+s)/2\}.$$ Apply Theorem <a href="#thm:ren-wang" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:ren-wang">11</a> with output loss $\alpha/4$. Choose $\eta$ sufficiently small that $C\eta<\eta_0(\alpha/4,s,d)$ and $C\eta<\alpha/4$, and then choose $\rho_1$ sufficiently small for all preceding bounds and fixed constants. The theorem yields $$CQM\gtrsim_{\alpha}
 \rho^{-\chi+\alpha/4}M_0
 \ge \rho^{-\chi+\alpha/4+C\eta}Q .$$ Absorbing the fixed constants by another loss less than $\alpha/2$ gives <a href="#eq:weighted-projection-finite" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:weighted-projection-finite">[eq:weighted-projection-finite]</a>.

For the last assertion, apply the finite theorem at any fixed $\alpha>0$. Its hypotheses eventually hold because their losses are subpower. Comparison with the assumed projection count gives $l\ge\chi-\alpha$; let $\alpha\downarrow0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rem-projection-incidence-laws"></a>
<div id="rem:projection-incidence-laws" class="remark">

*Remark 13* (Incidence laws and conditional applications). Often an incidence graph is supplied by a trimmed subprobability $\sigma$ rather than directly by $\mu\times\nu$. If $\sigma(G)\ge m$ and $\sigma\le K\mu\times\nu$, then $$(\mu\times\nu)(G)\ge m/K.$$ Thus subpower mass and subpower product domination give exactly the graph hypothesis of Theorem <a href="#thm:planar-projection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:planar-projection">12</a>. Uniform lower bounds on retained conditional atom masses give the required projection support counts. Uniform upper bounds at every fixed prefix, followed by a sufficiently fine finite scale mesh, give the required ball-mass bounds. The conditioning and homogenization results in Section <a href="#sec:entropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:entropy">2</a> justify those operations when applied in the prescribed order. In each application below we specify which point population and parameter population are being compared; an entropy lower bound without this uniformization is not a substitute for <a href="#eq:projection-populations" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:projection-populations">[eq:projection-populations]</a>.

</div>

<a id="sec:classical-extremality"></a>
### Extremal positive transport and its aspect

Fix $0<\gamma<1$, and put $$w(b,a)=(1+\gamma)b+(1-\gamma)a
       =a+b-\gamma(a-b),\qquad 0\le b\le a.$$ All entropies in this section are divided by $\log(1/\epsilon)$. The particle $T$ is a random variable carrying two bounded vectors $V(T),A(T)\in\mathbb R^2$; its position at time $c$ is $X(c)=A+cV$. The bounded real variable $c$ may have any joint law with $T$. The observations used below are finite. For a finite label $Y$ and arbitrary $T$, $\mathsf H(Y\mid T)$ denotes the average entropy of the conditional probabilities $\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{Y=y\}}\mid\sigma(T)]$, divided by $\log(1/\epsilon)$, and $\mathsf I(T;Y)=\mathsf H(Y)-\mathsf H(Y\mid T)$. Thus no entropy of $T$ is used. A fixed enlargement of the bounded domains is allowed. There is no Planck parameter in this section.

<a id="pm-h-15"></a>
#### Apertures and the universal growth rate

Use nested grids for time and write $C_t$ for the cell of $c$ of length comparable to $\epsilon^t$, together with its chosen representative. At $t=0$ one cell contains the time domain and its representative is zero. The finitely many boundary choices in this convention have entropy $O(1/\log(1/\epsilon))$. For an unoriented normal $R$, let $Q_R$ be an orthogonal frame whose first vector is tangent and whose second vector is normal. Orientations of aspect $e$ are recorded in cells of angular size comparable to $\epsilon^e$. Nested angular grids, or a finite collection of nested slope grids, may be used. Choose a representative normal for each recorded angular cell; both rectangular grids use its frame.

<a id="stmt-def-classical-aperture"></a>
<div id="def:classical-aperture" class="definition">

**Definition 14** (Standard aperture observation). At duration $t$ and horizon $L$, a standard observation $G$ records $$(t,b,a,C_t,R_{a-b},[V]_{b,a;R},
                   [X(C_t)]_{b+t,a+t;R}),
 \qquad 0\le b\le a,\quad a+t\le L.$$ Here the bracket denotes the rectangular grid cell, in the recorded frame, with side lengths $\epsilon^b,\epsilon^a$, or respectively $\epsilon^{b+t},\epsilon^{a+t}$. Its aperture weight is $w(G)=w(b,a)$. The shape and orientation may be chosen by a stochastic kernel; extra finite labels are permitted. Equivalently, a label may locate the data in bounded enlargements of the indicated rectangles. Adding the actual grid cells then costs $O(1/\log(1/\epsilon))$ information.

</div>

Depths can be rounded on a mesh $\xi=\xi_\epsilon\downarrow0$ with $\log(1/\xi)=o(\log(1/\epsilon))$. The number of shape choices in a bounded triangle is then subpower. In this terminology a factor is subpower if its normalized logarithm tends to zero. Dyadic spatial widths give a finite menu of apertures: choose orientation spacing comparable to the minor-to-major axis ratio and translates spaced by the corresponding widths. Every rectangle is contained in a fixed enlargement of one in this menu. Indeed an angular error at most a constant times the axis ratio moves a tangent uncertainty into at most a constant multiple of the normal uncertainty. This verifies the assertion for both columns. Discarding extra labels never increases particle information. Define the root supremum by $$\tau_L(T)=\sup_{D\text{ at duration }0}
       \{\mathbb Ew(D)-\mathsf I(T;D)\}.$$ The supremum is taken for the current particle law and the current precision, before any limit. For a fixed finite menu it is a supremum over all stochastic assignments to compatible caps. Rounding depths down on the mesh and adjoining the actual target cells costs $O(\xi)+O(1/\log(1/\epsilon))$ in root score, uniformly on fixed domain, horizon, and enlargement bounds. Thus these menus recover the unrestricted root supremum in the limit.

The score balances three quantities. The aperture weight rewards finer localization, particle information charges what the observation reveals about $T$, and conditional time entropy measures the time information left after the particle is known. The root supremum provides the zero-duration benchmark for this balance.

<a id="eq:classical-score"></a>
<a id="eq:classical-provisional"></a>
Write $S_t=\mathsf H(C_t\mid T)$ and $$\mathcal F_t(G)=\mathbb Ew(G)-\mathsf I(T;G)+2S_t,
 \qquad
 \beta=\sup\limsup_{\epsilon\to0}
       \frac{\mathcal F_t(G)-\tau_L(T)}{t}.
 \label{eq:classical-score}$$ The supremum ranges over all fixed $0<t\le L<\infty$ and all sequences of the systems just defined. Domain bounds are fixed within each sequence. Fixed affine normalizations put them in one bounded domain without changing a limit. The label $G$ determines, up to bounded ambiguity, a root aperture of the same shape: recover $A=X(C_t)-C_tV$ and coarsen its position rectangle. Consequently $\mathcal F_t(G)-\tau_L(T)\le2S_t+o(1)\le2t+o(1)$. For a single particle and independent uniform time, the choices $b=a=L-t$ give $\tau_L=2L+o(1)$ and $\mathcal F_t=2L+o(1)$. Thus $$0\le\beta\le2.
 \label{eq:classical-provisional}$$

<a id="stmt-thm-classical-growth"></a>
<div id="thm:classical-growth" class="theorem">

**Theorem 15** (Positive-transport growth). *For the aperture systems of Definition <a href="#def:classical-aperture" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="def:classical-aperture">14</a>, the rate in <a href="#eq:classical-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-score">[eq:classical-score]</a> satisfies $\beta\le\gamma$.*

</div>

We prove this bound by examining a sequence whose growth approaches $\beta$. Localization and the least-aspect construction produce a saturated path. Its tangent reduction has two alternatives: an isotropic system, excluded in Section <a href="#sec:isotropic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:isotropic">5</a>, or a path whose aspect grows in proportion to time. Sections <a href="#sec:characteristic-plane" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:characteristic-plane">6</a> and <a href="#sec:rate-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:rate-transfer">7</a> constrain the local information rates of the latter path; Section <a href="#sec:classical-closure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:classical-closure">8</a> combines those constraints with saturation to finish the proof. Until that point we use only <a href="#eq:classical-provisional" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-provisional">[eq:classical-provisional]</a> and the definition of $\beta$.

The rate in <a href="#eq:classical-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-score">[eq:classical-score]</a> is unchanged if the underlying probability spaces are required to be finite. Fix the complete finite root menu and project $G$ to its geometric coordinates, which can only decrease particle information. For every possible output/time pair $(g,k)$, use the two compatibility tests for $V$ and $A+\bar c_kV$, where $\bar c_k$ is the recorded time representative. Partition particles by all these tests and by membership in every root cap. The finite signature $\kappa(T)$ depends on $T$ alone, not on the sampled time. Choose an actual $(V,A)$ in each positive signature, with finite particle index $T^{\mathrm f}$. Give $(T^{\mathrm f},G,C_t)$ the old law of $(\kappa(T),G,C_t)$, and realize each time label by a point in its actual cell. The resulting finite law is compatible and has the same expected weight, with $$\mathsf I(T^{\mathrm f};G)\le\mathsf I(T;G),\qquad
 \mathsf H(C_t\mid T^{\mathrm f})\ge\mathsf H(C_t\mid T).$$ For roots, averaging a compatible kernel within signatures preserves its output marginal and weight and decreases information; conversely, every signature kernel lifts through $\kappa(T)$ with equal information. The frozen-menu root suprema therefore agree exactly. The uniform menu error above is $o(1)$, so every general-law score excess is at most that of a finite law plus $o(1)$. We take these finite laws before forming the conditional systems and independent copies below.

<a id="eq:classical-uniform"></a>
We make explicit the uniformity implicit in that definition. For any fixed domain bound $B$, $K<\infty$, and $t_{\min}>0$, there is a function $\omega_\epsilon(B,K,t_{\min})\to0$ such that $$\mathcal F_t(G)\le\tau_L(T)+\beta t+
 \omega_\epsilon(B,K,t_{\min}),\qquad t_{\min}\le t\le L\le K.
 \label{eq:classical-uniform}$$ Here the menu, its depth mesh, and its fixed enlargement convention are chosen as deterministic functions of $\epsilon$, common to all systems in the supremum. It also applies to every conditional system with these bounds. To see this, a failure selects systems and parameters with a fixed positive excess and a convergent subsequence of $(t,L)$. Changing depths by $\nu$ costs at most $C_{K,\gamma}\nu+o(1)$: cover the larger rectangle by the finer cells, including its changed frame in the count. Coarsening time by $\nu$ loses at most $\nu+o(1)$ of conditional time entropy. Transport to the coarser time uses an uncertainty $\epsilon^{t-\nu}$ times the measured velocity rectangle, which fits the earlier position rectangle. Finally, coarsening both depths of a root test by at most $\nu$ loses at most $2\nu+o(1)$ in weight; this proves the same continuity for the root supremum when its horizon changes by $\nu$. Fixed parameter slack therefore converts the selected systems to a sequence contradicting <a href="#eq:classical-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-score">[eq:classical-score]</a>. The same argument at $t=0$ uses the root supremum directly, with no division by time.

Whenever we use conditional arrays below, we first fix the finite list of observations, the depth mesh, all trimming thresholds, and the positive time increments. Their exceptional probabilities and normalized errors are then bounded by one deterministic function $q_\epsilon\to0$ on every retained cell. Cell coordinate bounds and covering multiplicities are common constants. Thus every selection of one retained system per precision remains an admissible sequence in <a href="#eq:classical-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-score">[eq:classical-score]</a>. The conditional-array selection principle at the end of Section <a href="#sec:entropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:entropy">2</a> applies to precisely this array; it does not require a uniform rate over unspecified subpower envelopes.

<a id="pm-h-16"></a>
#### Splitting and cap bounds

Call an observation saturated if, along the sequence under discussion, $\mathcal F_t(G)-\tau_L(T)\to\beta t$. An extremizer below always means such a sequence, not a maximizing measure at finite precision.

<a id="stmt-lem-classical-splitting"></a>
<div id="lem:classical-splitting" class="lemma">

**Lemma 16** (Splitting saturated laws). *Let $Z$ be a finite tag. If $\Delta=\beta t+\tau_L(T)-\mathcal F_t(G)$, and $\Delta_z$ is the corresponding deficit for the law conditional on $Z=z$, then $$\mathbb E\Delta_Z\le\Delta+3\mathsf H(Z).$$ In particular subpower splittings preserve saturation on typical parts, simultaneously for any fixed finite list of saturated observations.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-classical-splitting"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-classical-splitting</summary>

*Proof.* Combining conditional root tests and including $Z$ in their label gives $\mathbb E\tau_L(T\mid Z)\le\tau_L(T)+\mathsf I(T;Z)$. The exact chain rules give $$\mathbb E\mathcal F_t(G\mid Z)-\mathcal F_t(G)
 =-\mathsf I(T;Z\mid G)+\mathsf I(T;Z)-2\mathsf I(C_t;Z\mid T).$$ Subtract and use that each of the last two nonnegative costs is at most $\mathsf H(Z)$. By <a href="#eq:classical-uniform" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-uniform">[eq:classical-uniform]</a>, each conditional deficit is at least $-\omega_\epsilon$, uniformly over the cells. Its positive part therefore tends to zero in mean when the original deficit and tag entropy do. Markov’s inequality proves the last assertion. No lower bound on an individual cell probability is used for this selection. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-classical-cap-regularization"></a>
<div id="lem:classical-cap-regularization" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:classical-cap-bounds"></a>
**Lemma 17** (Greedy cap regularization). *After a subpower splitting and removal of probability $o(1)$, a particle law can be restricted to classes with a bounded number $h$ such that $$\Pr_T(\operatorname{cap}(D))
       \le\epsilon^{w(D)-h-o(1)},\qquad \tau_L(T)=h+o(1).
 \label{eq:classical-cap-bounds}$$ The cap bound is uniform over the root menu and its fixed enlargements. For a further law $Q\le\epsilon^{-\eta}\Pr_T$ on such a class, $\tau_L(Q)\le h+\eta+o(1)$. Hence a subpower restriction or tilt preserving the displayed score profiles preserves saturation.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-classical-cap-regularization"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-classical-cap-regularization</summary>

*Proof.* In the finite root menu, repeatedly select a cap maximizing $w(D)+\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(\mu_{\rm rem}(\operatorname{cap}(D))\right)$ and remove its remaining contents. Selected contents $E_i$ are disjoint and cover the law. A selected cap cannot be selected again with positive mass, so the procedure is finite. The successive maxima $h_i$ decrease. Split the indices into intervals $[h,h+\xi]$ and keep each entire $E_i$ in its bin. At the first removal in this bin every cap has remaining mass at most $\epsilon^{w(D)-h-\xi}$. The absolute mass of its intersection with the whole bin has the same upper bound.

Let the bin have probability $p$. Under its normalized law every cap thus has mass at most $p^{-1}\epsilon^{w(D)-h-\xi}$. The deterministic assigned-cap test has score $$\sum_{i\text{ in bin}}\frac{\mu(E_i)}p
       \left(w(D_i)+\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(\frac{\mu(E_i)}p\right)\right)
 =\mathbb E[h_i\mid\text{bin}]+\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(1/p\right).$$ Conversely, for any compatible stochastic test $D$, conditional relative entropy on its cap gives $$\mathsf I(T;D)\ge
   \mathbb E\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(\frac 1{\Pr_T(\operatorname{cap}(D))}\right).$$ The two estimates put the conditional root supremum between $h+\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(1/p\right)$ and $h+\xi+\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(1/p\right)$, up to the menu ambiguity. The same inequality proves the assertion about $Q$.

For completeness, very negative bins can be discarded: a fixed number of zero-depth caps cover the domain, so a remaining maximum below $-\lambda$ forces remaining probability at most $C\epsilon^\lambda$. The other maxima are at most $2L+o(1)$. Choose the mesh slowly, and discard bins of mass less than $\epsilon^{\eta_\epsilon}$, where $\eta_\epsilon\downarrow0$ slowly enough that the number of bins times $\epsilon^{\eta_\epsilon}$ tends to zero. Then $\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(1/p\right)=o(1)$ on every retained bin. This proves <a href="#eq:classical-cap-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-cap-bounds">[eq:classical-cap-bounds]</a>. Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-splitting">16</a> when the input is saturated. Before any later subpower tilt, impose the uniform probability bins of Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a>; its conditional relative-entropy estimate preserves the stipulated profiles. Their score tends to $\beta t+h$, while the cap bound gives $\tau_L(Q)\le h+o(1)$ and <a href="#eq:classical-uniform" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-uniform">[eq:classical-uniform]</a> gives the reverse inequality. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-17"></a>
#### Anisotropic localization

<a id="stmt-lem-classical-localization"></a>
<div id="lem:classical-localization" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:classical-local-first"></a>
<a id="eq:classical-local-second"></a>
**Lemma 18** (Localization and composition). *Let $G$ have fixed shape $(b,a)$ at $t$, put $e=a-b$, and fix $0\le r<t$, $0\le d\le e$. Let $J$ be the aperture at $r$ of shape $(b,b+d)$ whose frame is the depth-$d$ prefix of the frame of $G$. Set $\zeta=\mathsf H(R_d\mid T,C_r)$. Conditional on $J$, there are bounded line systems with final shape $(0,e-d)$, duration $t-r$, and horizon $L'=e-d+t-r$. With $\tau'_J$ their root suprema, $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal F_t(G)
 &\le\beta(t-r)+w(b,b+d)-\mathsf I(T;J)\notag\\
 &\qquad{}+2S_r+\mathbb E\tau'_J+2\zeta+o(1),
 \label{eq:classical-local-first}\\
 w(b,b+d)-\mathsf I(T;J)+2S_r+\mathbb E\tau'_J
 &\le\beta r+\tau_L(T)+o(1).
 \label{eq:classical-local-second}
\end{aligned}$$ Here parameters are fixed before $\epsilon\to0$. Uniform versions have errors $C\xi+C\log(C_0)/\log(1/\epsilon)+\omega_\epsilon$ for depth-rounding mesh $\xi$, fixed enlargement bound $C_0$, and the compact parameter bounds in <a href="#eq:classical-uniform" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-uniform">[eq:classical-uniform]</a>. If $\zeta=o(1)$ and $G$ is saturated, typical conditional systems are saturated and near-maximizing compositions give a saturated predecessor at $r>0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-classical-localization"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-classical-localization</summary>

*Proof.* Write $v_J,x_J$ for the velocity and position representatives of $J$, $c_J$ for its time representative, and $S=Q_{R_d}\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon^b,\epsilon^{b+d})$. The coordinates $$v'=S^{-1}(V-v_J),\quad
