 a'=\epsilon^{-r}S^{-1}(A+c_JV-x_J),\quad
 c'=\epsilon^{-r}(c-c_J)$$ are bounded on this conditional system, and its trajectory is $a'+c'v'$. More explicitly, $$a'+c'v'=\epsilon^{-r}S^{-1}
       \bigl(A+cV-x_J-(c-c_J)v_J\bigr),$$ so the moving anchor being subtracted is known from $J$. Both columns use the same spatial map; the position column has the additional factor $\epsilon^{-r}$. If $\theta$ is the angle from the coarse frame to the final frame, then $|\sin\theta|\le C\epsilon^d$. In these units the final velocity uncertainty matrix, with its harmless scalar factor removed, is $$N=\operatorname{diag}(1,\epsilon^{-d})
       Q_\theta\operatorname{diag}(1,\epsilon^e).$$ Its largest singular value lies between positive fixed constants: the first column has length at least one and all entries are bounded. Its determinant has absolute value $\epsilon^{e-d}$. Its other singular value is therefore comparable to $\epsilon^{e-d}$. The final position matrix is $\epsilon^{t-r}N$. This proves the asserted final aperture.

The same calculation proves the needed determination of $J$ by $G$. Rotate the velocity uncertainty to the coarse frame, coarsen its normal width from $a$ to $b+d$, and transport the position uncertainty from $C_t$ to $C_r$. Since $|C_t-C_r|\le C\epsilon^r$, the transported velocity uncertainty fits the position widths $\epsilon^{b+r},\epsilon^{b+d+r}$. Thus only a bounded number of cells is possible. This argument compares uncertainty rectangles, and imposes no bound on the displacement of their centers. In particular $$\mathsf H(J\mid G)=o(1),\qquad
 \mathsf H(J\mid T,C_r)\le\zeta+o(1).$$ After adding the actual transformed cells at bounded cost, the final label $G'$ satisfies $\mathsf I(T;J)+\mathsf I(T;G'\mid J)\le\mathsf I(T;G)+o(1)$. Also, since $J$ includes $C_r$, $$0\le S_t-S_r-\mathsf H(C_t\mid T,J)
      =\mathsf I(C_t;J\mid T,C_r)\le\zeta+o(1).$$ The local final weight is exactly $w(0,e-d)=w(b,a)-w(b,b+d)$. Apply <a href="#eq:classical-uniform" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-uniform">[eq:classical-uniform]</a> in each conditional system and average; these identities give <a href="#eq:classical-local-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-local-first">[eq:classical-local-first]</a>.

For composition, take a local root test of shape $(B,A)$, $0\le B\le A\le L'$, and frame $Q_\phi$. Its global uncertainty is $$M=S Q_\phi\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon^B,\epsilon^A).$$ Let $p\le q$ be its two singular-value depths. The determinant identity, the upper bound for the largest singular value, the lower bound for the smallest one, and submultiplicativity of the condition number give $$\begin{gathered}
 p+q=2b+d+A+B+o(1),\qquad
 q-p\le d+A-B+o(1),\\
 p\ge b+B-o(1),\qquad
 q\le b+d+A+o(1)\le a+t-r+o(1).
\end{gathered}$$ Consequently $$w(p,q)\ge w(b,b+d)+w(B,A)-o(1),\qquad q+r\le L+o(1).$$ The position column has the same singular directions and the extra factor $\epsilon^r$, so this is an admissible global aperture at $r$. Rounding its depths down removes the displayed horizon slack at a vanishing cost. Include $J$ in the composed label and add its actual cells at bounded ambiguity. Its information is at most $\mathsf I(T;J)+\mathsf I(T;D'\mid J)+o(1)$. Choose conditional root tests within any prescribed $\eta>0$ of $\tau'_J$, apply the global bound at $r$, and then let $\eta\downarrow0$. At $r=0$ use the defining root supremum instead. This proves <a href="#eq:classical-local-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-local-second">[eq:classical-local-second]</a>.

Finally, if both endpoints of these inequalities agree in the limit, their nonnegative limiting deficits have zero mean. The uniform lower bounds on all conditional deficits permit the same Markov selection as in Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-splitting">16</a>. The composition of the chosen conditional root tests gives the predecessor assertion. The finite errors quoted in the statement come respectively from rounding, bounded covering multiplicities, and <a href="#eq:classical-uniform" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-uniform">[eq:classical-uniform]</a>. ◻

</details>

The case $r=d=0$ removes the common depth $b$. Replacing the local horizon by its smallest permitted value $e+t$ cannot lower a score minus its root supremum; the universal upper bound then forces saturation. Replacing $\epsilon$ by $\epsilon^t$ makes the duration one and divides all depths, weights, and normalized entropies by $t$.

<a id="pm-h-18"></a>
#### The least aspect and saturated predecessors

<a id="eq:classical-rectangle-gain"></a>
We first isolate the rectangle comparison used twice below. Two equal-shape apertures $(b,b+e)$ with angular separation of depth $v\in[0,e]$ have a common coarsening of shape $(b,b+v)$ and an intersection aperture of shape $(b+e-v,b+e)$. The common label is determined by either original label, once an angle-depth bin of width $\xi$ is supplied, at information cost $O(\xi)+o(1)$. For the intersection, one normal constraint has width $\epsilon^{b+e}$; solving the other normal constraint along its tangent gives width $C\epsilon^{b+e}/|\sin\theta|$. The safe endpoint of the angle bin gives the asserted tangent depth with an $O(\xi)$ loss. Coarsening to normal depth $b+v$ proves the common-rectangle assertion. These arguments apply separately to both columns, with the common time factor when the duration is positive. The weight gain is $$w(b+e-v,b+e)+w(b,b+v)-2w(b,b+e)=2\gamma(e-v).
 \label{eq:classical-rectangle-gain}$$

Figure <a href="#fig:aperture-geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="fig:aperture-geometry">1</a> shows the two rectangles responsible for this weight gain.

<figure id="fig:aperture-geometry">

<figcaption>Aperture geometry for two common-shape observations. The centered schematic has $0 < ϵ < 1$, $b ≤ a$ and $0 ≤ v ≤ a − b$, with angle $θ ≍ ϵ^{v}$. Here $a = b + e$ in the notation of <a href="#eq:classical-rectangle-gain" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-rectangle-gain">[eq:classical-rectangle-gain]</a>; the two comparison rectangles give its weight gain. The dashed common rectangle contains both apertures up to fixed factors; the shaded intersection is contained in a rectangle with depths $(a−v,a)$. All indicated side lengths are orders of magnitude, and the picture displays an interior value of $v$. The same calculation applies to the position column at duration $r$ after multiplying both side lengths by $ϵ^{r}$.</figcaption>

<a id="stmt-prop-least-aspect"></a>
<div id="prop:least-aspect" class="proposition">

**Proposition 19** (Least-aspect limiting extremizer). *There exists a saturated sequence at duration one with $b=0$, endpoint aspect $e=m$, and horizon $1+m$, where $m\ge0$ is the least aspect of any such saturated sequence. One may moreover require $Y_j$ conditional on $X_j$ to be homogeneous for a prescribed countable list of finite pairs $(X_j,Y_j)$, provided that for each fixed $j$ there is $0\le A_j<\infty$, independent of $\epsilon$, such that $|\mathcal Y_j|\le\epsilon^{-A_j}$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$. No cardinality bound is imposed on $X_j$, which may include the exact particle $T$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-least-aspect"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-least-aspect</summary>

*Proof.* Choose systems whose normalized rates tend to $\beta$, split by narrow shape bins, remove $b$ by localization, and normalize time. Each individual inner sequence now has a fixed finite aspect $e$; its rate defect can be made arbitrarily small. We need a bound for $e$ independent of which sequence was selected.

Sample two final labels independently given $T$, and let $D_1,D_2$ be their root coarsenings of shape $(0,e)$. If the rate defect is $\eta$, then, since $S_1\le1+o(1)$ and $\beta\ge0$, $$\mathsf I(T;D_j)\le(1-\gamma)e-\tau_L(T)+2+\eta+o(1).$$ Tag their separation depth $v$ on a fixed mesh and use the common and intersection labels above. Conditional independence gives $$\begin{aligned}
 2e-(1+\gamma)\mathbb Ev-\tau_L(T)
 &\le\mathsf I(T;D_1,D_2)+O(\xi)+o(1)\\
 &\le2\big((1-\gamma)e-\tau_L(T)+2+\eta\big)
       -\big((1-\gamma)\mathbb Ev-\tau_L(T)\big)
       +O(\xi)+o(1).
\end{aligned}$$ Indeed the information identity for the pair subtracts $\mathsf I(D_1;D_2)$, which is at least the common-label entropy minus its two determination errors. That entropy is at least its particle information, and the root test bounds the latter below by its weight minus $\tau_L$. The separation tag has entropy $o(1)$ at each fixed mesh. Rearrangement yields $$2\gamma\mathbb E(e-v)\le4+2\eta+O(\xi)+o(1).$$ Thus a fixed $K=K_\gamma<\infty$ gives a positive, uniformly bounded below probability of agreement within a bounded number of cells at depth $(e-K)_+$. For each $T$, maximize the conditional probability of a coarse orientation cell. The conditional collision probability of two independent draws is at most a fixed constant times this maximum. This deterministic predictor therefore succeeds, to bounded cell ambiguity, on an event of probability at least $c_\gamma>0$. On that event the coarse orientation has conditional entropy $o(1)$ given $T$. Binary splitting preserves a rate defect tending to zero on this event. Localization with $r=0$, $d=(e-K)_+$ produces a conditional system with residual aspect at most $K$ and rate defect tending to zero. Uniform conditional deficit bounds justify selecting one such system even when the conditioning cells are numerous.

It remains to take the least aspect. The preceding construction, followed by a diagonal, produces at least one saturated sequence with bounded aspect and reduced horizon. Let $m$ be the infimum of its possible limiting aspects. Choose such sequences with aspects $e_j\to m$. For the $j$th sequence choose its precision small enough that its score defect, finite-menu errors, and the errors for the first $j$ requested profiles are less than $1/j$. Coarsen an endpoint of aspect $e_j$ to aspect $m$ when $e_j\ge m$; if needed allow a depth error $|e_j-m|$ before this coarsening. The score loses at most $C_\gamma|e_j-m|+o(1)$, whereas reducing the horizon to $1+m$ reduces the subtracted root supremum. The universal bound forces the resulting diagonal to saturate. For the homogeneity assertion, apply Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a> to finite initial lists of these pairs under the stated bounds on the child alphabets, and choose their meshes and errors before the corresponding precision. Lemma <a href="#lem:profile-diagonal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:profile-diagonal">10</a> then retains the countable list. In the applications below the children are finite tuples of grid observations at fixed depths in bounded coordinates; the exact particle and other unrestricted conditioning data occur only among the parents. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-prop-saturated-path"></a>
<div id="prop:saturated-path" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:classical-coherence"></a>
**Proposition 20** (Saturated path and coherence). *The sequence in Proposition <a href="#prop:least-aspect" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:least-aspect">19</a> can carry, on one joint law of $(T,c)$, saturated observations $G_u$ at every positive dyadic time $u\le1$. Their shapes satisfy $$b(1)=0,\quad a(1)=m,\quad
 b(r)\ge b(t),\quad a(r)+r\le a(t)+t\quad(r<t),
 \qquad e(u):=a(u)-b(u)\ge mu.$$ They can be constructed so that $\mathsf H(R_{e(u)}\mid T,C_u)=o(1)$. There is a constant $K_\gamma$, independent of $r,t$, for which the orientations at $r<t$ agree with probability tending to one at every positive depth $$d<\min(e(r),e(t))-K_\gamma
       \bigl(|b(r)-b(t)|+|a(r)-a(t)|+t-r\bigr).
 \label{eq:classical-coherence}$$ All statements refer to the inner $\epsilon$ limit with the times fixed.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-saturated-path"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-saturated-path</summary>

*Proof.* On a finite dyadic mesh, work backwards from $1$ using Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-localization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-localization">18</a> with $d=0$. A composed predecessor has minimum depth at least the later $b$ and maximum depth at most the later $a$ plus the time difference. Split its variable shape into narrow bins and use Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-splitting">16</a> to preserve all equalities already imposed. Drop redundant labels. Before making this split, sample each incoming predecessor from its kernel given $(T,C_r)$, independently of the previously retained finer time and later labels. This operation preserves its law with $(T,C_r)$ and preserves the entire later joint law. In particular the underlying time variable is never resampled.

Subsequent finite binning and trimming introduce at most their normalized entropy or relative-entropy cost into the averaged conditional mutual information, by Lemma <a href="#lem:entropy-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:entropy-splitting">4</a>. Retain typical parts on which this cost and all finitely many score defects are bounded by a common deterministic $q_\epsilon\to0$, using Markov thresholds fixed before selecting parts. The same lemma justifies the kernel resampling with base $(T,C_r)$; at this stage no observation involving a free replica is fixed. Passing to finer finite meshes, and then to a diagonal, gives the asserted common sequence and its dyadic shapes. Shape bounds follow from the fixed horizon. A saturated observation at $u$, localized with $r=d=0$ and normalized to duration one, has aspect $e(u)/u$; minimality gives $e(u)\ge mu$.

Here are details of coherence. Put $D=|b(r)-b(t)|+|a(r)-a(t)|+t-r$. Convert the observation at $t$ to the shape $(b(r),a(r))$ at $r$, using its recorded frame rounded to the target precision and recording the actual target cells. Its additional conditional log-cardinality is at most $C D+o(1)$. To check this bound, rotate the old uncertainty into the new frame: the tangent uncertainty entering the normal coordinate has exponent at least $b(t)+e(r)\ge a(r)-|b(t)-b(r)|$. The other side-length changes cost at most the absolute differences of the two depths. Transport from $C_t$ to $C_r$ adds $\epsilon^r$ times the velocity uncertainty, which has the same bound in position units divided by $\epsilon^r$. Counting the finer cells in each resulting rectangle gives the stated estimate. The weight changes by at most $2D$, and $S_t-S_r\le t-r+o(1)$. Thus this converted test and the original test at $r$ have total deficit at most $C_\gamma D+o(1)$ at duration $r$.

Call these two labels $D_1,D_2$, their common label $D_c$, and their intersection label $D_i$. They contain $C_r$, and their remaining coordinates are deterministic functions of $T,C_r$ and their respective orientations. The resampling construction therefore gives $$\mathsf I(D_1;D_2\mid T)\le S_r+o(1),\qquad
 \mathsf H(D_c\mid T)\ge S_r.$$ The pair information identity and common-label determination imply $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathsf I(T;D_i)
 &\le\mathsf I(T;D_1)+\mathsf I(T;D_2)-\mathsf H(D_c)
                   +\mathsf I(D_1;D_2\mid T)+O(\xi)+o(1)\\
 &\le\mathsf I(T;D_1)+\mathsf I(T;D_2)-\mathsf I(T;D_c)+O(\xi)+o(1).
\end{aligned}$$ Both $D_c,D_i$ have the same time $C_r$ and obey the original horizon. Apply the universal score bound to each. Their two time contributions cancel the corresponding contributions in $D_1,D_2$, giving $$2\gamma\mathbb E(e(r)-v)\le C_\gamma D+O(\xi)+o(1).$$ This inequality also holds on any separation event of fixed positive limiting probability: binary splitting preserves the two original saturations, and the extra conditional dependence costs only $o(1)$. On the event $v\le d$ its left side is at least $2\gamma(e(r)-d)$. Choose $K_\gamma$ larger than the preceding constant divided by $2\gamma$, and then let the angle mesh tend to zero. A positive limiting probability of separation at a depth in <a href="#eq:classical-coherence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-coherence">[eq:classical-coherence]</a> is impossible.

Apply the same comparison to two independent replicas of a single label given $(T,C_u)$. With $D=0$ they agree at every depth $e(u)-\nu$, $\nu>0$, with probability tending to one. For each base value, a coarse cell and its bounded neighbors then contain all but $o(1)$ of the conditional orientation mass on average. Choose such a cell deterministically from the base. The entropy bound obtained by separating this event from its complement is $o(1)$ at depth $e(u)-\nu$; refining the orientation costs at most $\nu+o(1)$. Let $\nu\downarrow0$. This proves the asserted zero conditional orientation entropy. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-19"></a>
#### Isotropic tangents or a matched aspect

<a id="stmt-prop-isotropic-reduction"></a>
<div id="prop:isotropic-reduction" class="proposition">

**Proposition 21** (Tangent reduction). *One of the following alternatives holds for the least aspect $m$.*

1.  *If $m=0$, there is a saturated sequence of duration and horizon one, with isotropic endpoint $(b,a)=(0,0)$ and homogeneous conditional time profile $$\mathsf H(C_u\mid T)=su+o(1),\qquad 0\le u\le1,
     \quad 0\le s\le1.$$*

<a id="eq:orientation-growth"></a>
2.  *If $m>0$, the saturated path can be represented by a single orientation $R$ with depth-$mu$ prefixes at time $u$, for every $0<u\le1$, and $\mathsf H(R_{mu}\mid T,C_u)=o(1)$. Its shapes satisfy $$e(u)=mu,\qquad b(u)\text{ is Lipschitz},\qquad
                     0\le-b'(u)\le1+m\quad\text{a.e.}$$ There is $\kappa>0$ such that its limiting conditional orientation entropies obey $$\mathsf H(R_{m(u+h)}\mid T,C_u)\ge\kappa h,
                      \qquad 0<u<u+h<1.
     \label{eq:orientation-growth}$$ The alternatives and the positive lower bound persist after homogeneous splittings that preserve the saturated path.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-isotropic-reduction"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-isotropic-reduction</summary>

*Proof.* The nesting inequalities make $b$ nonincreasing and $a(u)+u$ nondecreasing; extend them to their continuity points. In particular $e(u)+u$ is nondecreasing, so $e$ has bounded variation and its singular distributional derivative is nonnegative. Choose a common differentiability point $x\in(0,1)$ for these functions. Take dyadic $r<x<t$ with $\eta=t-r\downarrow0$ and with both distances from $x$ comparable to $\eta$. Differentiability gives uniform linear approximations throughout $[r,t]$, with error $o(\eta)$. Choose a finite dyadic chain $$r=u_0<u_1<\cdots<u_N=t$$ whose largest interval length is $o(\eta)$, and put $$D_j=|b(u_{j+1})-b(u_j)|+|a(u_{j+1})-a(u_j)|+u_{j+1}-u_j,
 \qquad D_{\max}=\max_jD_j.$$ The uniform linear approximations give $D_{\max}\le C\max_j(u_{j+1}-u_j)+o(\eta)=o(\eta)$. Here the chain may become longer as $\eta\downarrow0$, but it is finite and fixed at each inner small-parameter limit.

Let $e_{\min}=\min_j e(u_j)$ and choose a positive $\delta_\eta=o(\eta)$. Set $$d=\bigl(e_{\min}-K_\gamma D_{\max}-\delta_\eta\bigr)_+.$$ When $d>0$, it lies strictly below the coherence depth for every adjacent pair in the chain. Equation <a href="#eq:classical-coherence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-coherence">[eq:classical-coherence]</a> therefore makes all their frames agree at depth $d$, up to bounded neighboring cells, with probability tending to one. Transitivity costs at most a fixed number depending on this chain of neighboring cells, and the union of its finitely many exceptional events still has probability tending to zero. The frame at $r$ is determined by $(T,C_r)$ to zero normalized entropy at this depth. The entropy ambiguity bound hence gives the same determination for the terminal depth-$d$ frame. If $d=0$, no orientation information is required.

The uniform linear approximation for $e$ also gives $$e(t)-e_{\min}\le\max(e'(x),0)\eta+o(\eta).$$ Since $e_{\min}\ge0$, the definition of $d$ yields, in either case, $$e(t)-d\le e(t)-e_{\min}+K_\gamma D_{\max}+\delta_\eta
       \le\max(e'(x),0)\eta+o(\eta).$$ All depths, the chain, and its angular mesh are chosen before the inner limit. The depth loss is $K_\gamma D_{\max}$ at this one common depth; the number of links enters only the zero-cost angular ambiguity.

Localize the terminal observation at $r$, using its common depth $b(t)$ and this $d$. Its local horizon is $\eta+e(t)-d$. Saturation and zero conditional orientation entropy give saturated conditional systems. With small parameter $\rho=\epsilon^\eta$, their duration is one and their aspect is at most $\max(e'(x),0)+o(1)$. All local coordinate bounds are uniform, and their horizons stay bounded. Minimality of $m$ therefore implies $m\le\max(e'(x),0)$. If $m>0$, this yields $e'(x)\ge m$ almost everywhere. Since the singular derivative of $e$ is nonnegative, $$e(1)-e(u)\ge\int_u^1 e'(v)\,dv\ge m(1-u).$$ Together with $e(u)\ge mu$ and $e(1)=m$, this proves $e(u)=mu$. The original nesting inequalities now give $$0\le b(r)-b(t)\le(1+m)(t-r),$$ which proves the Lipschitz assertion and extends the path to every time.

We specify the selection of shrinking-scale limits, also for later use. For the $j$th interval first fix its endpoints, its finite coherence chain, and the first $j$ time-prefix fractions. Homogenize their joint and conditional probability bins, then choose the inner precision so that all depth errors, normalized conditional entropies, uniform-bound errors, and retained score deficits are less than $\eta_j/j^2$. Use uniform typical sets before any further restriction. The sum of the conditional deficits is then $o(\eta_j)$ in mean; select typical localization cells with each required error $o(\eta_j)$. Only afterwards divide by $\eta_j$ and take the outer diagonal. This is an application of Lemma <a href="#lem:profile-diagonal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:profile-diagonal">10</a> with the error measured in the new units. No modulus of differentiability uniform over profiles is used.

If $m=0$, use a common regular point with $e'\le0$ in the tangent construction above. The set of such points has positive measure: otherwise $e'>0$ almost everywhere, and its nonnegative singular derivative would force $e(1)>e(u)\ge0$, contrary to $e(1)=0$. The nondecreasing $1$-Lipschitz homogeneous time profile $S_u$ is differentiable almost everywhere, so the point can also be chosen regular for $S$. Put $s=S'(x)\in[0,1]$. At this point the residual aspect just constructed is $o(\eta)$.

For the conditional time calculation, fix the finite list $q=r+k\eta$ chosen above, and put $B=(T,C_r)$, $D_q=C_q$, $d_q=S_q-S_r$, and $\ell=\log(1/\epsilon)$. Let $\mathsf P$ be their joint law with the localization label $J$, before its value is fixed. The recorded conditional bins have one error $\omega_\epsilon=o(\eta)$ for this list outside probability $o(1)$, while the preceding parameter choice gives $\mathsf H^{\mathsf P}(J\mid B)=o(\eta)$. At sampled values, $$-\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf P(D_q\mid B,J)
 +\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf P(D_q\mid B)
 =\ell^{-1}\log
       \frac{\mathsf P(J\mid B)}{\mathsf P(J\mid B,D_q)}.$$ The two nonnegative $J$ surprises on the right have means at most $\mathsf H^{\mathsf P}(J\mid B)$. Choose $\delta_\epsilon=o(\eta)$ with $\mathsf H^{\mathsf P}(J\mid B)/\delta_\epsilon\to0$ and trim them by Markov’s inequality. Intersecting with the recorded bins leaves an event $E$ of probability $1-o(1)$ on which, simultaneously for the listed $q$, $$-\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf P(J\mid B)\le\delta_\epsilon,\qquad
 \left|-\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf P(D_q\mid B,J)-d_q\right|
       \le\alpha_\epsilon:=\omega_\epsilon+\delta_\epsilon=o(\eta).$$ The list is fixed before choosing the inner precision; its errors and exceptional masses are put under one deterministic vanishing envelope before the lists grow along the preceding diagonal.

Put $\mathsf P^E=\mathsf P(\,\cdot\mid E)$. Conditional relative entropy gives $$\mathsf H^{\mathsf P^E}(J\mid B)
 \le\mathbb E_{\mathsf P^E}[-\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf P(J\mid B)]
 \le\delta_\epsilon=o(\eta).$$ Since $J$ records $R_d$, this also bounds the orientation cost under $\mathsf P^E$. The binary tag $\boldsymbol1_E$ costs $O(1/\ell)=o(\eta)$. Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-splitting">16</a>, the original $o(\eta)$ deficits, and the common lower bound $-o(\eta)$ for the complementary deficits give $o(\eta)$ deficits on $\mathsf P^E$. Localization of this law has conditional laws $\mathsf Q_j=\mathsf P(\,\cdot\mid E,J=j)$, followed by the known $J$-dependent coordinate change. The shrinking-scale selection above therefore gives a set of $\mathsf P^E_J$-mass $1-o(1)$ on which the required local deficits are $o(\eta)$ under the same finite envelope.

Choose one $\lambda_\epsilon\downarrow0$ with $\log(1/\lambda_\epsilon)=o(\eta\ell)$, using $\eta\ell\to\infty$. Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:typical-conditioning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:typical-conditioning">3</a> to the event $E$, with $C=J$, $X=(B,J)$, $Y=D_q$, and all three exceptional thresholds equal to $\lambda_\epsilon$. Outside $\mathsf P^E_J$-mass at most $\lambda_\epsilon$, it gives $$\mathsf Q_j\le[\mathsf P(E)\lambda_\epsilon]^{-1}\mathsf P_j,
 \qquad \mathsf P_j=\mathsf P(\,\cdot\mid J=j).$$ On $J=j$, conditioning on $X$ is conditioning on $B$, and the bin on $E$ is for $\mathsf P(D_q\mid B,J)=\mathsf P_j(D_q\mid B)$. The lemma’s entropy and surprise conclusions therefore give $$\begin{gathered}
 \Omega_\epsilon:=
 \alpha_\epsilon+\ell^{-1}\log\frac1{\mathsf P(E)\lambda_\epsilon^2}
       =o(\eta),\\
 \left|\mathsf H^{\mathsf Q_j}(D_q\mid B)-d_q\right|\le\Omega_\epsilon,\qquad
 \mathsf Q_j\!\left\{
 \left|-\ell^{-1}\log\mathsf Q_j(D_q\mid B)-d_q\right|
       >\Omega_\epsilon\right\}\le2\lambda_\epsilon.
 \end{gathered}$$ These are uniform over the retained $j$ and the fixed finite list; the finite union bound is absorbed by the same diagonal. No original cell probability enters the error envelope.

Intersect these cells with the typical localization cells above. Since $C_r$ is fixed by $J$ and the local time grids correspond to $C_q$ up to bounded ambiguity, the estimates are conditional on the local particle. Differentiability gives $(S_q-S_r)/\eta=ks+o(1)$. The residual aspect and excess horizon are $o(1)$ in the new units; coarsen these vanishing depth errors and apply the universal bound to recover a saturated isotropic sequence. Increasing the finite prefix lists gives the homogeneous linear time profile and proves the first alternative.

Suppose henceforth $m>0$. Fix a dyadic $u>0$. On a sufficiently fine finite chain from $u$ to $1$, coherence and the Lipschitz width bounds identify all frames at every depth strictly below $mu$. The terminal orientation $R$ thus determines the frame at $u$ at that precision. Let the gap from $mu$ tend to zero. Both the old and new rectangles then determine each other with vanishing log-cardinality error; recording the same data in the endpoint-prefix frame preserves its score. Taking a diagonal over dyadic $u$, and then using Lipschitz interpolation of the widths and time grids, supplies the common-prefix representation at every $u$.

Finally, if no $\kappa>0$ satisfies <a href="#eq:orientation-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:orientation-growth">[eq:orientation-growth]</a>, there are fixed intervals $(u_j,u_j+h_j)$, chosen after their inner limits, with $$h_j^{-1}\mathsf H(R_{m(u_j+h_j)}\mid T,C_{u_j})\longrightarrow0.$$ Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-localization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-localization">18</a> to the saturated observation at $u_j+h_j$, with $r=u_j$, $b=b(u_j+h_j)$, and $d=e(u_j+h_j)$. Its conditional final shape is exactly isotropic and its local horizon is $h_j$. The error $2\zeta$ in <a href="#eq:classical-local-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-local-first">[eq:classical-local-first]</a> is $o(h_j)$. The other composition errors are made $o(h_j)$ by first fixing the interval and then choosing the inner precision. The local deficits consequently have mean $o(h_j)$ and a uniform lower bound of the same order. Select a local system with deficit $o(h_j)$ and replace $\epsilon$ by $\epsilon^{h_j}$. This produces a saturated isotropic sequence of horizon one, contrary to $m>0$. This contradiction proves the uniform positive constant. It uses neither a positive lower bound for $h_j$ nor one for $u_j$: both are fixed positive numbers at their own inner stage.

The same arguments apply after any homogeneous splitting preserving the path’s scores. Such a path is still a least-aspect extremizer, so the final contradiction again supplies a positive constant. One can also fix a projective orientation chart by a finite split. In that chart use rows $(1,0)$ and $(-R,1)$, with bounded slope $R$ and nested slope prefixes. The row frame and orthogonal frame have bounded condition number, angular and slope precisions are comparable, and the resulting rectangle observations differ by bounded covering multiplicities. All conclusions therefore hold in this row convention. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rem-classical-profile-inheritance"></a>
<div id="rem:classical-profile-inheritance" class="remark">

*Remark 22* (Homogeneous profiles for subsequent local arguments). In either alternative of Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-reduction">21</a>, one may first impose a fixed finite list of pairs $(X_j,Y_j)$ satisfying $|\mathcal Y_j|\le\epsilon^{-A_j}$ for fixed $0\le A_j<\infty$ and all sufficiently small $\epsilon$. The children may be joint grid observations or geometric prefixes. No cardinality bound is imposed on the conditioning variables $X_j$, which may include $T$. Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a> and Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-splitting">16</a>, select a saturated homogeneous component, and only then define its limiting profiles and choose a differentiability or trace point. The profiles need not equal those before this initial splitting. The positive constant in <a href="#eq:orientation-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:orientation-growth">[eq:orientation-growth]</a> is obtained for the selected component by the same least-aspect contradiction.

To spell out the later inheritance, suppose homogeneous probability bins for a parent $P$ and a refinement $Q$ have exponents $d_P,d_Q$ with error $\eta$; both may be conditional on an additional base $W$, including the exact particle. Here $d_P$ is the exponent for the child $P$, and $d_Q$ is the exponent for the joint child $(P,Q)$, identified with $Q$ when $Q$ already records $P$; both children are conditional on $W$. If the exact particle is present, it belongs to $W$. On their common uniform typical set, ratios of joint and parent masses give $$\Pr(Q=q\mid P=p,W=w)
       \le\epsilon^{d_Q-d_P-2\eta},\qquad
 \#\{q:\ (p,q,w)\text{ retained}\}
       \le\epsilon^{-(d_Q-d_P)-2\eta}.$$ These are respectively an upper conditional mass and an upper retained support count; they are stronger than an averaged entropy inequality. If a subsequent normalized law $\nu$ obeys $\nu\le\epsilon^{-\theta}\mu$, discard parent values whose marginal likelihood $\nu_{P,W}/\mu_{P,W}$ is below $\epsilon^\lambda$. Their $\nu$-probability is at most $\epsilon^\lambda$, and on the remaining parents the conditional mass bound loses at most $\theta+\lambda$ in its exponent. Support counts are inherited under restriction. The conditional relative-entropy identity in Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a> supplies the corresponding lower entropy bound with loss $\theta$. There is no factor depending on the number of parent values. Repeat this operation for the fixed finite list, then take a diagonal. For a block of length $h$, choose $\eta,\theta,\lambda=o(h)$ at its inner stage before using $\rho=\epsilon^h$ as the small parameter. Cap regularization may be imposed at the same stage to retain the root bound <a href="#eq:classical-cap-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:classical-cap-bounds">[eq:classical-cap-bounds]</a> under these operations.

</div>

<a id="sec:isotropic"></a>
### Exclusion of isotropic extremizers

We exclude the isotropic alternative in Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-reduction">21</a>. The argument has two geometric steps. Three sufficiently separated slopes would force more point entropy than saturation allows, so one can retain a slope population in a thin strip. That strip supplies an earlier anisotropic aperture; a two-slope projection estimate in the remaining block then forces a conditional time rate greater than one. Throughout both changes of scale we retain uniform conditional probability bounds on particle fibers, as well as the corresponding entropy inequalities.

<a id="stmt-prop-isotropic-exclusion"></a>
<div id="prop:isotropic-exclusion" class="proposition">

**Proposition 23** (Isotropic exclusion). *Suppose that $0<\gamma<1$ and that the classical universal growth rate satisfies $\beta>\gamma$. There is no saturated isotropic system of duration and horizon $1$ furnished by Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-reduction">21</a>, with homogeneous conditional time profile $\mathsf H(C_u\mid T)=su$, $0\leq u\leq1$.*

</div>

Here and below, a limiting assertion about homogeneous probabilities is used on the trimmed laws of Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a>. In particular, it supplies uniform probability bounds on the retained joint population. An exceptional set of small probability in an untrimmed conditional law is not treated as a uniform probability bound. We give the finite estimates that implement this distinction in the present argument.

<a id="pm-h-21"></a>
#### Finite incidence counts and regular increments

In the next two elementary estimates $\rho$ is a mesh size, and all coordinates belong to a fixed bounded set. Constants may depend on that set, but not on $\rho$. A point cell in dimension $d+1$ has coordinates $(c,x)\in\mathbb R\times
\mathbb R^d$, and a slope bin has representative $v\in\mathbb R^d$ and diameter $O(\rho)$. The intercept map is $$\pi_v(c,x)=x-cv.$$

<a id="stmt-lem-isotropic-intercepts"></a>
<div id="lem:isotropic-intercepts" class="lemma">

**Lemma 24** (Counting intercepts on retained fibers). *Suppose an incidence population uses at most $N$ point cells. For every retained exact particle and slope bin incident to it, suppose there are at least $m$ distinct retained time children in the same base cell and slope bin. Suppose further that these children lie on one line of true slope within $O(\rho)$ of the bin representative. Then, for each slope bin, all its retained incidences use at most $CN/m$ intercept cells of side $\rho$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-isotropic-intercepts"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-isotropic-intercepts</summary>

*Proof.* Fix the slope bin. A particle’s intercept $x-cv$ varies by $O(\rho)$ along its retained children. Its distinct time children give distinct point cells. For every occupied intercept cell $b$, choose one particle witnessing an incidence in $b$. The particle’s $m$ point cells have intercepts in a fixed bounded enlargement of $b$. A point cell can belong to the enlargements of only $C$ intercept cells, since $v$ is fixed. Counting the pairs consisting of an occupied intercept cell and one of these witnesses gives $m\#\{b\}\leq CN$. This counts point cells, and imposes no bound on the number or entropy of exact particles. The estimate concerns the population before replica labels are fixed; its support upper bound continues to hold on every subsequent subset. ◻

</details>

<a id="eq:isotropic-pair-comparison"></a>
<a id="eq:isotropic-star-comparison"></a>
<a id="eq:isotropic-pinning"></a>
We will use the following explicit form of the star calculation in Theorem <a href="#thm:finite-conditioning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:finite-conditioning">8</a>. Let $q$ be a normalized point–slope law with actual marginals $\mu,\nu$, and suppose $$q(p,v)\leq K\mu(p)\nu(v),\qquad \mu(p)\leq M^{-1}.
 \label{eq:isotropic-pair-comparison}$$ Sample $r$ slopes independently conditional on $p$. The resulting law $q_r$ satisfies both comparisons <a id="eq:isotropic-one-pair-comparison"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 q_r(p,v_1,\ldots,v_r)&\leq K^r\mu(p)\prod_{i=1}^r\nu(v_i),
 \label{eq:isotropic-star-comparison}\\
 q_r(p,v_1,\ldots,v_r)&\leq
 K^{r-1}q(p,v_j)\prod_{i\ne j}\nu(v_i)\quad(1\leq j\leq r).
 \label{eq:isotropic-one-pair-comparison}
\end{aligned}$$ These follow by multiplying $q(v_i\mid p)\leq K\nu(v_i)$, keeping one factor unestimated for the second inequality. If $\lambda$ is the slope-tuple marginal, then the tuples on which $\lambda/\prod_i\nu(v_i)<L^{-1}$ have $\lambda$-mass at most $L^{-1}$, by summing against the product probability. Outside that set, $$q_r(p\mid v_1,\ldots,v_r)\leq K^r L\mu(p).
 \label{eq:isotropic-pinning}$$ Thus fixing a typical tuple leaves at least $M/(K^rL)$ point cells. An event of independent slope probability $\eta$ has star probability at most $K^r\eta$. All applications below first trim pairs, discard point fibers of inadequate retention, and replace comparison marginals by the actual retained marginals using Theorem <a href="#thm:finite-conditioning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:finite-conditioning">8</a>. Consequently <a href="#eq:isotropic-pair-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-pair-comparison">[eq:isotropic-pair-comparison]</a> holds for the normalized retained law. The fixed labels will always be precisely these two or three slope replicas; no cyclic incidence configuration is used.

<a id="stmt-lem-isotropic-grid-projections"></a>
<div id="lem:isotropic-grid-projections" class="lemma">

**Lemma 25** (Two elementary projection inequalities). *Let $E$ be a set of occupied $\rho$-cells in a fixed bounded region.*

<a id="eq:isotropic-lw"></a>
1.  *In $\mathbb R^3$, let $v_1,v_2,v_3\in\mathbb R^2$ be bounded slopes and put $D=\abs{\det((1,v_1),(1,v_2),(1,v_3))}>0$. If $\pi_{v_i}(E)$ uses at most $N_i$ cells, with bounded enlargements permitted, then $$\abs E^2\leq C D^{-6}N_1N_2N_3.
     \label{eq:isotropic-lw}$$*

<a id="eq:isotropic-two-projections"></a>
2.  *In $\mathbb R^2$, for two bounded scalar slopes $v_1,v_2$ with $\abs{v_1-v_2}\geq\rho^a$, if their intercepts use at most $N_1,N_2$ cells, then $$\abs E\leq C\rho^{-2a}N_1N_2.
     \label{eq:isotropic-two-projections}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-isotropic-grid-projections"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-isotropic-grid-projections</summary>

*Proof.* For the first assertion choose a witness point in each occupied cell, and let $U$ have columns $(1,v_i)$. Replace each $U^{-1}z$ by its $\rho$-grid cell, obtaining a finite grid set $Y$. Since $\norm U\leq C$, each cell of $Y$ accounts for at most $C$ original cells, so $\abs E\leq C\abs Y$. The map $\pi_{v_i}U$ annihilates the $i$th coordinate. On the other two coordinates it is an invertible matrix of determinant of absolute value $D$ and inverse norm at most $C/D$. Thus each original intercept cell accounts for at most $CD^{-2}$ cells of the coordinate projection of $Y$ omitting coordinate $i$. Rounding $U^{-1}z$ adds only $O(\rho)$ to its intercept, because $\pi_{v_i}U$ has bounded norm.

For completeness, the discrete Loomis–Whitney inequality (Loomis and Whitney 1949) <a id="pm-cite-39"></a>[[LoomisWhitney1949](#ref-LoomisWhitney1949)] used here is $$\abs Y^2\leq\abs{\pi_{12}Y}\abs{\pi_{13}Y}\abs{\pi_{23}Y}.$$ To see it, write $f_{ij}$ for the indicators of the three projected sets. The sum $$\sum_{x,y,z}f_{12}(x,y)f_{13}(x,z)f_{23}(y,z)$$ majorizes $\abs Y$. Cauchy–Schwarz first in $z$ bounds this sum by $\sum_{x,y}f_{12}(x,y)\sqrt{b_x c_y}$, where $b_x=\sum_z f_{13}(x,z)$ and $c_y=\sum_z f_{23}(y,z)$. Cauchy–Schwarz in $(x,y)$ bounds its square by $\abs{\pi_{12}Y}(\sum_x b_x)(\sum_y c_y)$. Combining the three projection bounds proves <a href="#eq:isotropic-lw" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-lw">[eq:isotropic-lw]</a>. For the second assertion, the inverse of $(c,x)\mapsto(x-v_1c,x-v_2c)$ has norm at most $C\rho^{-a}$. Each pair of intercept cells therefore meets at most $C\rho^{-2a}$ point cells. Summing over the pairs proves <a href="#eq:isotropic-two-projections" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-two-projections">[eq:isotropic-two-projections]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="eq:isotropic-integrated-information"></a>
Here is the scale-selection fact needed twice below. Let $F_u$, $0\leq u\leq1$, be a filtration and let $X_h$ have normalized entropy at most $Dh$. For an optional fixed conditioning variable $Z$, put $g_h(u)=\mathsf I(X_h;F_u\mid Z)$. Nestedness and the chain rule give $$\int_0^{1-h}\mathsf I(X_h;F_{u+h}\mid Z,F_u)\,du
 =\int_0^{1-h}(g_h(u+h)-g_h(u))\,du
 \leq h\mathsf H(X_h\mid Z)\leq Dh^2.
 \label{eq:isotropic-integrated-information}$$ The middle inequality follows by canceling the two integrals on their common interval. For a sequence $h_j$ with $\sum_j\sqrt{h_j}<\infty$, Markov’s inequality and the elementary Borel–Cantelli argument show that, for almost every $u$, the integrand divided by $h_j$ is at most $\sqrt{h_j}$ eventually. The same points may be required to be differentiability points of any fixed finite collection of Lipschitz entropy profiles.

Our anchored observations are nested only to bounded ambiguity. Formula <a href="#eq:isotropic-integrated-information" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-integrated-information">[eq:isotropic-integrated-information]</a> is applied to their limiting profiles. Its exact finite counterpart can instead use the nested dyadic cells of the physical point $(c,A+cV)$: at every fixed depth $u$ these and $(C_u,[A+C_uV]_u)$ determine each other with a bounded number of possibilities. All entropy differences and conditional mutual informations consequently differ by $O(1/\log(1/\epsilon))$. This error is taken to zero before $h$.

<a id="pm-h-22"></a>
#### The isotropic entropy bounds

<a id="eq:isotropic-terminal-score"></a>
<a id="eq:isotropic-alpha"></a>
For a vector $Y$, write $[Y]_d$ or $Y_d$ for its isotropic grid observation at scale $\epsilon^d$. Assume the system in Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-exclusion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-exclusion">23</a> exists. Write $$O_u=(C_u,[A+C_uV]_u),\qquad O=O_1,\qquad
 \alpha=2-2s+\beta.$$ The exact particle $T$ determines $A,V$. In an anchored observation it leaves only the time label random, so $\mathsf H(O_u\mid T)=su$. Write $\tau$ for the root supremum, equivalently its uniformized cap level in the limiting system. The terminal weight is zero. Saturation therefore gives $$\beta=-\mathsf I(T;O)+2s-\tau=3s-\mathsf H(O)-\tau.
 \label{eq:isotropic-terminal-score}$$ Since $\tau\geq0$ and $\mathsf I(T;O)\geq0$, we have $\beta\leq2s$ and $$\mathsf H(O)\leq3s-\beta,\qquad
 \mathsf H(V_d\mid O)\geq\alpha d\quad(0\leq d\leq1).
 \label{eq:isotropic-alpha}$$ To prove the second inequality, test at duration $1-d$ with velocity depths $(d,d)$ and position depths $(1,1)$. Denote this observation by $\widetilde O$. Its weight is $2d$, and its conditional time entropy is $s(1-d)$. Universality and <a href="#eq:isotropic-terminal-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-terminal-score">[eq:isotropic-terminal-score]</a> imply $$\mathsf I(T;\widetilde O)-\mathsf I(T;O)\geq(2-2s+\beta)d.$$ The pair $(O,V_d)$ determines $\widetilde O$ to bounded ambiguity: transport over a time displacement $O(\epsilon^{1-d})$ with velocity uncertainty $O(\epsilon^d)$ has position error $O(\epsilon)$. The information difference is therefore at most $\mathsf H(V_d\mid O)$ in the limit. At $d=1$ the identical inequality follows from the definition of the root supremum at duration zero. Notice that $\alpha\geq\beta>0$.

<a id="eq:isotropic-velocity-mass"></a>
Homogenize jointly $O$, $V_d$, and their conditioning variables, for the finite lists of depths used below. Formula <a href="#eq:isotropic-alpha" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-alpha">[eq:isotropic-alpha]</a> then means, on the trimmed joint population, $$\mathbb P(V_d=q\mid O=o)\leq\epsilon^{\alpha d-\eta}
 \label{eq:isotropic-velocity-mass}$$ with arbitrarily small $\eta>0$ after taking the inner limit. Indeed the conditional probability exponent is the difference of the homogeneous joint and marginal exponents, and that difference is at least $\alpha d$. The same construction records the time probabilities conditional on the exact particle. It is legitimate on saturated homogeneous parts by the splitting and cap conclusions of Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-reduction">21</a>.

<a id="pm-h-23"></a>
#### Concentration of slopes in a thin strip

<a id="eq:isotropic-low-increment"></a>
<a id="eq:isotropic-first-increment"></a>
The profile $u\mapsto\mathsf H(O_u)$ is nondecreasing and $3$-Lipschitz, starts at zero, and has endpoint at most $3s-\beta$. There is consequently a set of positive measure of regular points $k\in(0,1)$ with $$p:=\partial_k\mathsf H(O_k)<3s-\beta/2.
 \label{eq:isotropic-low-increment}$$ Choose such a point satisfying <a href="#eq:isotropic-integrated-information" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-integrated-information">[eq:isotropic-integrated-information]</a> with $X_h=V_h$, whose entropy is at most $2h$. Along a sequence $h\downarrow0$, $$\mathsf H(O_{k+h}\mid O_k)=(p+o(1))h,\qquad
 \mathsf I(V_h;O_{k+h}\mid O_k)=o(h).
 \label{eq:isotropic-first-increment}$$

<a id="eq:isotropic-first-graph"></a>
Inside a typical $O_k$-cell translate time and position to the cell center and dilate both by $\epsilon^{-k}$. Put $\rho=\epsilon^h$, and call the child point observation $P$. Bounded changes from anchored to physical point cells do not affect any exponent. Homogeneity, the conditional fiber rule, and Lemma <a href="#lem:zero-information" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:zero-information">6</a>, followed by the actual-marginal conclusion of Theorem <a href="#thm:finite-conditioning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:finite-conditioning">8</a>, give a normalized retained pair law $q(P,V_h)$ satisfying the following bounds, with $e=e(h)\to0$: $$\begin{aligned}
 \#\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}P&\leq\rho^{-(p+e)},&
 \mu(P=z)&\leq\rho^{p-e},&
 q&\leq\rho^{-e}\mu\otimes\nu.
 \label{eq:isotropic-first-graph}
\end{aligned}$$ These conclusions hold outside base cells of probability tending to zero. One may enlarge $e(h)$ to absorb all fixed numerical constants and all $o(1)$ errors in <a href="#eq:isotropic-first-increment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-first-increment">[eq:isotropic-first-increment]</a>. To be explicit about the conditioning: the mean information in block units tends to zero; discard base cells where it exceeds its square root, apply the likelihood-ratio truncation in each remaining cell, and discard point fibers losing more than half their mass. Homogeneous joint and marginal bounds then supply the two point estimates in <a href="#eq:isotropic-first-graph" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-first-graph">[eq:isotropic-first-graph]</a>. This procedure introduces only another quantity tending to zero into $e$.

<a id="eq:isotropic-first-intercepts"></a>
We also trim on the exact particle fibers before sampling replicas. A retained time child, conditional on $T,C_k$ in the original base law, has probability at most $\rho^{s-e}$. Lift all pair restrictions to that law, and discard particle fibers whose conditional retention there is below $\rho^e$. If the pair restrictions have total retention $m_0$, these discarded fibers have normalized retained mass at most $\rho^e/m_0$, by <a href="#eq:retention-fibers" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:retention-fibers">[eq:retention-fibers]</a>. Here $m_0$ is bounded below before this step; more generally a subpower lower bound is absorbed by increasing $e$. Each remaining particle has at least $\rho^{-s+2e}$ distinct retained time children, by dividing its retained mass by the original child mass bound. Given $T,C_k$, the anchored base observation is fixed. Thus this is a statement in the very same base cell used for $P$; no particle entropy bound is involved. For a slope bin of size $\rho$, all these points have intercept within $O(\rho)$ of the particle’s intercept. Lemma <a href="#lem:isotropic-intercepts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:isotropic-intercepts">24</a> gives $$\#\pi_v(\text{retained neighbors of }v)
 \leq C\rho^{-(p-s+3e)}.
 \label{eq:isotropic-first-intercepts}$$ Apply one final simultaneous marginal core to this pruned law. Its retention is at least one half, by Lemma <a href="#lem:marginal-core" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:marginal-core">7</a>, and the pair comparison again uses its actual point and slope marginals. Increasing $e$ absorbs the finite factors, so <a href="#eq:isotropic-first-graph" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-first-graph">[eq:isotropic-first-graph]</a> and <a href="#eq:isotropic-first-intercepts" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-first-intercepts">[eq:isotropic-first-intercepts]</a> hold together for this final pair law. The core need not preserve the rich particle fibers: the intercept support bound was established before it, and survives by support inclusion. Use this same order of operations in the two-replica application below.

Fix $\vartheta>0$ so small that $12\vartheta<\beta/8$. We claim that, in every retained base cell, some strip of thickness $C\rho^\vartheta$ has slope mass at least $\rho^{5e}$, after enlarging $e(h)\to0$ once more. If all such strips had mass less than $\rho^{5e}$, two independent slopes would have distance at least $\rho^\vartheta$ except with probability $C\rho^{5e}$; a ball of that radius is contained in a strip of comparable thickness. Conditional on the first two, the third would lie at distance at least $\rho^\vartheta$ from their line except with the same probability. Hence, outside an independent event of probability $C\rho^{5e}$, $$\abs{\det((1,v_1),(1,v_2),(1,v_3))}\geq\rho^{2\vartheta}.$$ For the three-replica star, <a href="#eq:isotropic-star-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-star-comparison">[eq:isotropic-star-comparison]</a> bounds the exceptional probability by $C\rho^{2e}$. Choose $L=\rho^{-e}$ in <a href="#eq:isotropic-pinning" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-pinning">[eq:isotropic-pinning]</a>. A good tuple then leaves a point population of at least $\rho^{-p+5e}$ cells, and each projection has the support bound <a href="#eq:isotropic-first-intercepts" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-first-intercepts">[eq:isotropic-first-intercepts]</a>. Lemma <a href="#lem:isotropic-grid-projections" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:isotropic-grid-projections">25</a> implies $$2p-10e\leq3(p-s+3e)+12\vartheta+o_{\rho\to0}(1),
 \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
 p\geq3s-12\vartheta-19e-o_{\rho\to0}(1).$$ This contradicts <a href="#eq:isotropic-low-increment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-low-increment">[eq:isotropic-low-increment]</a> for all sufficiently small $h$, with $\rho$ taken sufficiently small afterwards. We take $e>0$ even when an error vanishes, so that the exceptional probabilities above tend to zero in this inner limit.

Choose one such strip measurably in each base cell, using a finite grid menu with bounded enlargement, and restrict incidences to it. The total retention is at least $\rho^{5e}$ times the mass of the retained base cells. No strip index is fixed globally: its index is a function of $O_k$ and will be included in the earlier test through that base label. With <a id="eq:isotropic-strip"></a>$$l=\vartheta h,
 \qquad \abs{V\cdot n(O_k)-w(O_k)}\leq C\epsilon^l,
 \label{eq:isotropic-strip}$$ round the unit normal and offset at precision $\epsilon^l$. This changes $C$ only. The Radon–Nikodym bound for the restriction is $\epsilon^{-O(eh)}$. Since $\vartheta$ is fixed and $e(h)\to0$, its normalized logarithmic cost is $o(l)$.

The bins for $O$, the required $V_d$, and the particle-conditional time probabilities are trimmed before this restriction. Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a> and its conditional retention rule therefore preserve their exponents with errors $o(l)$, including the particle-conditional time exponents and <a href="#eq:isotropic-velocity-mass" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-velocity-mass">[eq:isotropic-velocity-mass]</a>. The absolute root cap bound gives $\tau_{\rm new}\leq\tau+o(l)$. The terminal numerator before subtraction of $\tau$ changes by $o(l)$, because its observation and conditional time exponents were recorded. Consequently the new terminal score is at least $\beta-o(l)$, and universality bounds it above by $\beta+o(l)$. We henceforth use this retained law and its own root supremum; its terminal score is $\beta+o(l)$.

<a id="pm-h-24"></a>
#### An earlier anisotropic observation

Take $h$ small enough that $k<1-l$, and put $a=1-l$. In the frame with normal $n=n(O_k)$ and tangent $n^\perp$, form <a id="eq:isotropic-earlier-test"></a>$$B=\bigl(O_k,O_a,[(A+C_aV)\cdot n]_1\bigr).
 \label{eq:isotropic-earlier-test}$$ The coarse observation $O_a$ locates tangent position to depth $a$; its normal position is additionally located to depth $1$. The strip supplies normal velocity to depth $l$, and tangent velocity is bounded. The rounded frame is known to depth $l$. Thus $B$, with boundedly many additional data cells if necessary, is an admissible aperture with velocity depths $(0,l)$, duration $a$, horizon $1$, and weight $(1-\gamma)l$.

<a id="eq:isotropic-last-time"></a>
It is determined by $O$ to bounded ambiguity. Indeed $O$ coarsens to $O_k,O_a$ to bounded ambiguity, hence determines the chosen strip up to the same fixed number of choices. For its fine normal position use <a id="eq:isotropic-normal-transport"></a>$$(A+C_aV)\cdot n=(A+C_1V)\cdot n+(C_a-C_1)w+O(\epsilon),
 \label{eq:isotropic-normal-transport}$$ where the error is bounded by $C\epsilon^a\epsilon^l=C\epsilon$. Conversely every component of the anchored $B$ is fixed by $(T,C_a)$, since $C_a$ fixes $C_k$. In particular, $$\mathsf H(O\mid T,B)=sl+o(l).
 \label{eq:isotropic-last-time}$$ The conditional time profile on the retained law follows from the ratios of the recorded probabilities at depths $a$ and $1$; the strip restriction costs $o(l)$ on typical particle fibers. Adjoining standard data cells to $B$ uses deterministic functions of $(T,C_a)$ and leaves this argument unchanged.

<a id="eq:isotropic-information-saving"></a>
We prove the information saving $$\mathsf I(T;O)-\mathsf I(T;B)\geq sl-o(l).
 \label{eq:isotropic-information-saving}$$ The main point is a lower bound for the last block’s joint time and tangent position entropy.

<a id="pm-h-25"></a>
#### Slope bounds inside the last block

For $0\leq u\leq1$ let $F_u$ record, in addition to $B$, time to depth $a+ul$ and tangent position at that time to the same depth. Within a $B$-cell translate time and tangent position to their depth-$a$ centers and dilate both by $\epsilon^{-a}$. The resulting coordinates are bounded, the new mesh parameter is $\rho_*=\epsilon^l$, and the tangent slope $X=V\cdot n^\perp$ remains bounded. The filtration $F_u$ has capacity $2$ per unit depth. Its base $F_0$ adds at most bounded information to $B$, and $F_1$ is determined by $(O,B)$ to bounded ambiguity. Given $T,B$, its conditional entropy profile is $su+o(1)$ in block units, because its new data are fixed by the particle and the time cell.

<a id="eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent"></a>
For each fixed $d\in(0,1]$ and each fixed filtration depth $u$, the retained conditional tangent slope law satisfies $$\mathbb P\bigl(X\in J\mid B,F_u\bigr)
 \leq \rho_*^{\alpha d-o(1)}
 \quad\text{for intervals }J\text{ of length }\rho_*^d.
 \label{eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent}$$ Here, as throughout, the inequality is uniform on a further trimmed subprobability, followed by normalization on fibers of subpower retention. We verify this transfer, since a bare conditional entropy inequality would not suffice.

First apply <a href="#eq:isotropic-velocity-mass" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-velocity-mass">[eq:isotropic-velocity-mass]</a> at velocity depth $dl$ on the jointly trimmed law. Adjoin the finite list of labels $(B,F_u)$ to $O$. Each such list has at most $K$ possible values given $O$, where $K$ is fixed when the list is fixed. For a positive tolerance $\zeta$, discard realized values whose conditional likelihood given $O$ is below $\rho_*^\zeta$. Their total probability is at most $K\rho_*^\zeta$. On the remaining values, conditioning on the adjoined label multiplies a conditional velocity-bin probability by at most $\rho_*^{-\zeta}$. More explicitly, write $\kappa_h=O(e(h)/\vartheta)$ for an upper bound on all prior restriction costs in last-block units. Whenever a retained subprobability has mass at least $\rho_*^{\kappa_h}$, discard conditioning fibers whose retention is below $\rho_*^{\kappa_h+\zeta}$. Formula <a href="#eq:retention-fibers" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:retention-fibers">[eq:retention-fibers]</a> bounds their normalized retained mass by $\rho_*^\zeta$; normalization costs at most $\kappa_h+\zeta$ in the conditional exponent. For the fixed finite number of such operations, the total extra loss is $C\kappa_h+C\zeta$. It tends to zero by first taking the inner limit, then $h\downarrow0$ and $\zeta\downarrow0$. It incurs no factor involving the number of $O$-cells or $B$-cells.

For a fixed $B$-cell, its normal strip has thickness $O(\epsilon^l)$. Its intersection with a tangent interval of length $\epsilon^{dl}$ meets only $C$ velocity grid cells of depth $dl$, since $d\leq1$. Thus the same uniform upper bound holds for this tangent interval conditional on $O,B,F_u$. Averaging over compatible $O$-labels gives <a href="#eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent">[eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent]</a>, with the explicit extra exponent loss $\zeta$ and the retention losses. Taking those losses to zero proves the asserted form. Every bound is imposed on the retained joint population before averaging; no exponentially small bound for untrimmed exceptional probabilities is needed.

We now make the order of limits precise. Fix $\vartheta$ first. Choose the regular sequence $h\downarrow0$ above. For each fixed $h$ record the finite lists of $O,V_d$, and particle-conditional time bins before the strip choice. Construct $B,F_u$ and perform the transfer just proved after choosing the strip. The later increment binnings are performed after this transfer. Take $\epsilon$ small enough that all inner mesh and bin errors, divided by $l$, tend to zero. A diagonal, with $h\downarrow0$, gives last-block systems with parameter $\rho_*$, exact limiting time profile $su$, and <a href="#eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent">[eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent]</a> at a countable dense list of $(u,d)$. Bounded coordinate capacities extend the entropy profiles to other depths. For the conditional mass bound at a subsequently chosen fixed filtration depth $u$, repeat the direct $O\to(B,F_u)$ determination and likelihood truncation above; it has the same bounded multiplicity. A requested slope depth $d$ is obtained by using recorded depths $d'<d$ and then letting $d'\uparrow d$. Thus the mass bound is inherited from that comparison, independently of continuity of entropy. A later increment length $r>0$ is held fixed before each inner limit; only then is $r\downarrow0$. Thus errors $o(l)$ from the first construction are never divided by an unchosen infinitesimal $r$. No bound on $\mathsf H(B)/l$ is asserted or needed.

<a id="pm-h-26"></a>
#### Two-slope expansion and the score contradiction

<a id="eq:isotropic-last-entropy"></a>
We show, in the last-block limits just constructed, that $$\mathsf H(F_1\mid B)\geq2s
 \quad\text{in units }\log(1/\rho_*).
 \label{eq:isotropic-last-entropy}$$ Write $f(u)=\mathsf H(F_u\mid B)$ in these units. It is nondecreasing and $2$-Lipschitz, with $f(0)=0$. Apply <a href="#eq:isotropic-integrated-information" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-integrated-information">[eq:isotropic-integrated-information]</a> to $X_r$, the tangent slope prefix of depth $r$, conditional on $B$. Its entropy is at most $r$, so the integrated mutual information is at most $r^2$. At almost every regular interior $u$ there is consequently a sequence $r\downarrow0$ for which the increment has negligible information about $X_r$, in units of its own length.

In a typical $(B,F_u)$-cell let $P_1$ be the time–tangent-position increment, at mesh $\rho=\rho_*^r$. Homogenize its probabilities and the pair with $X_r$. Let $p_1$ denote its point exponent. The likelihood-ratio and actual-marginal steps used in <a href="#eq:isotropic-first-graph" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-first-graph">[eq:isotropic-first-graph]</a> give, with $e\to0$ along the regular sequence, $$\#\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}P_1\leq\rho^{-(p_1+e)},\qquad
 \mu_1(z)\leq\rho^{p_1-e},\qquad
 q_1\leq\rho^{-e}\mu_1\otimes\nu_1.$$ The particle-conditional time exponent is $s$. Trimming exact particle fibers and applying Lemma <a href="#lem:isotropic-intercepts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:isotropic-intercepts">24</a> therefore bounds every retained intercept support by $C\rho^{-(p_1-s+3e)}$.

Fix $0<a_0<1$. Formula <a href="#eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent">[eq:isotropic-inherited-tangent]</a>, at depth $a_0r$, gives the actual retained slope marginal the interval bound $\nu_1(J)\leq\rho^{\alpha a_0-o(1)}$ for intervals of length $\rho^{a_0}$. The two-replica star consequently has $\abs{v_1-v_2}\geq\rho^{a_0}$ outside a set of probability $O(\rho^{\alpha a_0-2e-o(1)})$. Since $\alpha>0$, this probability tends to zero by taking $r$ sufficiently far along the regular sequence and then the inner small-parameter limit. Pin a good tuple using <a href="#eq:isotropic-pinning" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-pinning">[eq:isotropic-pinning]</a> with $L=\rho^{-e}$. At least $\rho^{-p_1+4e}$ point cells remain. Their original intercept support bounds are still valid. Formula <a href="#eq:isotropic-two-projections" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-two-projections">[eq:isotropic-two-projections]</a> now gives $$p_1-4e\leq2(p_1-s+3e)+2a_0+o(1),
 \qquad p_1\geq2s-2a_0-10e-o(1).$$ First let the regular-increment errors vanish, and then let $a_0\downarrow0$. This proves the lower entropy rate $p_1\geq2s$.

Here is why the cellwise argument yields $f'(u)\geq2s$ almost everywhere, even if new homogeneous parts have different point exponents. Their conditional increment entropies average to $f(u+r)-f(u)$, and all have capacity at most $2r+o(r)$. If $f'(u)<2s$ by a fixed amount, a positive fraction of the conditional population must have point exponents below $2s$ by a smaller fixed amount. The mean conditional information is $o(r)$, so Markov’s inequality removes a vanishing fraction while imposing the pair comparison above. The uniform time and slope bounds survive on the remaining typical fibers. Homogenizing a finite list costs a subpower, and thus selects a part with all these properties and the same fixed deficit. The preceding statement about inherited bounds can also be checked directly: in a fixed conditional cell, restriction to a part $E$ of mass $m$ gives $\nu_E(J)\leq m^{-1}\nu(J)$. Here $m=\rho^{o(1)}$, so the slope exponent is preserved. Discard exact particle fibers retaining less than $m\rho^\zeta$ of their original conditional time law; their normalized retained mass is at most $\rho^\zeta$. The time exponent therefore loses at most $\log_{1/\rho}(1/m)+\zeta=o(1)+\zeta$. These estimates justify the simultaneous selection without any count of conditioning cells. The two-slope inequality contradicts the fixed deficit. Since $f$ is Lipschitz, integrating $f'(u)\geq2s$ proves <a href="#eq:isotropic-last-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-last-entropy">[eq:isotropic-last-entropy]</a>.

Returning to the original units, <a href="#eq:isotropic-last-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-last-entropy">[eq:isotropic-last-entropy]</a> and the determination of $F_1$ by $(O,B)$ give $$\mathsf H(O\mid B)\geq2sl-o(l).$$ Together with <a href="#eq:isotropic-last-time" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-last-time">[eq:isotropic-last-time]</a>, this gives $\mathsf I(T;O\mid B)\geq sl-o(l)$. Since $\mathsf H(B\mid O)=o(l)$, the information chain rule proves <a href="#eq:isotropic-information-saving" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:isotropic-information-saving">[eq:isotropic-information-saving]</a>.

Finally let $Q_G$ denote the undivided score numerator, including subtraction of the root supremum of the retained law. The same root supremum occurs for $B$ and $O$. Their time entropies differ by $sl+o(l)$, so $$\begin{aligned}
 Q_B-Q_O
 &=(1-\gamma)l+\mathsf I(T;O)-\mathsf I(T;B)-2sl+o(l)\\
 &\geq(1-\gamma-s)l-o(l).
\end{aligned}$$ On the other hand terminal saturation and the universal duration bound give $Q_O=\beta+o(l)$ and $Q_B\leq\beta(1-l)+o(l)$. Divide by $l$ and pass through the specified limits to obtain $$1-\gamma-s\leq-\beta,
 \qquad s\geq1+\beta-\gamma>1.$$ This contradicts the scalar time capacity $s\leq1$ and proves Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-exclusion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-exclusion">23</a>.

<a id="sec:characteristic-plane"></a>
### The matched plane and its traces

The trace construction applies to the matched process of Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-reduction">21</a> for any least aspect $m>0$. In the proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:classical-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:classical-growth">15</a>, this is the alternative remaining under $\beta>\gamma$ after Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-exclusion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-exclusion">23</a>. Its saturated apertures have shapes $$(b(u),a(u))=(b(u),b(u)+mu),\qquad 0<u<1,$$ with horizon $L=1+m$, a Lipschitz function $b$, and $0\le-b'\le1+m$ almost everywhere. Their labels use one common time filtration and the prefixes of one orientation, as supplied by Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-reduction">21</a>.

<a id="pm-h-28"></a>
#### The information profile and the contact relation

<a id="eq:trace-variables"></a>
<a id="eq:trace-domain"></a>
Work in one bounded slope chart, using the row frame from the end of Proposition <a href="#prop:isotropic-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:isotropic-reduction">21</a>. The particle $T$ carries $(V,A)$. At label time $v$ put $E_v=(C_v,R_{mv})$ and set $$\label{eq:trace-variables}
 X=V_1,\qquad Y=A_1+C_vX,\qquad
 W=V_2-R_{mv}X,\qquad
 Z=A_2+C_vV_2-R_{mv}Y.$$ For data depths $\mathbf L=(L_X,L_Y,L_W,L_Z)$ let $O(\mathbf L,v)$ record $E_v$ and these four variables at their respective grid precisions. We allow the depths to vary on compact subsets of $$\label{eq:trace-domain}
 \begin{aligned}
 L_Y-L_X&\le v,& L_W-L_X&\le mv,\\
 L_Z-L_W&\le v,& L_Z-L_Y&\le mv,
 \qquad 0<v<1.
 \end{aligned}$$ They may range over any fixed bounded extension of the depths of the apertures; a negative depth gives only boundedly many bins.

When $m=1$, impose $L_Y=L_W=L_U$ at this point and regard $U=(Y,W)$ as one datum of capacity two, with $\mathbf L=(L_X,L_U,L_Z)$. The profile and all the trace statements below are then defined on this grouped domain, and the middle datum has one joint trace rate.

<a id="eq:matched-aperture-region"></a>
The finite matched apertures occupy a particular plane in the depth domain. At time $u$, an aperture with common depth $i$ has velocity depths $(i,i+mu)$ and position depths $(i+u,i+(1+m)u)$. Define <a id="eq:matched-plane"></a>$$\label{eq:matched-plane}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pi_m(i,u)&=(i,i+u,i+mu,i+(1+m)u,u), &&m\ne1,\\
 \Pi_1(i,u)&=(i,i+u,i+2u,u), &&m=1.
 \end{aligned}$$ The coordinate orders are $(L_X,L_Y,L_W,L_Z,v)$ and $(L_X,L_U,L_Z,v)$, respectively. The finite matched observation is $O(\mathbf L,u)$ with $(\mathbf L,u)=\Pi_m(i,u)$. Every inequality in <a href="#eq:trace-domain" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:trace-domain">[eq:trace-domain]</a> is an equality on this plane. The part corresponding to admissible apertures is $$\label{eq:matched-aperture-region}
 \mathcal A_m=\{(i,u):0<u<1,\quad i\ge0,\quad i+(1+m)u\le L\}.$$ The path observations are the points $i=b(u)$, up to the zero-cost grid choices already established for the common row frame. The bounded extension of the data depths gives a neighborhood within this plane across the boundary of $\mathcal A_m$. The full depth domain still has the one-sided faces in <a href="#eq:trace-domain" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:trace-domain">[eq:trace-domain]</a>.

We now make one homogeneous choice before defining the limiting functions. Start with a countable dense family of admissible depth configurations and the countable family of all finite tuples formed from their observations, including the versions conditional on $T$. Also include the score observations at dyadic path times. At each stage use only a finite initial list and finitely many path times. Apply the cap regularization of Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-cap-regularization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-cap-regularization">17</a>, then the uniform bins of Lemma <a href="#lem:homogenization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:homogenization">5</a>. By Lemma <a href="#lem:classical-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:classical-splitting">16</a>, select typical components whose finitely many score deficits lie under one deterministic vanishing envelope. Let the lists grow and the bin meshes shrink slowly with the precision. The diagonal of Lemma <a href="#lem:profile-diagonal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:profile-diagonal">10</a>, as in Remark <a href="#rem:classical-profile-inheritance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rem:classical-profile-inheritance">22</a>, gives one sequence of finite laws $p_\epsilon$ carrying all the listed homogeneous profiles. Every listed path observation is saturated along this sequence in the limit. Only after this sequence is chosen do we define $$f_\epsilon(\mathbf L,v)=\mathsf I^{p_\epsilon}(T;O(\mathbf L,v)),\qquad
 S_\epsilon(v)=\mathsf H^{p_\epsilon}(C_v\mid T).$$ Lemma <a href="#lem:profile-diagonal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:profile-diagonal">10</a> and the box comparisons below give a limiting profile $f$ on <a href="#eq:trace-domain" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:trace-domain">[eq:trace-domain]</a>; write $S$ for the limiting time profile. The finite root suprema are bounded, so pass to a further subsequence and write $\tau$ for the limit of $\tau_L(T)$. The limiting score along the path is continuous: $b,S$ are Lipschitz, and the box comparisons give continuity of $f$ along $\Pi_m(b(u),u)$. Saturation at the dense dyadic times therefore extends to every $0<u<1$. The positive constant in <a href="#eq:orientation-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:orientation-growth">[eq:orientation-growth]</a> is obtained for this selected component by the least-aspect argument; it need not be the constant before the split. The symbols $f,S,\tau$ below refer to this component, whose profiles may differ from those before the split. Later, a trace point and a positive block length will be chosen for this fixed $f$ before the required real-depth bins and finite precision are selected.

<a id="eq:matched-plane-profile"></a>
<a id="eq:closure-obstacle"></a>
The information of a matched aperture is therefore the restriction $$\label{eq:matched-plane-profile}
 \Phi(i,u)=f\bigl(\Pi_m(i,u)\bigr).$$ The weight of the aperture at $(i,u)$ is $2i+(1-\gamma)mu$. Rearranging the universal score bound and using saturation on the path gives $$\Phi(i,u)\ge
 2i+(1-\gamma)mu+2S(u)-\beta u-\tau,
 \qquad\text{with equality when }i=b(u).
 \label{eq:closure-obstacle}$$ We call this equality the contact relation. The local projection arguments will constrain the information rates at almost every plane point with $i>0$, while saturation is known on this particular contact curve. We therefore need both local affine approximations on the plane and control of how the rates cross the curve.

At a differentiability point of $b$ put $p=-b'(u)$. A direction $V_c=\partial_u-c\partial_i$ preserves the data depth $i+cu$, and its crossing factor at the contact curve is $p-c$. Here the clocks are $0,1,m,1+m$, with the two middle clocks grouped when $m=1$. Figure <a href="#fig:characteristic-plane" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="fig:characteristic-plane">2</a> shows these relations.

<figure id="fig:characteristic-plane">

<figcaption>The resolution triangle $i ≥ 0$, $u ≥ 0$, $i + (1+m)u ≤ L$ and the characteristic directions $di/du =  − c$, where $c ∈ {0, 1, m, 1 + m}$. Each direction $V_{c} = ∂_{u} − c∂_{i}$ preserves the corresponding data depth $i + cu$. The explicit example on the left has $m = 2$ and contact slope $p =  − b′(u) = 3/2$; its two axes use different drawing scales. The right panel uses equal scales for the local increments. The signs mark $± (i−b(u)) > 0$. At a transverse contact, $p ≠ c$, the crossing factor is $V_{c}(i−b(u)) = p − c$. Existence of one-sided traces and the associated jump identities use the hypotheses of Lemma <a href="#lem:curve-traces" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:curve-traces">28</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

```latex
    \node[font=\normalsize] at (0.80,0.75) {$+$};
    \node[font=\normalsize] at (-0.85,-0.73) {$-$};
    \node[font=\footnotesize,anchor=west] at (0.54,1.39)
      {$V_c=\partial_u-c\partial_i$};
  \end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Right panel ("Directions at a contact point"): axes $\Delta i$ (horizontal) and $\Delta u$ (vertical); dashed tangent line with negative slope labeled "tangent: $\Delta i = -p\,\Delta u$"; four directional vectors $V_c = \partial_u - c\partial_i$ extending from origin labeled $c = 0$, $c = 1$, $c = m = 2$, and $c = 1 + m = 3$; regions on either side of tangent line marked with "$+$" and "$-$".

Ambient almost-everywhere differentiability does not solve the local problem: the entire matched plane lies on the boundary of <a href="#eq:trace-domain" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:trace-domain">[eq:trace-domain]</a>, and could lie in the ambient exceptional set. We will obtain the needed traces from the signs of the mixed derivatives. Their affine approximation will produce finite entropy blocks for Section <a href="#sec:rate-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:rate-transfer">7</a>; their measure identities will later pass those rate constraints to the contact curve.

Here are the properties of $f$ supplied by the finite observations. It is locally Lipschitz and nondecreasing in every coordinate; its data derivatives lie between zero and the capacity of that coordinate. Its label derivative is nonnegative and locally bounded. Every mixed derivative involving two different coordinates, including a data coordinate and $v$, is a nonpositive distribution in the interior. We verify the signs, especially the one involving the label.

<a id="eq:trace-frame-change"></a>
Advance $v$ to $v'>v$. Write $a=C_{v'}-C_v$ and $r=R_{mv}-R_{mv'}$. Nested labels give $|a|\lesssim\epsilon^v$, $|r|\lesssim\epsilon^{mv}$, and the change of data is $$\label{eq:trace-frame-change}
 X'=X,\quad Y'=Y+aX,\quad W'=W+rX,\quad
 Z'=Z+aW+rY+arX.$$ In a data box, the uncertainty in $Y'$ is bounded by a constant times $\epsilon^{L_Y}+\epsilon^{v+L_X}$, and that in $W'$ by a constant times $\epsilon^{L_W}+\epsilon^{mv+L_X}$. The uncertainty in $Z'$ is bounded by $$C\bigl(\epsilon^{L_Z}+\epsilon^{v+L_W}
       +\epsilon^{mv+L_Y}+\epsilon^{(1+m)v+L_X}\bigr).$$ The four inequalities in <a href="#eq:trace-domain" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:trace-domain">[eq:trace-domain]</a> bound these by the respective target widths. The inverse shear has the same bounds. Consequently, conditional on $E_{v'}$, the old and new data descriptions at fixed admissible depths determine each other with bounded ambiguity. This assertion also holds at each corner of any coordinate rectangle contained in the domain.

At fixed labels, a data refinement is determined by the particle and labels. Its increase in particle information is therefore exactly its conditional entropy, up to the bounded bin ambiguities. A further data refinement can only decrease this conditional entropy. For a label refinement, express both ends of the data refinement in the old frame conditional on $E_{v'}$, using <a href="#eq:trace-frame-change" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:trace-frame-change">[eq:trace-frame-change]</a>. The two information increments being compared are then $$\mathsf H(D_{\rm fine}\mid E_v,D_{\rm coarse})
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \mathsf H(D_{\rm fine}\mid E_{v'},D_{\rm coarse}),$$ up to $O(1/\log(1/\epsilon))$; the latter is no larger than the former. Here $D_{\rm coarse}$ includes every other data coordinate. Thus each mixed rectangle difference of $f_\epsilon$ is nonpositive up to an error vanishing as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Passing to the limiting profile proves the mixed signs, first for rectangle differences and then for distributions, by integrating the rectangle inequalities against nonnegative smooth test functions and shrinking the rectangles.

Refining a scalar datum by $d$ costs at most $d+O(1/\log(1/\epsilon))$ in normalized entropy; for $U$ the bound is $2d+O(1/\log(1/\epsilon))$. Advancing the labels by $d$ costs at most $(1+m)d+O(1/\log(1/\epsilon))$. The old data are recoverable from the new observation, and the change of data conditional on the new labels has bounded ambiguity. These facts give monotonicity and the asserted Lipschitz bounds.
