For each such $Q$, let $\mathcal T_{J,Q}\subset\mathcal T_J$ consist of the atoms at this $P$ whose transported positions are within $C_0 R s$ of that cell, where $R=\epsilon^{-\theta}$ and $C_0$ is a fixed constant large enough for the transport and cell-boundary enlargements. Absorb $C_0$ into the fixed constants in the coherence estimates. Write $N_{J,Q}=\#\mathcal T_{J,Q}$ and $$h_{J,Q}=\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_{J,Q}}c_Tg_T.$$ Let $Z=Z(J,O)$ add to $Q$ the output position at precision $\sigma$ along $n(P)$ in the elongated case and in both directions in the isotropic case. These labels are functions of the geometric endpoint observation and the fixed grid and normal table; they do not include the arbitrary extra labels carried by $\omega$. On the full sample space write $Q(\omega)=Q(J(\omega),O(\omega))$ and likewise for $Z(\omega)$.

<a id="eq:repayment-winning-candidate-tail"></a>
<a id="eq:repayment-winning-candidate"></a>
The winning superposition $h_J$ is fixed, while $h_{J,Q}$ depends on $Q$. On every retained endpoint site, the buffered property and the transport order fixed after the winning map give $$|\mathfrak a_O(h_J)-\mathfrak a_O(h_{J,Q(J,O)})|
       \le C_{\rm tr}\epsilon^{A_{\rm tr}}\|f\|_2 .
 \label{eq:repayment-winning-candidate-tail}$$ The coefficient and count comparison in the original construction is still available: the squared summed tail has exponent beyond $B+1$ after the $Q_0$ count loss. For the score we use the stronger information that the winning amplitude itself has the floor <a href="#eq:repayment-winner-floor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-winner-floor">[eq:repayment-winner-floor]</a>. Set $$q_{\rm tr}=
 \frac{C_{\rm tr}S_\epsilon}{1-q_0}
       \epsilon^{A_{\rm tr}-A_0/2}.$$ The choices $B>2A+3Q_0+10$, $A>A_0/2+1$, and <a href="#eq:repayment-transport-order" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-transport-order">[eq:repayment-transport-order]</a>, together with the subpower bound on $S_\epsilon$, make $q_{\rm tr}\to0$ at fixed finite parameters. Choose $\epsilon$ small enough that $q_{\rm tr}<1/2$. Equations <a href="#eq:repayment-winner-floor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-winner-floor">[eq:repayment-winner-floor]</a> and <a href="#eq:repayment-winning-candidate-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-winning-candidate-tail">[eq:repayment-winning-candidate-tail]</a> then imply $$m_O(h_J)\le(1-q_{\rm tr})^{-2}m_O(h_{J,Q(J,O)}).
 \label{eq:repayment-winning-candidate}$$ In particular $m_O(h_{J,Q(J,O)})>0$ and $N_{J,Q(J,O)}>0$ on every retained sample. Replacing the winning mass by this candidate-truncated mass costs at most <a id="eq:repayment-candidate-score-cost"></a>$$3\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(1/(1-q_{\rm tr})\right)
 \label{eq:repayment-candidate-score-cost}$$ in the score’s mass term. This cost is included in $\eta$.

<a id="eq:repayment-candidate-mass"></a>
For a fixed $J,Q$, define $$m_Z=\sum_{\substack{O\mapsto Z\\ O\ {\rm in\ the\ localizer}}}
             m_O(h_{J,Q}) .
 \label{eq:repayment-candidate-mass}$$ The sum uses every geometric output site mapping to $Z$ once, with the allowed bounded lattice multiplicity and its chosen site-dependent amplitude; it does not sum over copies of a site in $\Omega$. Because $Z$ includes $Q$, the entire fiber uses one input $h_{J,Q}$. Thus $m_Z$ is exactly the candidate-truncated mass to which the next lemma applies. The input $h_{J,Q}$ varies with $Q$. These masses are used only to bound an entropy expression under $\pi$; they are not treated as a new admissible packet system for a growth estimate.

<a id="pm-h-61"></a>
#### The repayment estimate

The prepared cut supplies $\mu$ and the capacity bound <a href="#eq:velocity-fiber-regularity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:velocity-fiber-regularity">[eq:velocity-fiber-regularity]</a>. The remaining estimate shows that a near-maximal endpoint score increases the fine-velocity credit.

<a id="stmt-prop-finite-repayment"></a>
<div id="prop:finite-repayment" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:repayment-saturation-input"></a>
<a id="eq:finite-packet-repayment"></a>
**Proposition 48** (Finite packet repayment). *Fix $0<\gamma<1$ and a comparison rate $b_{\mathrm q}\in[0,1]$. For the prepared cut constructed above, let $\eta$ bound the composition budget $\mathcal R$, $\theta+\xi+(\log C)/\ell$, all logarithmic class, winner, tail, and label costs, the current mean $\mathbb E_\pi d_1$, and the finite classical growth error on the fixed class of lines, after a fixed increase of $C_*$. The selected endpoint and earlier replacement and composition deficits required in the construction are at most $\eta$ on their specified current laws, including the two conditional prediction marginals. The common shape and count bins have width at most $\eta$; in the isotropic case they also give the error in <a href="#eq:repayment-isotropic-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-isotropic-score">[eq:repayment-isotropic-score]</a>. When $k_f>0$, assume <a href="#eq:repayment-selected-credit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-selected-credit">[eq:repayment-selected-credit]</a> under $\pi$ with its accumulated error $\alpha_f\le\eta$. Finally suppose $$P_t\ge B_r+2b_{\mathrm q}h-\Delta .
 \label{eq:repayment-saturation-input}$$ Then the prepared statistic $P,n(P),W,k$ under $\mu$ satisfies $$0\le k\le d h+C_*\eta,\qquad
 k\ge k_f+(4b_{\mathrm q}-2\gamma)h-2\Delta-C_*\eta,
 \quad
 d=\begin{cases}1&\text{elongated},\\2&\text{isotropic}.
                 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:finite-packet-repayment}$$ Its pointwise probability bound is <a href="#eq:repayment-outgoing-credit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-outgoing-credit">[eq:repayment-outgoing-credit]</a>. In the elongated case the continued aperture normal is within $C\epsilon^h$ of $n(P)$. The returned score satisfies <a href="#eq:repayment-earlier-scores" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-earlier-scores">[eq:repayment-earlier-scores]</a> in that case and <a href="#eq:repayment-isotropic-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-isotropic-score">[eq:repayment-isotropic-score]</a> in the isotropic case. All these bounds are finite at fixed $\epsilon$.*

</div>

<a id="pm-h-62"></a>
#### A coherent estimate on the full set of output sites

We next prove the mass estimate before introducing any positive law on candidate packets. The output amplitudes may be chosen separately at every site.

<a id="stmt-lem-packet-coherence"></a>
<div id="lem:packet-coherence" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:finite-coherence"></a>
**Lemma 49** (Packet coherence on a strip or a cell). *Use local coordinates with root time $r$, endpoint duration $2h$, and put $$\rho=\epsilon^u,\qquad s=\epsilon^{u+h},\qquad
 \sigma=\epsilon^{u+2h}=s^2/\rho,\qquad
 \lambda_{\rm loc}=s^{-2}.$$ Fixed multiplicative errors in these relations change only constants. Let $P$ be a buffered isotropic cell of width $\rho$. Let $Q$ specify $P,C_t$ and a position cell of side $s$ at $C_t$. Candidate atoms have this $P$, velocity spacing $s$, earlier position spacing $s$, and transported position within $Rs$ of that cell, where $R=\epsilon^{-\theta}$. Let $N_Q$ be their number, and suppose $$|c_T|^2\leq\epsilon^{-\xi}m.$$ Partition their velocities into $K\leq\epsilon^{-k-\xi}$ bins of width $s$, in a fixed normal direction for $d=1$ or in both directions for $d=2$. Let $Z$ add to $Q$ the output position at precision $\sigma$ in those $d$ directions. Let $m_Z$ be the sum of squared packet tests over all output sites mapping to $Z$, on the input truncated to these candidates. Then $$\sum_{Z\mid Q}m_Z\leq C\epsilon^{-\xi}N_Qm,\qquad
 m_Z\leq C\epsilon^{dh-k-2\theta-2\xi}N_Qm.
 \label{eq:finite-coherence}$$ The constant is uniform over all admissible choices of the site-dependent amplitudes. Without candidate truncation, the square root of the mass estimate has the additive tail error provided by Lemma <a href="#lem:packet-decomposition" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:packet-decomposition">37</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-packet-coherence"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-packet-coherence</summary>

*Proof.* The first inequality is the synthesis Bessel estimate followed by the analysis Bessel estimate of Lemma <a href="#lem:packet-bessel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:packet-bessel">36</a>. It holds for any subset of output sites and any subset of atoms.

Suppose first that $d=2$. If $A_{OT}$ is the normalized atom/test matrix, then $$|A_{OT}|\leq C\rho^{-1}\|g_T\|_1
          \leq C s/\rho=C\epsilon^h.$$ A full velocity bin contains a bounded number of velocity lattice centers. At each such center the proximity condition leaves at most $CR^2$ position centers. Each $Z$ contains a bounded number of output sites. Cauchy–Schwarz first within one bin and then across its $K$ bins gives $$m_Z\leq CKR^2\epsilon^{2h}\sum_T|c_T|^2
       \leq C\epsilon^{2h-k-2\theta-2\xi}N_Qm.$$

<a id="eq:one-bin-strip"></a>
For $d=1$, write $n$ for the bin normal and $\tau$ for its orthogonal unit tangent. Fix one velocity bin $W$. There are at most $CR^2$ candidate atoms per tangent velocity interval of length $s$. We claim $$\sum_{O\mapsto Z}\left|
       \sum_{T\in W}c_T A_{OT}\right|^2
 \leq CR^2\epsilon^h\sum_{T\in W}|c_T|^2.
 \label{eq:one-bin-strip}$$

Here are details that also justify using all output sites with independently chosen amplitudes. Write $v=V_P+\rho z$ on a common bounded patch and surround each output center $X_O$ by a square $B_O$ of side comparable to $\sigma$. For $x\in B_O$, remove the scalar value at $v=V_P$ from $$\psi_O((v-V_O)/\rho)
 \exp\{i\lambda_{\rm loc}
       [\Phi(C_t,X_O,v)-\Phi(C_t,x,v)]\}.$$ All derivatives in $z$ are uniformly bounded, because $\lambda_{\rm loc}\rho\sigma=1$. A common bump and a Fourier series on a fixed enlarged patch therefore give coefficients $b_\nu(O,x)$ satisfying $$|b_\nu(O,x)|\leq C_M(1+|\nu|)^{-M}$$ uniformly in both $O$ and $x$. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the squared transform at $X_O$ by a fixed rapidly summable combination of squared transforms at $x$, each with a common bump and a linear modulation $e^{i\nu\cdot(v-V_P)/\rho}$. These factors are independent of $x$. No derivatives with respect to the site index have been used.

<a id="eq:strip-normalization"></a>
Integrate this bound on $B_O$, divide by its area, and sum. The squares have bounded overlap, and their union lies in a strip of normal width $C\sigma$ and tangent length $Cs$. The normalization outside the resulting continuous position integral is $$\rho^{-2}\sigma^{-2}=s^{-4}.
 \label{eq:strip-normalization}$$ It is enough to prove the estimate for each of the common bump/modulation factors, uniformly in its Fourier index; the factor has bounded modulus and is independent of $x$.

For fixed normal position, integrate against a smooth majorant of the tangent interval of length $Cs$. For velocities in the same $W$, their normal difference is $O(s)$. Symmetry and uniform definiteness of $\partial_p\zeta$ give $$\partial_\tau\{\Phi(C_t,x,v)-\Phi(C_t,x,v')\}
       =\tau^{\mathsf T}A(x,v,v')(v-v'),$$ where $A$ is an average of those definite matrices. If the tangent separation is a sufficiently large multiple of $s$, this derivative has magnitude at least $c|(v-v')\cdot\tau|$. Higher $x$-derivatives are bounded by $C_j|v-v'|$. Repeated integration by parts in the rescaled tangent variable thus bounds its kernel by $$C_Ms\left(1+\frac{|(v-v')\cdot\tau|}{s}\right)^{-M}.$$ For smaller separation the same bound, with another constant, follows directly by integration over the interval. Earlier normalized atoms have $L^1$ norm at most $Cs$. Including the normal integration and <a href="#eq:strip-normalization" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:strip-normalization">[eq:strip-normalization]</a>, the corresponding Gram entry is therefore at most $$C_Ms^{-4}\sigma s\,s^2
  \left(1+\frac{|(V_T-V_{T'})\cdot\tau|}{s}\right)^{-M}
 =
 C_M\epsilon^h
  \left(1+\frac{|(V_T-V_{T'})\cdot\tau|}{s}\right)^{-M}.$$ The possible overlap of velocity supports changes only the constant in this estimate. Sum the rapidly decreasing kernel over tangent intervals, using the multiplicity $CR^2$. The Schur bound proves <a href="#eq:one-bin-strip" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:one-bin-strip">[eq:one-bin-strip]</a>. Finally Cauchy–Schwarz over the $K$ bins proves the second inequality of <a href="#eq:finite-coherence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:finite-coherence">[eq:finite-coherence]</a> for $d=1$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-63"></a>
#### The candidate law and its entropy bound

<a id="eq:repayment-candidate-expression"></a>
We now prove Proposition <a href="#prop:finite-repayment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:finite-repayment">48</a>. For a value $J=j$ of positive $\pi_J$-probability, let $\pi_j$ denote the selected endpoint law conditional on $J=j$. Define the finite entropy expression $$\mathcal E_j=
 \mathsf H_{\pi_j}(Z)+\tfrac12\mathsf H_{\pi_j}(Z\mid D)
 +\tfrac32\mathbb E_{\pi_j}\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m_Z\right)
 +\tfrac12\mathbb E_{\pi_j}w_{\rm loc}(D).$$ All entropies here concern the displayed geometric observations, rather than the entire sample $\omega$. The latter carries extra labels only so that later augmentation preserves them. Finite composition first compares the original score with the conditional winning scores. Equation <a href="#eq:repayment-winning-candidate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-winning-candidate">[eq:repayment-winning-candidate]</a> then replaces their masses by the candidate-truncated masses. Finally, conditional log-sum on each $O\mapsto Z$ fiber bounds the two entropy–mass terms by those in $\mathcal E_j$. The unconditional fiber calculation uses all sites mapping to $Z$; conditional on $D$, its support is a subset of those sites. Thus $$P_t\le \mathsf H_\pi(J)+b_*+\mathbb E_{\pi_J}\mathcal E_J
       +\mathcal R+3\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(1/(1-q_{\rm tr})\right).
 \label{eq:repayment-candidate-expression}$$ This is a comparison of finite expressions under the same endpoint law. No growth bound has been applied to the $Q$-dependent inputs.

Lemma <a href="#lem:packet-coherence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:packet-coherence">49</a> now gives its two exact bounds for the masses $m_Z$ in <a href="#eq:repayment-candidate-mass" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-candidate-mass">[eq:repayment-candidate-mass]</a>. Only after these analytic inequalities do we introduce a positive candidate law. Adjoin an earlier atom to the full endpoint sample by <a id="eq:repayment-candidate-law"></a>$$\widetilde\pi(\omega,T)=\pi(\omega)
   \frac{\boldsymbol1_{\{T\in\mathcal T_{J(\omega),Q(\omega)}\}}}
        {N_{J(\omega),Q(\omega)}} .
 \label{eq:repayment-candidate-law}$$ The denominator is positive on every sampled value, as proved above. This law has exactly the endpoint marginal $\pi$, including $P_f,W_f$ and every stochastic incoming tag. Conditional on $(J,Q)$, the atom is uniform on the candidate set and independent of every other endpoint label. Its marginal on atoms is generally biased; it is different from $\mu$, which is uniform within each retained class.

For the next calculation fix $J=j$, and write $\mathsf H_j,\mathbb E_j$ for entropy and expectation under $\widetilde\pi(\,\cdot\mid J=j)$. Put $$B_{1,j}=\mathbb E_j\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(N_{J,Q}\right),\qquad
 S_{t,j}=\mathsf H_j(C_t\mid T),\qquad
 \mathcal M_j=\mathbb E_j\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m_Z\right).$$ Since $Z$ includes $Q$, the sampling rule gives exactly $$\mathsf H_j(T\mid Z,D)=\mathsf H_j(T\mid Z)=B_{1,j}.$$ Candidate proximity gives $\mathsf H_j(Q\mid T,C_t)\le C_*\eta$. It also gives $\mathsf H_j(Z\mid T,D)\le C_*\eta$. For the latter bound, $T,C_t$ locate the position to precision $s$, while $D$ supplies its normal component at precision $\sigma$. In the elongated case the current prediction $\angle(n(D),n(P))\le C\epsilon^{4h}$ moves a residual of size at most $\epsilon^{-\theta}s$ by at most $C\epsilon^{4h-\theta}s< C\sigma$. In the isotropic case the aperture supplies both fine components. The remaining costs are the stated lists and boundary-depth errors.

<a id="eq:repayment-entropy-chain-one"></a>
<a id="eq:repayment-entropy-chain-two"></a>
<a id="eq:coherent-entropy-repayment"></a>
The chain rule gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathsf H_j(Z)&\le \mathsf H_j(T)-B_{1,j}+S_{t,j}
                 +\mathsf H_j(Z\mid Q)+C_*\eta,
 \label{eq:repayment-entropy-chain-one}\\
 \mathsf H_j(Z\mid D)+B_{1,j}
       &\le \mathsf H_j(T\mid D)+C_*\eta.
 \label{eq:repayment-entropy-chain-two}
\end{aligned}$$ Conditional log-sum applied to the aggregate coherence bound, and the logarithm of its pointwise bound, respectively give $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathsf H_j(Z\mid Q)+\mathcal M_j
     &\le B_{1,j}+\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m(j)\right)+C_*\eta,\\
 \mathcal M_j&\le B_{1,j}+\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m(j)\right)+k-dh+C_*\eta .
\end{aligned}$$ Use the first inequality with coefficient $1$ and the second with coefficient $1/2$ in <a href="#eq:repayment-entropy-chain-one" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-entropy-chain-one">[eq:repayment-entropy-chain-one]</a>–<a href="#eq:repayment-entropy-chain-two" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-entropy-chain-two">[eq:repayment-entropy-chain-two]</a>. Every occurrence of $B_{1,j}$ cancels. The result is $$\mathcal E_j\le
 \mathsf H_j(T)+\tfrac32\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m(j)\right)
 +\tfrac12\{\mathbb E_jw_{\rm loc}(D)+\mathsf H_j(T\mid D)
                    +2S_{t,j}+k-dh\}+C_*\eta .
 \label{eq:coherent-entropy-repayment}$$ Here the common $k$ bin absorbs its stated finite bin error.

<a id="eq:coherent-entropy-repayment-averaged"></a>
We assemble these conditional kernels under $\pi_J$ before using incoming information. Averaging <a href="#eq:coherent-entropy-repayment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:coherent-entropy-repayment">[eq:coherent-entropy-repayment]</a> gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{\pi_J}\mathcal E_J
 &\le \mathsf H_{\widetilde\pi}(T\mid J)
       +\tfrac32\mathbb E_\pi\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m(J)\right)\notag\\
 &\quad+\tfrac12\bigl\{
       \mathbb E_\pi w_{\rm loc}(D)
       +\mathsf H_{\widetilde\pi}(T\mid D,J)
       +2\mathsf H_{\widetilde\pi}(C_t\mid T,J)
       +k-dh\bigr\}+C_*\eta .
 \label{eq:coherent-entropy-repayment-averaged}
\end{aligned}$$ The incoming conditional probability bound will be used under this assembled law, not separately on each $J$ fiber.

<a id="pm-h-64"></a>
#### A faithful aperture and the incoming information

The candidate atoms carry exact straight lines through their earlier positions with their assigned velocities. In a localizer $J$, let $F_T$ record $C_t$ and both columns of this line at isotropic width $u-h$ at the endpoint. Its local position precision is $\epsilon^{u+h}=s$. Thus $F_T$ is a function of $(T,C_t,J)$; conditional on $J$, it need not be a function of $T$ alone.

In the elongated case coarsen the orientation of $D$ and its aperture data to widths $0,u-h$, computing the latter from the center given by $F_T$. In the isotropic case use widths $u-h,u-h$. Denote this intermediate observation by $Y$. Transport proximity makes $Y$ determined by $D$, conditional on $J$, up to a list of size at most $\epsilon^{-C_*\eta}$.

Enlarge each rectangle of $Y$ by one fixed factor so that it contains the entire corresponding isotropic $F_T$ cell. The factor works for every orientation: projections of a square have length at most its diagonal, and rounding the center adds only a fixed grid spacing. This costs at most $(\log C)/\ell$ in depth. Call the enlarged label $\bar Y$. It is a function of $Y$, so it has the same conditional list bound from $D$. Let $\kappa(g\mid F_T,J)$ be the conditional law of $\bar Y$ under $\widetilde\pi$, and adjoin $G$ by that kernel: $$\widetilde\pi(\omega,T,G)
   =\widetilde\pi(\omega,T)\kappa(G\mid F_T,J).$$ We keep the same notation for the augmented law. It preserves the entire old law of $(\omega,T)$ and the joint law of $(F_T,J,\bar Y)$ with $\bar Y$ replaced by $G$. The new $G$ is independent of $T$ conditional on $(F_T,J)$, contains $C_t$, and is faithful for every line with that $F_T,J$ value. No $T$-dependent cell is appended to its label.

<a id="eq:faithful-classical-bound-averaged"></a>
Apply Theorem <a href="#thm:classical-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:classical-growth">15</a> in each localizer with duration $2h$ and horizon $u+h$. The strict eccentricity condition, or $b_*=0$ with $u_t>h$, gives $u>h$. Its root caps have widths at most $u+h=u_r-b_*$, and the endpoint horizon $a+t\le L$, with its stated depth error, also places them inside the local packet menu. For every such root test $F$, the support upper bound gives $$\mathsf H_j(T\mid F)+\mathbb E_j w(F)\le g(j)+C_*\eta.$$ This uses only the retained support, so it holds for the biased candidate marginal. The positive root supremum is consequently at most $g(j)-\mathsf H_j(T)+C_*\eta$. Positive growth yields, on each $J=j$ fiber, <a id="eq:faithful-classical-bound"></a>$$\mathbb E_j w(G)+\mathsf H_j(T\mid G)+2S_{t,j}
       \le g(j)+2\gamma h+C_*\eta .
 \label{eq:faithful-classical-bound}$$ Averaging these inequalities under the same $\pi_J$ as before, $$\mathbb E_{\widetilde\pi}w(G)+\mathsf H_{\widetilde\pi}(T\mid G,J)
       +2\mathsf H_{\widetilde\pi}(C_t\mid T,J)
 \le \mathbb E_\pi g(J)+2\gamma h+C_*\eta .
 \label{eq:faithful-classical-bound-averaged}$$

<a id="eq:information-before-credit"></a>
All information in the remainder of this subsection is under the assembled augmented law $\widetilde\pi$. Both $D$ and $G$ contain $C_t$, and $F_T$ is a function of $(T,C_t,J)$. The common time information cancels in the exact chain rule <a id="eq:time-correct-information-splitting"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \mathsf I(T;D\mid J)-\mathsf I(T;G\mid J)
 &=\mathsf I(F_T;D\mid C_t,J)-\mathsf I(F_T;G\mid C_t,J)
       \notag\\
 &\quad+\mathsf I(T;D\mid F_T,J)-\mathsf I(T;G\mid F_T,J).
 \label{eq:time-correct-information-splitting}
\end{aligned}$$ The last term is zero by the resampling kernel. Data processing for $\bar Y$, followed by preservation of its joint law with $(F_T,J)$, bounds the first line below by $-C_*\eta$. Therefore $$\mathsf I(T;D\mid J)-\mathsf I(T;G\mid J)
       \ge \mathsf I(T;D\mid F_T,J)-C_*\eta .
 \label{eq:information-before-credit}$$

<a id="eq:credit-information"></a>
When $k_f>0$, the preserved endpoint marginal supplies an averaged information lower bound $$\mathsf I(T;D\mid F_T,J)\ge k_f-C_*\eta .
 \label{eq:credit-information}$$ Here is the finite-list verification. In absolute units, $F_T$ and $P_f$ have identical velocity depth $u_t-h$ and position depth $t+u_t-h$. The candidate position differs from the observed one by at most $\epsilon^{-\theta}\epsilon^{r+u_r}$, exactly an $\epsilon^{-\theta}$ multiple of that position unit, and the velocity difference is $O(\epsilon^{u_t})$. The localizer has the coarser width in <a href="#eq:repayment-localizer-depth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-localizer-depth">[eq:repayment-localizer-depth]</a>; its remaining tags have the charged conditional count. It follows that $$\mathsf H(F_T,J\mid P_f)\le C_*\eta,\qquad
 \mathsf H(P_f\mid F_T,J)\le C_*\eta .$$ Because $\widetilde\pi_\Omega=\pi$, <a href="#eq:repayment-selected-credit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-selected-credit">[eq:repayment-selected-credit]</a> still holds for its endpoint labels. It is not asserted after conditioning separately on $J$. The chain rule gives $$\mathsf H(W_f\mid F_T,J)
 \ge \mathsf H(W_f\mid P_f)-\mathsf H(F_T,J\mid P_f)
 \ge k_f-C_*\eta .$$

Neither coarse label alone determines $W_f$. The pairs $(D,F_T,J)$ and $(T,F_T,J)$, however, each determine a list of at most $\epsilon^{-C_*\eta}$ possibilities. First list the possible $P_f$’s supplied by $F_T,J$. For each listed value, $n_f(P_f)$ is known, with no continuity assumption on this function. Use that value’s coarse velocity center as reference. The remaining velocity has size $O(\epsilon^{u_t-h})$. The incoming alignment of the normal of $D$ with $n_f(P_f)$ is $O(\epsilon^h)$, so changing between them changes the measured component by $O(\epsilon^{u_t})$, one $W_f$ unit. Thus $D$ resolves that component to the stated list. The exact velocity of $T$ does so as well, since it differs from the output velocity by $O(\epsilon^{u_t})$. For isotropic tests use both velocity coordinates. Consequently $$\mathsf H(W_f\mid D,F_T,J)+\mathsf H(W_f\mid T,F_T,J)\le C_*\eta .$$ The elementary information inequality $$\mathsf I(T;D\mid F_T,J)\ge
 \mathsf H(W_f\mid F_T,J)-\mathsf H(W_f\mid D,F_T,J)
                         -\mathsf H(W_f\mid T,F_T,J)$$ proves <a href="#eq:credit-information" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:credit-information">[eq:credit-information]</a>. This is a conditional information averaged over $J$ under $\widetilde\pi$, which is exactly what the averaged bounds need. If $k_f=0$, use nonnegativity of conditional mutual information instead.

Combining <a href="#eq:information-before-credit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:information-before-credit">[eq:information-before-credit]</a> and <a href="#eq:credit-information" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:credit-information">[eq:credit-information]</a> with <a href="#eq:faithful-classical-bound-averaged" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:faithful-classical-bound-averaged">[eq:faithful-classical-bound-averaged]</a> gives $$\mathbb E_{\widetilde\pi}w(G)+\mathsf H_{\widetilde\pi}(T\mid D,J)
       +2\mathsf H_{\widetilde\pi}(C_t\mid T,J)
 \le \mathbb E_\pi g(J)+2\gamma h-k_f+C_*\eta .$$ The weight change on each localizer is $$w_{\rm loc}(D)-w(G)=
 \begin{cases}
 (1-\gamma)h+O(\eta),&d=1,\\
 2h+O(\eta),&d=2,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 w_{\rm loc}(D)-w(G)\le dh+C_*\eta .$$ Also $\mathsf H_{\widetilde\pi}(T\mid J)\le
\mathbb E_\pi\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(N(J)\right)$, since every candidate lies in its retained class. Insert these bounds into <a href="#eq:coherent-entropy-repayment-averaged" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:coherent-entropy-repayment-averaged">[eq:coherent-entropy-repayment-averaged]</a>, then use <a href="#eq:repayment-candidate-expression" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-candidate-expression">[eq:repayment-candidate-expression]</a>. The tail comparison costs are included in $\eta$, so after returning to the original units, $$P_t\le B_r+\gamma h+\tfrac12(k-k_f)+C_*\eta .$$ Comparison with <a href="#eq:repayment-saturation-input" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-saturation-input">[eq:repayment-saturation-input]</a> proves the lower bound in <a href="#eq:finite-packet-repayment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:finite-packet-repayment">[eq:finite-packet-repayment]</a>. Its upper bound is <a href="#eq:velocity-fiber-regularity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:velocity-fiber-regularity">[eq:velocity-fiber-regularity]</a>.

Under $\mu$ at time $r$, $P$ has depth $u_t=u_r-h$ and $W$ has depth $u_r$. Thus <a href="#eq:repayment-outgoing-credit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-outgoing-credit">[eq:repayment-outgoing-credit]</a> and the earlier aperture and score bounds supply the next cut’s incoming data. That cut may use a new atom decomposition: the coarse-label lists carry the observable $W\mid P$ bound, without identifying the two temporary candidate populations. This completes Proposition <a href="#prop:finite-repayment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:finite-repayment">48</a>.

<a id="pm-h-65"></a>
#### A finite backward chain

Suppose, for a contradiction, that $\beta_{\mathrm q}>\gamma/2$, and set $$c=4\beta_{\mathrm q}-2\gamma>0.$$ Choose an integer $q$ with $qc>2$. Proposition <a href="#prop:boundary-alternatives" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:boundary-alternatives">44</a> supplies $q$ backward steps of a common positive length $2h$, with all times positive and $u_t>h$. In the forced alternative first take $h$ sufficiently small compared with the fixed aspect gap times $\gamma$; this verifies <a href="#eq:repayment-eccentricity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-eccentricity">[eq:repayment-eccentricity]</a>. In the other alternative all the back tests are exactly isotropic.

Fix this chain and start with $k_0=0$. At cut $i$, apply the rule for a prepared cut and call its final endpoint law $\pi_i$; the returned $\mu_i$ is the next endpoint law. Let $\Delta_i,\eta_i$ be the actual selected errors for $\pi_i$, with $J$-averages under $(\pi_i)_J$. They include the exceptional-fiber score splits and the accumulated $\zeta+\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(1/p_A\right)$ with every $p_A$ measured in its current law. Choose the finitely many retention parameters and current-law branches so this finite cost sum is as small as required.

Within each fixed outer row $j$, choose the finite inner parameters $\theta,\xi$ and the finitely many $\zeta$’s, then the initial packet tail orders and coefficient cutoff, the later transport order, and finally the precision $\epsilon$. These choices make the inner errors, including both mass-comparison costs, arbitrarily small in that row. Finite composition and <a href="#eq:repayment-input-bridge" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:repayment-input-bridge">[eq:repayment-input-bridge]</a> leave the selected deficits bounded by that row’s $\Delta_j$, with the fixed finite selection factors, plus those inner errors. With the target shape and $g$ accuracies fixed before choosing the late row, these factors are bounded across the subsequence: only uniformly positive current masses of qualifying unions and retained complements divide deficits, while individual tag probabilities enter only logarithmic costs. The selected deficits are not sent to zero inside the row. Only then choose a sufficiently late outer row, with $q$ and $h$ already fixed across the subsequence, and choose finite inner precision in that row so that the total error bound below holds. No transport order uniform in unbounded outer aspect parameters is required.

Apply Proposition <a href="#prop:finite-repayment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:finite-repayment">48</a> with $b_{\mathrm q}=\beta_{\mathrm q}$. Iteration of <a href="#eq:finite-packet-repayment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:finite-packet-repayment">[eq:finite-packet-repayment]</a> gives $$k_q\geq qch-\sum_{i=1}^q(2\Delta_i+C_*\eta_i),
 \qquad
 k_q\leq2h+C_*\eta_q.$$ Choose the finite errors so that $$\sum_{i=1}^q(2\Delta_i+C_*\eta_i)+C_*\eta_q
                  <(qc-2)h.$$ The two inequalities are incompatible. Consequently $\beta_{\mathrm q}\leq\gamma/2$, completing the proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:packet-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:packet-growth">35</a>.

<a id="sec:multiplier"></a>
### Oscillatory integrals and Bochner–Riesz multipliers

We now turn packet growth into the multiplier bound. The first step is an oscillatory integral estimate with loss $\lambda^\nu$ for every $\nu>0$, uniform over fixed phase and amplitude classes. After a change of variables, this gives norm $O_{\delta,\nu}(\lambda^{-\delta+\nu})$ for a Bochner–Riesz kernel shell of radius $\lambda$. Choosing $\nu<\delta$ makes the dyadic shell sum converge. We keep the data bounds explicit because the shell amplitudes vary with the scale.

<a id="stmt-thm-oscillatory-estimate"></a>
<div id="thm:oscillatory-estimate" class="theorem">

<a id="eq:oscillatory-estimate"></a>
**Theorem 50** (Oscillatory integral estimate). *Fix bounded input and output regions $K_v,K_x\subset\mathbb R^2$. For the input patch $K_v$, fix a class of smooth real phases satisfying the phase assumptions of Section <a href="#sec:packet-structure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:packet-structure">9</a>, with common domain $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^2\times U_v$, where $U_v$ is an open neighborhood of $K_v$. All enlarged patches required by the decomposition, expressed in the original $v$ coordinates, are contained in $U_v$ and obey common bounds. The translated systems are considered on the corresponding bounded rescaled patches described in that section, with the resulting uniform bounds. Throughout the phase domain, $$\partial_v\Phi(c,x,v)=\zeta(v,x-cv).$$ For each phase and each required original input patch $V$, the matrix $\partial_p\zeta$ is symmetric and satisfies either $$a_0I\le\partial_p\zeta(v,p)\le a_1I
 \qquad(v\in V,\ p\in\mathbb R^2),$$ or the same inequality with $-\partial_p\zeta$ in place of $\partial_p\zeta$, with common constants $a_0>0$ and $a_1$ for the class. On these original patches, every mixed $v,p$ derivative of total order $j$ of this matrix is bounded by $A^{j+1}(j!)^3$ for a common $A\ge1$. Fix these constants and all the seminorm bounds of a class of smooth amplitudes $B$ supported in $[0,1]\times K_x\times K_v$. For every $\nu>0$ there is a constant $C_\nu$, depending only on these fixed data and $\nu$, such that, for every $\lambda\ge2$, every phase and amplitude in the specified classes, and every $f\in L^3(\mathbb R^2)$ supported in $K_v$, $$\label{eq:oscillatory-estimate}
 \left\|E_\lambda f\right\|_{L^3([0,1]\times K_x)}
 \le C_\nu\lambda^{-1+\nu}\|f\|_3,
 \qquad
 E_\lambda f(c,x)=\int e^{i\lambda\Phi(c,x,v)}B(c,x,v)f(v)\,dv.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-oscillatory-estimate"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-oscillatory-estimate</summary>

*Proof.* Fix $0<\gamma<1$ and a loss $\eta>0$. Apply Theorem <a href="#thm:packet-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:packet-growth">35</a> with $$\epsilon=\lambda^{-1},\qquad H_{\mathrm P}=t=L=1.$$ Thus its finite conclusion is $P_1\le K_0+\gamma/2+\eta$ for all sufficiently large $\lambda$, uniformly in the data under consideration. Here and until the endpoint sum below, logarithms in scores have base $\epsilon^{-1}$.

Suppose first that $|f|\le\mathbf 1_F$, where $F\subset K_v$ is measurable. The case $f=0$ is immediate. At the root the packet radius is $\rho_0=\lambda^{-1/2}$. Write $m_O$ for the canonical root masses. The Bessel bound of Lemma <a href="#lem:packet-bessel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:packet-bessel">36</a> gives $$M:=\sum_Om_O\le C|F|.$$ If $D$ is any admissible root aperture of widths $b\le a\le1/2$, its velocity centers lie in a rectangle with side lengths comparable to $\epsilon^b,\epsilon^a$. All the corresponding test windows lie in the $100\rho_0$ enlargement of this rectangle. Since $\rho_0\le\epsilon^a\le\epsilon^b$, that enlargement has area at most $C\epsilon^{a+b}$. Applying the same Bessel estimate to $f$ restricted to the enlarged rectangle yields <a id="eq:restricted-root-cap"></a>$$\label{eq:restricted-root-cap}
 M_D:=\sum_{O\text{ compatible with }D}m_O
 \le C\epsilon^{a+b}.$$ This estimate holds separately for each label, including labels that are assigned stochastically. Its constant includes the fixed lattice and window multiplicities.

<a id="eq:restricted-root-score"></a>
For any law of $(O,D)$ supported on compatible pairs, log-sum gives $$\mathsf H(O)+\mathbb E\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m_O\right)\le\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(M\right),
 \qquad
 \mathsf H(O\mid D)+\mathbb E\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m_O\right)\le\mathbb E\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(M_D\right).$$ Consequently every root score is at most $$\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(|F|\right)
 +\tfrac12\mathbb E\bigl[w(b,a)-a-b\bigr]
 +\frac{C}{\log\lambda}
 \le \log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(|F|\right)+\frac{C}{\log\lambda},$$ because $w(b,a)-a-b=-\gamma(a-b)\le0$. The norm option in $K_0$ has the same upper bound: indeed $$\|f\|_2^3\le |F|^{3/2}\le |K_v|^{1/2}|F|.$$ We have therefore proved $$\label{eq:restricted-root-score}
 K_0\le\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(|F|\right)+\frac{C}{\log\lambda}.$$

At $t=H_{\mathrm P}=1$ the velocity radius is one. Cover the input region by a fixed number of such velocity patches, and partition the output region into boxes with time and position side lengths comparable to $\lambda^{-1}$. We may work with one input patch at a time. For each output box let $m_O$ be a test mass controlling the supremum of $|E_\lambda f|^2$ on that box, up to a fixed factor. These tests are admissible endpoint masses. To see the asserted uniformity, if $(C,X)$ is the box anchor, absorb $$\exp\!\left(i\lambda\bigl[
 \Phi(c,x,v)-\Phi(C,X,v)
 -\Phi(c,x,v_*)+\Phi(C,X,v_*)\bigr]\right)$$ into the amplitude, where $v_*$ is fixed in the input patch. Every positive-order $v$ derivative of the phase difference is $O(\lambda^{-1})$, by the defining identity for $\partial_v\Phi$ and the uniform bounds on $\partial_p\zeta$. The displayed factor thus has uniformly bounded derivatives. Sitewise choices approaching a supremum are permitted by the packet theorem; no regularity between the choices at distinct boxes is required.

<a id="eq:restricted-oscillatory"></a>
Only the aperture widths $b=a=0$ are allowed at the endpoint. Choose their labels with a fixed orientation. For any endpoint law its score is at least $\mathsf H(O)+\tfrac32\mathbb E\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m_O\right)$. Taking the law proportional to $m_O^{3/2}$, or omitting zero masses, gives the exact log-sum value $$\mathsf H(O)+\tfrac32\mathbb E\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(m_O\right)
 =\log_{1/\epsilon}\!\left(\sum_Om_O^{3/2}\right).$$ The packet theorem and <a href="#eq:restricted-root-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:restricted-root-score">[eq:restricted-root-score]</a> imply <a id="eq:endpoint-packet-sum"></a>$$\label{eq:endpoint-packet-sum}
 \sum_Om_O^{3/2}\le C_{\gamma,\eta}
 \lambda^{\gamma/2+\eta}|F|.$$ Each output box has volume $O(\lambda^{-3})$. Summing the integrals over boxes, and then the fixed number of input patches, proves $$\label{eq:restricted-oscillatory}
 \|E_\lambda f\|_3
 \le C_{\gamma,\eta}\lambda^{-1+\gamma/6+\eta/3}|F|^{1/3}
 \qquad (|f|\le\mathbf 1_F).$$ All constants are uniform over the fixed classes. In particular, the passage from limiting packet growth to the finite bound used here is uniform: otherwise a sequence of offending scales, inputs, phases, amplitudes, and laws would contradict the sequence quantifier in Theorem <a href="#thm:packet-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:packet-growth">35</a>.

For a general input normalize $\|f\|_3=1$. The two tails satisfy $$\|f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le\lambda^{-10}\}}\|_1
 \le |K_v|\lambda^{-10},\qquad
 \|f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|>\lambda^{10}\}}\|_1\le\lambda^{-20}.$$ The trivial $L^1$ to bounded-region $L^3$ estimate controls their contributions. Split the remaining input into $N=O(\log\lambda)$ dyadic levels $f_k$, with $2^k<|f|\le2^{k+1}$ on $F_k$. Equation <a href="#eq:restricted-oscillatory" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:restricted-oscillatory">[eq:restricted-oscillatory]</a>, followed by Hölder in $k$, gives $$\left\|\sum_k E_\lambda f_k\right\|_3
 \le C_{\gamma,\eta}\lambda^{-1+\gamma/6+\eta/3}
 \sum_k2^{k+1}|F_k|^{1/3}
 \le 2C_{\gamma,\eta}\lambda^{-1+\gamma/6+\eta/3}N^{2/3}.$$ Choose $\gamma,\eta>0$ so that $\gamma/6+\eta/3<\nu/2$ and absorb $N^{2/3}$ in the remaining positive power of $\lambda$. Bounded values of $\lambda$ are covered by the trivial estimate. Homogeneity proves <a href="#eq:oscillatory-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:oscillatory-estimate">[eq:oscillatory-estimate]</a> for every input. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-67"></a>
#### The radial kernel and its dyadic pieces

Use the Fourier convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx$. For real $\delta>0$ put $$m_\delta(\xi)=(1-|\xi|^2)_+^\delta,
 \qquad K_\delta=\mathcal F^{-1}m_\delta.$$

<a id="stmt-lem-br-kernel"></a>
<div id="lem:br-kernel" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:br-kernel-symbol"></a>
**Lemma 51** (Endpoint expansion of the kernel). *The kernel is bounded on $\mathbb R^3$. For $R\ge1$ it has an expansion $$\label{eq:br-kernel-symbol}
 K_\delta(Re_3)=e^{2\pi iR}b_+(R)+e^{-2\pi iR}b_-(R),
 \qquad
 |b_\pm^{(j)}(R)|\le C_{\delta,j}R^{-2-\delta-j}
 \quad(j\ge0).$$ In particular $K_\delta\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ whenever $\delta>1$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-br-kernel"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-br-kernel</summary>

*Proof.* Boundedness follows from $m_\delta\in L^1$. Integrating first over the disks perpendicular to $e_3$ gives the exact formula $$K_\delta(Re_3)=\frac{\pi}{\delta+1}
 \int_{-1}^1e^{2\pi iRz}(1-z^2)^{1+\delta}\,dz.$$ Choose a smooth partition into neighborhoods of the two endpoints and a compact subinterval of $(-1,1)$. At $z=1$ write $t=1-z$ and extract $e^{2\pi iR}$. Its remaining integral has amplitude $t^{1+\delta}a(t)$, with $a$ smooth and supported in a fixed small interval $[0,t_0)$. Its $j$th $R$ derivative has amplitude a constant times $t^{1+\delta+j}a(t)$. The part $t\le R^{-1}$ is bounded by $CR^{-2-\delta-j}$. On a smooth dyadic shell $t\asymp h\ge R^{-1}$, $N$ integrations by parts give the bound $$C_{\delta,j,N}R^{-N}h^{2+\delta+j-N}.$$ For an integer $N>2+\delta+j$ the sum over these shells is at most $C_{\delta,j}R^{-2-\delta-j}$. The same argument at $z=-1$ gives the other symbol. The middle integral and every derivative decrease faster than any inverse power of $R$; after multiplication by $e^{-2\pi iR}$ it can be included in $b_+$. This proves <a href="#eq:br-kernel-symbol" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-kernel-symbol">[eq:br-kernel-symbol]</a>. Radial integration of its absolute-value bound gives $\int_1^\infty R^2R^{-2-\delta}\,dR<\infty$ when $\delta>1$. ◻

</details>

<a id="eq:br-rescaled-shell"></a>
<a id="eq:br-unit-shell"></a>
Take a smooth radial partition of unity into a bounded region and shells $|x|\asymp\lambda$, $\lambda=2^j\ge2$. The bounded piece of $K_\delta$ is integrable. By Lemma <a href="#lem:br-kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:br-kernel">51</a>, each shell is the sum of two kernels $$\lambda^{-2-\delta}e^{\pm2\pi i|x|}
 a_{\lambda,\pm}(x/\lambda),$$ where the amplitudes are supported in a fixed annulus and all their derivatives are bounded uniformly in $\lambda$. In the convolution operator set $x=\lambda z$, $y=\lambda y'$. The factor from volume is $\lambda^3$, so the rescaled operator is $$\label{eq:br-rescaled-shell}
 \lambda^{1-\delta}A_{\lambda,\pm}f(z),\qquad
 A_{\lambda,\pm}f(z)=
 \int e^{\pm2\pi i\lambda|z-y|}a_{\lambda,\pm}(z-y)f(y)\,dy.$$ The input and output dilation factors cancel in its $L^3$ operator norm. We next prove $$\label{eq:br-unit-shell}
 \|A_{\lambda,\pm}\|_{L^3(\mathbb R^3)\to L^3(\mathbb R^3)}
 \le C_\nu\lambda^{-1+\nu} \qquad(\nu>0).$$

<a id="pm-h-68"></a>
#### The distance phase

<a id="eq:distance-phase"></a>
<a id="eq:distance-hessian"></a>
Partition input and output space into unit cubes with smooth cutoffs of bounded overlap. The annular support in <a href="#eq:br-rescaled-shell" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-rescaled-shell">[eq:br-rescaled-shell]</a> allows only a bounded number of input neighbors for each output cube, and conversely. For one such pair, translate both cubes together to a fixed bounded region. A finite smooth angular partition and fixed rotations reduce the phase to regions where $$0<d_0\le z_3-y_3\le d_1<\infty,$$ with fixed constants. The dyadic shell operators have the Carleson–Sjölin distance-phase form treated by Guo et al. (2025) <a id="pm-cite-43"></a>[[GuoOhWangWuZhang2025](#ref-GuoOhWangWuZhang2025)]; we use their subsequent pseudoconformal change of variables. Fix the slice variable $y_3$, and set $$s=(z_3-y_3)^{-1},\qquad Z=s(z_1,z_2),\qquad v=(y_1,y_2).$$ Then, for $g(q)=\sqrt{1+|q|^2}$, $$|z-y|=s^{-1}g(Z-sv),\qquad
 \left|\det\frac{\partial(Z,s)}{\partial z}\right|=s^4.$$ Choose a fixed positive interval $[s_*,s_*+D]$ containing the range of $s$, and put $s=s_*+Dc$, $Z=Dx$. Both the coordinate change and its inverse have bounded derivatives and Jacobians on the relevant regions, uniformly in the slice. Direct differentiation gives <a id="eq:distance-zeta"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \Phi(c,x,v)&=\pm2\pi(s_*+Dc)^{-1}
 g\bigl(Dx-(s_*+Dc)v\bigr),\label{eq:distance-phase}\\
 \partial_v\Phi(c,x,v)&=\zeta(v,x-cv),\qquad
 \zeta(v,p)=\mp2\pi\nabla g(Dp-s_*v),\label{eq:distance-zeta}\\
 \partial_p\zeta(v,p)&=\mp2\pi D\nabla^2g(Dp-s_*v).
 \label{eq:distance-hessian}
\end{aligned}$$ The eigenvalues of $\nabla^2g(q)$ are $(1+|q|^2)^{-1/2}$ and $(1+|q|^2)^{-3/2}$. They are bounded away from zero on the fixed argument region of the integral, but the smaller eigenvalue tends to zero at infinity. The packet decomposition uses global definiteness when solving <a href="#eq:packet-gradient-matching" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:packet-gradient-matching">[eq:packet-gradient-matching]</a> for every Fourier mode. We therefore modify $g$ outside the argument region to obtain the global hypothesis of Theorem <a href="#thm:oscillatory-estimate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:oscillatory-estimate">50</a>.

Choose $R_0>1$ so that all arguments in <a href="#eq:distance-phase" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:distance-phase">[eq:distance-phase]</a> have norm less than $R_0$. Let $\chi$ be a nondecreasing smooth function, zero on $(-\infty,R_0]$, one on $[R_0+1,\infty)$, with $$|\chi^{(j)}(r)|\le C^{j+1}(j!)^2.$$ Such a function is obtained by integrating and normalizing the bump $\exp[-1/t-1/(1-t)]$ on $0<t<1$, extended by zero. For completeness, Cauchy’s estimate on a complex disk of radius a small fixed multiple of $t$ gives a derivative bound $j!(C/t)^j e^{-c/t}$ near $t=0$. Maximizing $t^{-j}e^{-c/t}$ gives $C^{j+1}(j!)^2$; the estimate at $t=1$ is identical, and away from the endpoints analyticity gives the bound directly.

Let $h(r)=0$ for $r\le R_0$ and, for $r>R_0$, let $$h(r)=\int_{R_0}^r(r-u)\chi(u)\,du.$$ Replace $g(q)$ by $\widetilde g(q)=g(q)+h(|q|)$. The added Hessian has radial and tangential eigenvalues $\chi(r)$ and $h'(r)/r$, both nonnegative and at most one. For $r\ge2(R_0+1)$ they are at least $1/2$. On the remaining compact region the original Hessian is uniformly positive. Thus $$c_0 I\le\nabla^2\widetilde g\le C_0 I\quad\hbox{on }\mathbb R^2.$$ The modification vanishes on the argument region. Its Hessian has derivative bounds $A_0^{j+1}(j!)^3$: on the transition annulus this follows by the chain rule from the displayed Gevrey bounds and the analyticity of $q\mapsto|q|$ away from zero. More explicitly, grouping the terms in a derivative of order $j$ by the $k$ derivatives landing on the outer scalar function bounds their sum by $$C^j j!\sum_{k=1}^j C^k k!\binom{j-1}{k-1}
 \le C_1^{j+1}(j!)^2.$$ The analytic factors $q/|q|$ in the radial Hessian obey the same bound after the product rule. Outside the transition annulus, $h(r)$ is a quadratic polynomial in $r$ plus a linear term and a constant, whose radial Hessian has the same bounds. Near the origin there is no modification. The original $g$ has uniform analytic Hessian bounds. Formula <a href="#eq:distance-hessian" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:distance-hessian">[eq:distance-hessian]</a>, with $\widetilde g$ in place of $g$, therefore satisfies all the required global hypotheses, including the mixed $v,p$ derivative bounds.

For each fixed $y_3$, Theorem <a href="#thm:oscillatory-estimate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:oscillatory-estimate">50</a>, applied after this change of variables, bounds the sliced integral by $$C_\nu\lambda^{-1+\nu}\|f(\cdot,y_3)\|_{L^3(\mathbb R^2)}$$ in $L^3$ of the output variables. The transformed amplitudes have uniform seminorms, and the output Jacobians are uniformly bounded. Minkowski’s inequality and then Hölder’s inequality on the bounded interval of $y_3$ prove the corresponding three-dimensional bound for the selected cube pair. Finally, if $a_k$ is the input $L^3$ norm in cube $k$, the output norm in cube $j$ is at most $C_\nu\lambda^{-1+\nu}\sum_{k\sim j}a_k$. The inequalities $$\sum_j\left(\sum_{k\sim j}a_k\right)^3
 \le C\sum_k a_k^3$$ follow from the bounded neighbor counts in both directions. Summing the finite angular partition proves <a href="#eq:br-unit-shell" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-unit-shell">[eq:br-unit-shell]</a>.

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-br-kernel-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-br-kernel</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:bochner-riesz" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:bochner-riesz">1</a>.* Combining <a href="#eq:br-rescaled-shell" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-rescaled-shell">[eq:br-rescaled-shell]</a> and <a href="#eq:br-unit-shell" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-unit-shell">[eq:br-unit-shell]</a> shows that the shell of radius $\lambda$ has $L^3$ operator norm at most $C_{\delta,\nu}\lambda^{-\delta+\nu}$. For each fixed $\delta>0$, choose $\nu=\delta/2$. The sum over $\lambda=2^j$ converges, and the bounded kernel piece is controlled by Young’s inequality. The resulting operator is bounded on $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$.

For a Schwartz input, convolution with $K_\delta$ equals $\mathcal F^{-1}(m_\delta\widehat f)$: writing $K_\delta$ as the inverse transform, Fubini is justified by $\|m_\delta\|_1\|f\|_1<\infty$. The spatial partition also converges to this convolution pointwise by dominated convergence, since $K_\delta$ is bounded and $f\in L^1$. Its operator-norm sum therefore represents the same multiplier. Density of Schwartz functions in $L^3$ supplies the asserted bounded extension. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-69"></a>
#### The full strict range

We record the consequence for other exponents. Its proof uses the positive-order theorem at arbitrarily small, fixed orders; no uniformity as the order tends to zero is needed.

<a id="stmt-lem-br-complex-order"></a>
<div id="lem:br-complex-order" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:br-complex-bound"></a>
**Lemma 52** (Complex orders from a real order). *For $\Re z>0$ and $R>0$, let $T_{z,R}$ have multiplier $(1-|\xi|^2/R^2)_+^z$, and write $T_z=T_{z,1}$. Suppose $r>0$ and $T_r$ is bounded on $L^q$ for $1\le q<\infty$. If $a>r$ and $N$ is an integer with $N>r+1$, then $$\label{eq:br-complex-bound}
 \|T_{a+i\tau}\|_{q\to q}
 \le \|T_r\|_{q\to q}
 \prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(1+\frac{\tau^2}{(a-r+k)^2}\right)^{1/2}.$$ The same conclusion holds for $q=\infty$ if $K_r\in L^1$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-br-complex-order"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-br-complex-order</summary>

<a id="eq:br-beta-mixture"></a>
*Proof.* Conjugation by the $L^q$ isometry $f(x)\mapsto R^{3/q}f(Rx)$ shows that $\|T_{r,R}\|_{q\to q}=\|T_r\|_{q\to q}$. For $\Re z>r$, the beta integral gives $$\label{eq:br-beta-mixture}
 T_z=\frac{\Gamma(z+1)}{\Gamma(r+1)\Gamma(z-r)}
 \int_0^1(1-u)^{z-r-1}u^rT_{r,\sqrt u}\,du.$$ Indeed, at a frequency with $s=|\xi|^2<1$ the integral of the multiplier on the right is $$\int_s^1(1-u)^{z-r-1}(u-s)^r\,du
 =(1-s)^z B(r+1,z-r);$$ both sides vanish if $s\ge1$. For finite $q$, the integral in <a href="#eq:br-beta-mixture" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-beta-mixture">[eq:br-beta-mixture]</a> converges absolutely in $L^q$ on every input: dilation is strongly continuous for positive radii and the scalar majorant $(1-u)^{a-r-1}u^r$ is integrable. The multiplier identity first holds on Schwartz inputs and then extends by density. For $q=\infty$, integrate instead the dilated kernels $u^{3/2}K_r(\sqrt u\,\cdot)$ in $L^1$; their norms are constant, and their resulting Fourier transform gives the same identity.

<a id="eq:br-gamma-bound"></a>
Taking norms in <a href="#eq:br-beta-mixture" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-beta-mixture">[eq:br-beta-mixture]</a> yields $$\label{eq:br-gamma-bound}
 \|T_{a+i\tau}\|_{q\to q}
 \le \|T_r\|_{q\to q}
 \frac{\Gamma(a-r)}{\Gamma(a+1)}
 \left|\frac{\Gamma(a+1+i\tau)}{\Gamma(a-r+i\tau)}\right|.$$ One can bound this quotient without asymptotics. The gamma recurrence and another beta identity give $$\frac{\Gamma(z+1)}{\Gamma(z-r)}
 =\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}(z-r+k)
 \frac{B(z+1,N-r-1)}{\Gamma(N-r-1)}.$$ Since $|B(a+1+i\tau,N-r-1)|\le B(a+1,N-r-1)$, substitution in <a href="#eq:br-gamma-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-gamma-bound">[eq:br-gamma-bound]</a> and cancellation prove <a href="#eq:br-complex-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-complex-bound">[eq:br-complex-bound]</a>. In particular the boundary norms grow at most polynomially in $|\tau|$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-cor-full-bochner-riesz"></a>
<div id="cor:full-bochner-riesz" class="corollary">

<a id="eq:full-br-range"></a>
**Corollary 53** (Strict Bochner–Riesz range in three dimensions). *Let $1\le p\le\infty$ and $$\label{eq:full-br-range}
 \delta>\max\left\{0,\,3\left|\frac1p-\frac12\right|-\frac12\right\}.$$ Then the multiplier $(1-|\xi|^2)_+^\delta$ is bounded on $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$. The same bounds hold uniformly for every positive radius after dilation. This assertion concerns the strict inequality <a href="#eq:full-br-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:full-br-range">[eq:full-br-range]</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cor-full-bochner-riesz"><summary>Proof of stmt-cor-full-bochner-riesz</summary>

*Proof.* First let $3<p<\infty$. Put $$\theta=1-\frac3p\in(0,1),\qquad c=\delta-\theta>0,
 \qquad z(w)=c+w.$$ On the boundary $\Re w=0$, Lemma <a href="#lem:br-complex-order" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:br-complex-order">52</a> with $r=c/2$ and Theorem <a href="#thm:bochner-riesz" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:bochner-riesz">1</a> give a polynomially growing $L^3$ bound for $T_{c+i\tau}$. On $\Re w=1$, apply the same lemma with $r=1+c/2>1$. Lemma <a href="#lem:br-kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:br-kernel">51</a> supplies an integrable real-order kernel and hence a polynomially growing $L^\infty$ bound for $T_{1+c+i\tau}$.

This is an admissible analytic family. For Schwartz functions $f,g$ its scalar pairing is the integral over the unit ball of $$(1-|\xi|^2)^{c+w}\widehat f(\xi)\overline{\widehat g(\xi)};$$ on compact subsets of $\Re w>-c$ all its derivatives are dominated by integrable powers of $|\log(1-|\xi|^2)|$. On the closed strip $0\le\Re w\le1$, its $L^2$ norm is at most one. Approximation by Schwartz functions therefore extends weak analyticity in the open strip and scalar continuity on the closed strip to all $L^2$ pairs, including bounded simple functions of finite support. Indeed, the scalar pairings converge uniformly on the strip by the $L^2$ bound. These are admissible tests for analytic interpolation. To make the polynomial boundary growth harmless, fix $\kappa>0$ and use the analytic family $$e^{\kappa(w-\theta)^2}T_{c+w}.$$ Its boundary norms are bounded because the scalar factor has modulus $e^{\kappa((\Re w-\theta)^2-(\Im w)^2)}$. The analytic interpolation theorem (Stein 1956) <a id="pm-cite-44"></a>[[Stein1956](#ref-Stein1956)], applied between $L^3$ and $L^\infty$, gives an $L^p$ bound at $w=\theta$, since $$\frac1p=\frac{1-\theta}{3},
 \qquad c+\theta=\delta.$$ The Gaussian factor equals one there, so this is the required bound for $T_\delta$.

For $2\le p\le3$, interpolate the fixed real operator $T_\delta$ between its $L^2$ bound from Plancherel and its $L^3$ bound from Theorem <a href="#thm:bochner-riesz" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:bochner-riesz">1</a>; here <a href="#eq:full-br-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:full-br-range">[eq:full-br-range]</a> is exactly $\delta>0$. Its real multiplier is self-adjoint on Schwartz functions, so duality proves the corresponding bounds for $1<p<2$. The symmetry of <a href="#eq:full-br-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:full-br-range">[eq:full-br-range]</a> under $p\leftrightarrow p'$ gives precisely the asserted range. Finally, for $p=1$ or $p=\infty$ the condition is $\delta>1$, and Lemma <a href="#lem:br-kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:br-kernel">51</a> and Young’s inequality give the result directly. Dilation gives the assertion about radii. ◻

</details>

For completeness, the norm-convergence assertion in the introduction follows from the same uniform radius bounds. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $\widehat f\in C_c^\infty$, then $T_{\delta,R}f\to f$ in the Schwartz topology: on the fixed Fourier support, every derivative of $(1-|\xi|^2/R^2)^\delta$ converges to the corresponding derivative of $1$. Inverse Fourier transforms of $C_c^\infty$ functions are dense in $L^p$. The uniform bounds and a density argument therefore give $T_{\delta,R}f\to f$ in $L^p$ for all $f$ in that space whenever <a href="#eq:full-br-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:full-br-range">[eq:full-br-range]</a> holds.
